div.head: CHINESE CHILDREN.
div.p: CHINESE CHILDREN.

A Chinese baby is rolled up in clothes till ho looks like a ball and is cradled in a bam- boo cradle that has rockers of such a size and that makes such a noise that one wonders 'where the somnolent effect of the rocking is obtained. He has a red cord round his wrist to keep him from being naughty when he grows up, and a string of coins round his neck to keep away evil spirits.

NAMING THE CHILD. He has a real name that belongs to him as a citizen and a member of his family, and a nickname, so ugly, that when the evil spir- its hear him called by it, they come to the conclusion that he is worth very little and so leave him alone. We say "he" advised- ly in what we are writing, for though some of our remarks are applicable to girls it is only the boy that counts in the Chinese fam- ily. A girl has been known often enough to receive the uncomplimentary nickname of "Not Wanted" as a mark of her parents' disappointment at the sex of their infant. When the boy goes to school for the first time he has his head shaved and his face washed and is given a fairly spick and span appearance. He carriee in a bag a pen which has a brush in lieu of a nib, a cake of ink, a stone slab on which to mix the ink with water and a set of books. He is given a new name that belongs to him while he is at school and which is generally fairly compli- mentary. If the boy is intended for a clerk he learns arithmetic from a clerk or a shop- keeper, not from the regular schoolmaster who despises such utilitarian arts. The chief instruction in the class-room is the learning by heart of thousands of lines from the Chinese classics. Whether lit, understands them aright or not does not matter as long as he can say them without error. Each boy says his lesson aloud and as everybody is learning a different line at the same time there is a fine noise when the boys are dill. gent.

div.head: HOW CHINESE CHILDREN A.RE TAUGHT TO witrrE. –
div.p: HOW CHINESE CHILDREN A.RE TAUGHT TO witrrE. -

When the scholar is perfect in his repeti- tion. he is taught to write, which he does by painting over o. number of red characters with black ink. He proceeds to tracing and then to unaided writing. Perhaps the chief subject that demands his attention is essay - writing in which he must become proficient if he wishes for service under the Govern. meat. k

There is a curious similarity between some of the games played in China and in this country, as for instance, in a variety of "blind man's buff" called "Catching ,fishes in the dark," and in a modification of "I spy" known as "Waiting for the seekers." Shuttlecock is played with the feet instead of the hands and kites are exhibited of many wonderful forms including the figures of birds, butterflies, centipedes and different varieties of fish.

'The ffnest trait in the • character of the Chinese child is his reverence for his par- This is no lip service but a very real regard for the commands and wishes of thore whom he- calle.: by the name of father and mother: One,young man who lost his mo- ther at an early age 'could not be persuaded that her death was not due in any other CallSe than sone ixet of filial disobedience of his own, and to free himself from this ima- ginary guilt he undertook a painful pilgrim- age of sixty In Hes in the course of which he bowed to the earth over 15,000 times., The reverence paid to the parents is extended to those who occupy their places for the pur- pose of education and tie teacher is treated in a way that would-dtiight the heart, of any Western pedarrhgne.

div.head: WIT AND WISDOM ON WINDOW TICKETS.
div.p: WIT AND WISDOM ON WINDOW TICKETS.

The average shop-keeper does not exhibit much originality in the window cards and price tickets he displays in his ;windows. He generally labels his window goods with cards on which are inscribed "Latest Styles," and other mere platitudes. These hackneyed ex- pressions carry no weight, and certainly dc not attract customers.

There are however enterprising shop-keep- ers who dare to be original. They realise the fact that clever, catchy window an- nouncements are a valuable aid in attracting customers; Many of • the cards exhibited by these up-to-date tradesmen are clever as well as humorous, and attract the attention of the passer-by.

div.head: ARRESTING ANNOUNCEMENTS.
div.p: ARRESTING ANNOUNCEMENTS.

The following arresting announcement ap- peared in the window of a shop at a busy junction in North London: "Mr. Joseph Chamberlain said, 'What I have said, I have said.' I say, 'What I say I DO, I DO do.'" It would be surprising if this tradesman did not meet with the success that his clever window-card deserved. An Indianapolis store-keeper made a novel use of a window-card, which he displayed in the most prominent position in his window. On the card was this notice. "This card is for the people who owe me money, and don't come inside to pay. Watch this space; their names will appear." , It is said that the' an- nouncement attracted much attention and comment, but the merchant did not find it necessary to insert any names in the space provided on the card. In the window of a dealer in fancy goods, some grotesque novelties were ticketed as follows: Say! Don't you think your friends would smile if they saw me on your shelf ?" "I've seen you before. You're so fond of looking at me, that I wonder you don't buy me altogether. I cost is." "There's no reason why I shouldn't decorate your home, instead of wasting my time here, is there ?" "I'm a little bargain that the shopman put in this corner because there are not many of my sort. If you want one like me, you'll have to hurry." "LookinNor me? I'm yours for ever—for is." Sometimes a shop-keeper, in trying to be too original, overshoots the mark. One am- bitious tradesman affixed to his window the following bill: "Others fail in succeeding otLethslt.h pirnogni to please you. We succeed in failing to please you. Try our goods." Ile was ra- ther proud of his effort, until the absurdity ill promptly come aay iinteddowanut to him, when . C)ccaslicmiallY a ladies' outfitter will give himself away by having "Black Ladies' Gloves ed ' " . • • and "Short Ladies' Vests" ticket- or sale.

A. STARTLING STATEMENT. A chemist with unconscious humour exhib- ited a small bill in his window, on which was Printed the following startling statement: "Do not poison your system with other so- called cough mixtures. Try ours." The chemist forgot to add that, if you had quite decided to poison youraelf, he also sold the following other poisons: arsenic, strychnine, or carbolic acid, all of which would be equal- ly effective. A Glasgow boot-dealer, in attempting to Impress upon his patrons the desirability of a prompt acceptance of hie offer, conveyed to them quite a different impression in this window bill "A chance for bargain-hunters. Boots and Shoes at half cost. Snap them up, they won't last long." Boot and shoe dealers as a class however generally display smartness and originality in the window an- nouncements and tickets attached to their goods. Here are two good specimens: "Eng- land is still a free country, and you can pay more for your shoes if you want to; but your doing so is nothing more nor less than extravagance." "Ladies' feet are in the fa- if they're in S— Shoes." The following are a sucoessful and an un- successful attempt to expresS the same idea: "If you don't see what you want in the window, come inside and get what you DO want." "If you see what yoff don't want in the window, step insidc." Unconscious wit was exhibited in the fol- lowinm window cards: "Annual Sale now on
_ j

Don't go elsewhere to be cheated, come in here." Mr. Brown, Furrier, begs to an- nounce- that he will make up gowns, capes, etc., for ladies out of their own skin." "Wanted—a boy to be partly outside and partly behind the counter. In the window of a photographer's shop was exhibited the following gruesome notice "Babies taken and finished in ten minutes." An ironmonger who was. having a clear- ance sale of joiner's tools, including ham- mers, mallets, etc., placed in his window the tallying forcerful 'announcement: "When you have finished looking at my goods in the window, just step inside. We have 60104' 'striking' goods at 'knock-down' prices." TRAMCAR ADVERTISEMENTS.

One of the advantages of a window an- nouncement in a public vehicle is that, like a stirring story, it always carries the reader with it. He can't get away from it till his journey ends; that. is if it is printed in bold clear type, large enough to be seen easily from any part of the car. Many of the cards and transparencies in tramcars are very entertaining. Just ima- sine the awful dulness of a journey in a tram In which there were no advertisements. It is certain that if a vote was taken of the hab- itual riders in tramcars, a vast majority would be found in favour of retaining the advertisements. It is ranch more interesting to read the surprising proverbs which are used to recommend particular soaps, or the verses which set forth the virtues of certain tinned foods, than to gaze gloomily at your opposite neighbour, or to stare out of the window. .

An American whisky firm ion a series of very successful cards in the street cars of New York. The first and last lines of the matter were printed in red, and the rest ID black. This made the cards very conspicu- ous. Here are two specimens: "One test. Empty a glass of most whis- ky except McHenry, and hold it upside down over a heated stove. The glass will smell of prune juice or some other adulterant. Test McHenry in the same way, and the glass 'will smell like a rye grain field. Than purity. McHenry." "A man starts in the whisky business to- day. Offers ten year old whisky to-mcrrrow. Where does he get it? I, give up. Out my way, we can't live ten years overnight. I am able to sell old whisky because I have an old business. McHenry, founded 1812. Costi you no more." On one of the horse trams ftnning between two districts in London, the' somewhat un- usual instance is displayed of an -advertiser openly warring againsethe proprietors of the medium used for his announcement. The advertisement extends the whole length and height of the top railing of the car, and reads: "You don't want to ride, if you wear Easy Miles. J. Al and Son, Bootmakers."

div.head: CLEVER SCHEME.
div.p: A CLEVER SCHEME.

• Thieves entered the store of a New York clothing firm, and took away a great many of the newest things for Spring; but the proprietors by a clever scheme turned this seeming misfortune to good account. They inserted, in the window, a copy of a news- paper with the paragraph containing an ac- count of the burglary marked with blue pen- cil. On each side of the newspaper they placed a large placard. on which was printed in large type the, following: "We hate to be robbed, but we cannot help but admire the good taste of the thieves. People are going to have our stylish suite, even if they have to steal them." 'Another example of how a mishap was made the opportunity for obtaining ,a splen- did advertisement was shown by an enter- prising tradesman. A run-away horse and' trap crashed into the window of his ,little shop, and he was compelled to put up the shutters. div.head: MARKET GATE.
div.p: MARKET GATE.
Lively Discussion Over the Fate of the Market Hall.
"ONLY A HARBOUR FOR RATS."
Building to be Demolished to Make
-Room for the Circus.

There was a lively discussion at 'Warrington Council on Tuesday night in regard to the alterations at Market Gate, where, to camplete the proposed space to be known as a circus, the prbjeet is to remove the old Market Hall. It was stated that the Improvements Committee had received a report from the Borough Sur- veyor on the laying out of the land at Market Gate, which would be available for re-sale after the widening of Sankey-street, which would in- volve the removal of the Market Hall. Alderman BENNETT, the committee chairman. , who was understood to move the adoption of ,1 the proposal, created a surprise by declaring that he was not convinced of the necessity of so ' drastic a step as the removal of the Market Hall, which had cost £12,000. The present idea of the Council seemed to be to disturb every- thing. (" No.")
Alderman Tnimos: Speak for yourself. Alderman BENNETT : I didn't say you; I said somebody.

Alderman TINNiox : You looked* very hard at me. (Laughter.) "Never Happy." • Alderman BENNETT : It seems we are never happy unless we are pulling something down. (Councillor PEMBERTON: Indeed!) There is no economy in pulling down, unless .you are 'going to erect something better. The market cost £12,000, and now the income is .P.,300 a year. There is no need to demolish this building. _ . _

Alderman TINN lON : Question! Alderman BENNETT : I cannot see any utility in the proposal. We do not gain an inch of land and from an asthetic and financial point of view this is absolutely a, fatal step. Alderman' TINNION : Let us know where we are. Here is a gentleman who sets out to move the confirmation of minutes, and he is doing nothing but speak against them. It seenis to be alto- gether out of order. Dr. JOSEPH then proposed the minutes. Alderman Bennett's Objections. Alderman BENNETT moved the minutes back, and wished to express his strong personal opinion,, which he had, no oppoitunity to do at the committee meeting. He objected to the Market and Corporation-street being removed. The object was said to be one to get straight streets, but that scheme would end in the streets not facing each other. Their scheme was to get still more ugly streets than they had. They , were spending half a million on their scheme, and in spending such a fabulous 'sum, he thought they should try to get the best pos- sible results, which the proposed scheme did not give,

If they were to scrap the Market Hall, let them follow the example of Continental towns, and make a square in the centre worthy of the town, but the idea to remove the market and put up shops behind was a scheme not 'worthy of consideration. He felt very keenly about the proposal. Councillor BR OADTIVRST seconded, on the ground that the Council wanted more informa- tion.

Riding a Hobby Horse. Alderman JAMES EvAss was surprised at tlo.e course taken by Alderman Bennett, as the plfflh only showed what had received approval, again and .again from Alderman Bennett. It was merely to complete the circus, which Alderman Bennett had again and again urged, and it Vas to carry out that circus on economic and reason- able lines. (Hear, hear.) To do that, the Mar- ket Hall would have to be interfered with. The income from the Market was such as would not permit them to ride a hobby horse on the ques- tion. Alderman Bennett had talked about £3OO

div.p: from the market a year. The truth was the Council had been running a portion of the mar- ket at Or general expense of the ratepayers. Councillor PEMBERTON : Shame!
A Harbour for. Rats.

Alderman JAMES EVANS : We cannot get ten- ants for that part of the Market Hall. It is simply a harbour for rats, and it costs as much as we can get to keep it in repair. Councillor PEMBERTON supported the minutes, about which the committee were unanimous except the chairman, Alderman Bennett. In his opinion, the scheme had been too long de- layed, and as a business man he was not going to stand longer delay. If they did not provide space for shops, where were they going to put the tenants put out? They migtit even now have to face claims for compensation. Alderman TINNION said they had had to fight the chairman, Alderman Bennett, all the time. If they convinced him he was wrong at one meeting, the Alderman started again at the next with his fads.

"Only in His Fads." It was only in his fads that Alderman Bennett was unreasonable. (Laughter.) When he got fads into his head—well, it was no use arguing with him. (Laughter.) It was mainly through Alderman Bennett that they were to have "this splendid circus at Market Gate. There was certain land the Council had to purchase, and there were certain' businesses they would have to purchase, unless they made proper provision for the businesses to be trans- ferred somewhere else. They got Al to ..t4 a week gross rental from that part a the Market Hall. Nobody was proud of that market, to get into which they had to go up and down dirty steps into a dirty, sawdusty place, occupied by rats. Any man who wanted to preserve that place—he did not think he would say anything about such a man. Councillor PEMBERTON : Put him in the Museum. (Laughter.) Exceedingly Badly Spent.

Alderman—T—lNNlo;:- If the Market has cost A:12,000, the money has been exceedingly badly spent. We can use the land to much better purpose. Alderman BOLTON said the Market had its day and earned it money, au way for improvements d now must go to make Councillor OSBORNE supported the amendment to have the matter referred back, beCause the Council ought to have further particulars in regard to the scheme. Alderman BURTON thought the suggested scheme was the best for the town, but he thought it was premature to pass it then, fIS there was no hurry about the matter. Alderman Bennett's amendment was defeated, and the minutes were approved.

div.head: GARDEN AND THE REST.
div.p: A GARDEN AND THE REST.

Howard-place, according to a plan displayed at the Council on Tuesday, is to be converted into a garden, and in the garden is to be a • public convenience, about which there has been SO much controversy in the past. Councillor Wilson, as chairman of the Sanitary Works Committee, moved the proposal at the Council meeting on Tuesday. Councill9r HAWTHORN, in seconding, said once the scheme was completed there would be noth- ing to which the residents could object. Alderman BENNETT objected to the proposal. He did not think the place would be as orna- mental as the plan showed. He only wished the councillors had the gift of imagination, and they would not approve of the Scheme. (Laugh- ter.) He had hoped to see the space devoted to a statue of John Howard. Five, centuries after the people would wonder at the Council putting such a thing there. Alderman TINNION : We shall all be dead by then. (Laughter.) Dr. JOSEPH, the Deputy Mayor, thought if Howard-place was to be the ideal place it was painted, he would go and live there. (Laugh- ter.) •

, . Councillor PEMBERTON asked why they should not have two statues'-John Howard at one end and Alderman Bennett at the other. (Laugh- ter.) Ultimately, after further discussion, in the course of which it was said the inhabitants had withdrawn their previous objections, the com- mittee's scheme was approved by a Majority.

By that means the water would be purified and made soft. so as to be quite suitable for use in boilers. The Ship Canal Company .had given permission for the Water Committee to use the water on the payment of a low, meter fate. The water undertak,' big for some years had been extremely'consist- ent with regard to the percentage on the income. For ten years it had averaged 3.:3 per cent., and the estimated cost of the scheme would not exceed the annual increment of interest. There was not the slightest possibility that the pro- , posed expenditure would become prejudicial to the water undertaking from a financial stand- point. It would enable them to offer any future ' manufacturers a full supply of water suitablo for boiler purposes.

STERILISED MILK.
What the Loss of the Lime Salts May Mean.

Sir Almroth Wright, discussing with a repre- sentative of the " Times " Mr. Bobert Mond's statement that sterilised milk is dangerous to the children fed upon it, said Mr. Mond based his opinion on investigations conducted at his experimental farhe m at Coombe Bank, Sevenoaks, nidat t Infants' Hospital, Vincent-square. These investigations also indicated, according to Mr. Niond; that tuberculosis was not con- veyed by milk to human beings.

Sir "chin-oil). said that the question was one of the greatest importance, and required most careful investigation. It was a question the stale must take tip and. solve ; it could not be salved without scientific research. He had demonstrated that when •milk was boiled the lime 'arid magnesium salts were precipitated, and .settled at the bottom of the vessel. The upper portion of such milk would not Curdle with rennet, as fresh milk did._ If, however, a • drop of acid was added to the sterilised milk; the-lime .salts ere dgain diss.;fv,;d and 'spread through the milk. It then curdled at once with rennet. In the 'normal -process ci digestion, fresh milk, thanks to itSlime salts, was curdled in the stomach ; but in the case of sterilised milk_ the tendency Would be for the lime salts thrown down by hailing to be left deposited at ,the bat-. tom of the jug.. The child would therefore not - gel, them. It would be 'drinking a fluid other than normal milk, and differing from normal! milk in respect of curd formation. Milk a. complex fluid, beautifully balanced as regards its various constituents,' and containing the I essentials of nutrition,- One could not suppose that the loss or decrease of a particular consti- of course, uarnpoaslteerinatiaonspdeecliinbc- thent—cepting, ,safpfeeccii(the value of the milk. ce!ta's -1..'e1-‘37.oliTllddefafiolrtoa High niedical authorities had. stated that chil- dren led on sterilised milk were apt to contract scurvY. He suggested that the precipitation and consequent loss of iiiptchlebsiei ecsaasletss.waTs hreesbpoodny siblefor the condition re- quired those, salts, and could not remain healthy without- them. lie .thought • that too much was being made at present of so-called exclusion of infection and hygiene. Infection could not be completely excluded. The well-fed, well-nourished child possessed poWers of resist- ing disease which were its best protection.

div.head: EMPLOYMENT ON ,AVET DAYS.
div.p: EMPLOYMENT ON ,AVET DAYS.

if them is one thing more than another on which some farmers deserve a. little rebuke, says Farm and Home," it is upon the loss they incur through caress management. and the same remark applies with equal force to a good many smallholders. Manure, for /instance, is of tent left lying about the yard expoSed to the rain, ,and no notice is taken of the fact that its goodness is being washed into the drains. Again, many machines and tools, instead of being cleaned and greased and possibly painted alter use, are often left in the yards, and even in the fields,, unprotected and uncleaned ; while straw, and 'chaff: and heaps of wood 'are' allowed: to lie about in rank disorder. The repairing, painting, and general cleaning of the farm machinys and-premises on a well-conducted farm provide work for the labourers on wet days, when outdoor work is impossible. The lambi who cannot find anything for his men to do on \vet days is not a model farmer by any means, although, of course, there may be case's here and there where other causes render this course more or less unreasonable. As a general rule, however, a good deal of waste can be avoided and better feeling engendered between the firiiiir and his Men by the latter being given employillent on \vet as well as fine days.

The returns for thesweek ended December 27th show that there were 19 outbreaks of anthrax, as against 14, 22, and 30 in the three preceding years; the total since the opening of the year (52 weeks) is 594, as against 743 in 1912:905 in 1911, and 1,465 reported in 1910.. Of foot-ad- mouth disease no fresh outbreak is reported ; the total for the 52 weeks is 2, as against 83, 19, . and 2. Of glanders there were 7 outbreaks in the week, as against 1, 3 and 6; th 4 total since the beginning of the year is 162, as against 172, .and 346. Of parasitic mange there were 39 outbreaks ; in 19-12 there were 45; the total for the 52 weeks is 2,373, as against 2,8/3 in 1912. • There were 12 sheep scab outbreaks; the numbers in the three preceding years were 7, 20, and 35; the total since January is 236, as against 301; 434, and 514. Swine teve,r out- breaks numbered. 53, as against 32, 39, and 34; the total since the beginning of the year is 2,573, as against 2,920,2,466, and 1,5611

A boy had to be ' gi i directly he left school, and he was prob- ab , tY twenty-three or twenty-four years of age (he did not work fifty-three hours a week only) before he couldupddonall 'the work That was re- tkodaleaN fit' . gaundmethdatpc re- quired of him hlouaghri,elL, rl,vsutochadajsusttoandiarlic.lei land trim a hedge, to ofthreshing, Itself-bhi to ding reaping machine, otor ttioelit);llNo,tttti het. hdrench a bullock, time, to to assist attend generally to horses and with. the sheep at lathing fim 11 break in a colt, and the thousand and one other helpothe things incidental to life on a farm which a fitter, ou en- gineer or carpenter could not do. Why sh a man who was required to do such work as that. be called a " labourer "? It was ridiculous. Of course, the designatiOn had been handed down by tradition, and people who had never reflected upon the character of the work of the agriOultural " labourer " had never done him justice. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
WARRINGTON SHOW.
Another Loss Made Good by Sir Gilbert Greenall.
DATE OF THIS YEAR'S SHOW.

The annual meeting of they Warrington and District Agricultural Society was held in the Masonic • Hall, Bold-street, on Monday. In the .absence of the President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr: It C. Parr presided, and said that Lady Greenall had come to apologise for the absence of Sir Gilbert.

div.head: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.
div.p: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

..... Mr. A. lieoomz, the honorary. treasurer, read his statement of accounts, which showed : Sub- scriptions, .e 254 10s. 6d.• gate receipts, .2.122 135.; grand-stand receipts, £3l 25.; catalogues, .t.lO 13s. 5d.; catering rights, ..t10; and other receipts totalled £571 17s. 2d. The expenses were: For prizes, ..t463; show yard, ..tB6 lls. 11d.; and, after other expenses had been paid, there was a deficit of £136 ;6s. 9d. Sir, Gilbert Oreenall had •sent a special donation of ..Cl5O, and this, together with a balance of .143 is. 9d.• from 1912, and .11 10s. subscriptions paid in advance, less deficit balance, left the present finances of the society at 158 ss. in hand. .
On the proposition of Mr. J. M.. WEST the report was adopted..

THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.. Mr. J. BAINBRIDGE, secretary, in his report, said the twenty-fourth annual, show was held on Thursday, 21st August, in Walton Park, on the usual show ground. Fortunately for the society the country was free from foot.anddno.,iii dis- ease, which caused the withdrawal of the cattle and pig classes from the :912 show, and these classes were re-introduced. For thl first time for many years the classes for butter and cheese were omitted from the schedule, owing to the small entries which have been Made in these classes at the, last few shows. Thera were 58 classes in the schedule and 254 entries, as against 35 classes and 216 entries in 1912. The amOunt received for entries shows a marked decrease, owing to the small number ef entries in the riding and driving classes. The balance sheet as a whole is much better than last year, but subscriptions are a good deal less all J. .new mem- bers are badly wanted. The gate money is just over .640 7.10 re than 1912, and the grand-stand receipts are more accordingly. The increase in the attendance is doubtles due to the fact of the show being held on the usual site, and not in Walton Lea .Park; the Walton Hall gardens, Sic., were thrown open to the public, and this always attracts a large number of people. The other receipts on the balance sheet are about as usual, with on addi- tional .610 for catering rights. With rcgard to payments, the amount ,of prizes is nearly 4.110 less than in 1912, showyard expenses are slightly more, but the cost of printing and advertising is much reduced. The remaining items of expen- diture, are comparatively as usual. The whole of the catering was again in the hands of Messrs. Agar and Son, of Manchester, and gave general satisfaction.

div.head: Some Fine Exhibits.
div.p: Some Fine Exhibits.

Once again the thanks of the society are due to Sir Gilbert Greenall for the use of the show ground, the cost of erecting the rings, grand- stand, stalls for the exhibits, and other show- yard expenses, as well as his usual special dona- tion to meet the deficit on the year's working and special prizes in some of the sections. The at- traction of Lady Greenall's Flower Show was this year missing, and the number of inquiries from visitors as to whether it had been permanently given up, testifies to its popularity. Mr: H. B. Armitage honoured the society by accepting office as vice-president for the year, and he very kindly gave a special prize in the cattle sec- tion, in which section special prizes were also given by Mr. Alan T. Sykes, M,P., Mr. Joseph Palmer, and Mr. G. Norris Midwood. The thanks of the seciety are due to these gentlemen, as also to Mr. F. Stapleton Bretherton, Mr. John Coxon, Mr. J. Whittaker Kenworthy, Mr. James Gould, Mr. Dan Massey, and the Cheshire Hunt, who gave special prizes in the horse section. The three London Breed Societies offered their medals as usual. There was a wonderful exhi- bition of Shire mares and foals, and also of dairy cattle, and it will soon be as difficult to win at Walton in these classes as at any one- day show in the country. I should like to thank the stewards for the Willing and efficient manner in which they carried out their duties on the show day. The CHAIRMAN said the report was a very satis- factory one. It was adopted, on the proposition of Mr. BROOME, seconded by Mr. WEIR.

•„ THE OFFICE BEARERS. Sir Gilbert Greensll was re-elected President, on the proposition of Mr. JAMES WHITLOW, seconded by Mr. JOHN LONGSHAW. •Mr. WHITLOW said they had one of the nicest little shows in England. Lord Gerard was elected vice-president, on the proposition of Mr. J. W. BAINBRIDGE. The result of the election of eight members , on the Council was as follows :—North-East Messrs. A. J. Willett, 84; J. Mainwaring, 64; H. F. Greenough, 57; C. Hudson, 16. North-West : Messrs. E. L. Bent, Newton-le-Willows, '76; W. Longton, Newton-le-Willows, 54; Thomas Smith, Bold, 48; ill., T. Hulme, Bold, 42. South-East: Messrs. James Gould, Grappenhall, 73; Edward Marsh, Lymm, 70; John Bradford, Grappen- hall, 54. H. E. Gibbon, LYmm, 30. South-West': Messrs. 'John Whitlow, Appleton, 71; W. Fowles Hatton, 59; J. T. Baxter, Dutton, 53; J. T. Fryer, Keckwick, 45. The first two in each district were elected.

div.head: DATE OF THE NEXT SHOW.
div.p: DATE OF THE NEXT SHOW.

On the proposition of Mr. J. W. BAINBRIDGE, it was decided to recommend that the show be held on August 6th this year, with a view to inducing those showing at and visiting the Royal Lancashire Show the same week to visit Walton. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the business.

div.head: SHEER RAISING IN NOVA SCOTIA.
div.p: SHEER RAISING IN NOVA SCOTIA.

At Middletbn, Nova Scotia, a company has been organised with a capital of about 20,000 dollars, and are now beginning sheep raising on a scientific basis. There is every prospect of success, for in the last dozen years the prices for mutton and lamb have increased by 100 per cent. gAotodvrleasnendt fortlioi this and for wool'and pelts by 50 to 75 per cent., and therods an ever-increasing demand. An expert from :the Dominion Department of Agriculture was called in and as a result about 500 acres of a r e 2 e ehave n been bought. grounds, and, more are expected before the end of the year.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

The folloxying 'shrubs will be found suitable for the present planting of window boxes : Euonymuses, cupressus, box, golden privet, aueubas, silver hollies, and 'ivies, green and variegated. Use small plants,

The common bleediug heart, dielytra speeta- bilis, makes a good pot plant for early _flower- ing under glass. Those who grow this plant in the open know its gracefulness when in'ilower; and this is increased grown under glass._ It makes also tt, good association with other sub- jects in the greenhouse. Plant climbing plants, such as clematis, wis- tarias, polygonum, ivies, Virginian creepers, buddleias, ceanothus, and magnolias. Put them in firmly on well-trenched and manueed ground, and tie up securely after planting. Put a mulch of good manure round each plant, without coming into contact with the stems. When digging always use a bright, clean spade. Push it into the ground down to, the haft, almost verticatly. Turn the soil com- pletely over, and leave it as rough as p,,ssime. Digging should only be done when the weather is dry and the soil is free from, frost. • Scrape moss and lichen from the branches of fruit trees with a piOce of iron, and spray the trees with,at. alkali Wash to destroy insects.
, Throw up in ridges all vacant land when the weather conditions arc favourable, for the frost to penetrate and pulverise.

div.head: Map of Europe Changed and Social Reform in England Advances. –
div.p: Map of Europe Changed and Social Reform in England Advances. -
BY A WELL-KNOWN PUBLICIST.

It is impossible for one to look back upon the trail of 1913 without a sense of wonder at all that has been crowded into thi. little mile in the long journey through time. War and disaster spread a lurid light over much of the picture which the memories of the year recall,, the "muttering thunder" of labour unrest accompanies the traveller , nearly all the way, and one can remember a political. crisis, or what we were led to ,be-. lieve was a political Crisis, nearly . every day. It has, indeed, been a year eif crowded events. There has been little lagging in the drama. The map of the world has changed con- siderably, --l0 year opened With hopes of peace, in the Balkana, but revolt in Turkey and the lust for complete victory in Bulgaria brought them crashing to the ground. The conflict spread once more, and there came, after days of conflicting rumour, the fall of Adrianople at the elase oi" an historic siege, and a little later the' capture of stubbornly- fended Scutari by little Montenegro. One can only mention the amazing defiance of the combined Powers of the world by King Nicholas, and the signing of the Treaty of London which was Accomplished at St. James's Palace on May 30th. The significance of both events was blotted out by yet another conflagration. A war which began with the sympathy of many nations as a war of libera- tion ended in a tragic and sordid orgy of bloodshed among the Allies themselves over the spans of victory. The Powers warned in rain, and what might have been a glorious and united triumph ended in Turkey regain- ing Adrianople, and a great deal more than she could ever have taken pos'session of in face of a united foe, in the humiliation or Bulgaria, and in the patching-lip of a settle- ment the chief merit of which was that it ended the slaughter and avoided any inter- national complications,

Lands to supeevise all questions dealing with the land in town and country ; the appoint- ment of Commissioners with extensive powers in the fixing of rents, the securing of fixity of tenure, the granting of compensa- tion for disturbance, the vetoing of unrea- sonable evictions, and the acquiring of dere- lict and uncultivated land; a minimum wage and reasonable hours for the rural labourer; the State provision of cottages; reform of the Game La's; and' a great afforestation !scheme. Such is the rural policy, and the. Government's proposals for the towns are on quite as drastic lines, including as they do , redress of the town tenant's grievances, re- ' form of the leasehold system, the scheduling of the slum areas, and the compulsory ac- quisition of land at a fair price where con- siderations of health or town development demand it. Mention may be made here of the sensa- tion caused late in the year by the purchase of the Duke of Bedford's great Covent Gar- den estate by Mr. Mallaby-Deeley, a Conser- vative M.P. It was the biggest land deal on record, the amount of money involved being several millions.

div.head: HOTJND THE GLOBE.
div.p: HOTJND THE GLOBE.

Balkan struggle provides the chapters of the story of the ymeoAasrltthadobruraogmanda,ttileiteh e eyes of the world have been turned in many other directions from time to time. In France there was little of sensa- tional moment, despite the tremendous in- terest aroused, by the struggle over the Three Years' Service Bill, until close on the end of the year, when the Barthou Government was overthrown by a hostile vote on the proposal that the new stock of the fifty-two million loan should be immune from %ration. The Ministerial crisis was not easily solved, and the new Government under M. Dournergue came into being amid prophecies that it in turn would very soon collapse. In Germany, too, the event of the year was a militarist or, rather. an anti-militarist crisis. After four weeks' uproar in the little town of Zabern, in Aleace, over the conduct of a young lieutenant named Forstubr the question came before the Reichstag. The Chancellor's dealing with the matter led to ex- citing scenes, and in the end a crushing vote of censure upon him was carried by 293 votes to 54. The Kaiser speedily intervened, and a sternly- worded message disapproving the military excesses and the removal of the offending garrison from the town smoothed matters over. For the rest, there •44 been a gradual restoration of peace in troubled China, civil war in unruly ifelico, and a suc- cession of grave labour revolts in South Africa, involving first the whole of the Rand miners and later the. entire Indian commu- nity in Natal, peace, fortunately, has reigned supreme among the great Powers, and the year closed with the bonds of friendship between ourselves and the other nations of the world as strong and close as they have ever been

div.head: POLITICAL DRAMA.
div.p: THE POLITICAL DRAMA.

- - ---- , ---- The political drama a' "11le has been one of particular interest and importance. The great developments have taken place outside rather than inside parliament, a was a busy and fatigulng session lthough it at West- the provi- the former the latter by 347 to 244 uer minster. The other featuresof of the 1 session were the defeat 11 Women's Su once again of the ffrage Rill, the passing of the Scottish Temperance Bill by consent on lines of compromise, the reversal of the Osborne Judgment, the amendinet!t of the Insurance Act, and the trenchant debate on the report of the Marconi Committee. The proceedings of the Marconi Committee itself, during the sittings of which scarcely a day passed without somc. incident, were fol- since anv lowed with remarkable interest, and it is many years . ns , report of a Committee of the House of Comm? The scene in the crowded and tensely-excited House while the two arraigned Minis- ters made their statement s, and then walked from the Chamber to await the vertlict of their fellow-Members, `.,v,s-i3 full of the ele- ments of drama. iii the end it was de- cided by 346 votes to 268 that the House should ,t,cept the exPress'•ons of regret made by the two Ministers that theY had purchased shares in the America" Marconi Company, ecqui 't them of acting 0 ierwise than in good bate the cha faith, and repro bete rges of corrup• tion brought t agarnsthem, which had proved to be wholly false.

session THE DOMINANT ISSITEs. Parliament adjourned _ Political inactivity in the middle of August, but the spell of was short. Ulster reTna 'lied a topic of heated debate wherever politicians gathered, and a few weeks after the Parliameu - tar ended Lord Loreburn caused a sensation by his letter to the Times, appealing for a con- .ference of all parties. to try and devise ways and means of settling the Irish question. Events moved slowly, but -the utterances of the Prime Minister and Mr. Ronar Law both indicated a desire for settlement if. it could be devised without the sacrifice of vital prin- ciples. Then came the "no compromise " orations of Sir Edward Carson and the famous "full speed ahead 9, speech of Mr. Redmond, and, for a time, growing hopes of a peaceful solution were overcast. It became plain that the idea of a formal conference was not practicable, but hope was revived by the Prime Minister's expression of his will- ingness to take part in a free sand frank exchange of views, and the year closes amid the discussion ot a number of interesting sug- gestions as to the best basis for a settlement, and with the door still open to a peaceful issue. The other outstanding feature of the poli- tical year has, of course, been the opening of the Government's Land campaign. The an- nouncement of the Government's intentions was awaited with extraordinary interest, and the full policy outlined by Mr. LlZyd George in his series of speeches in the country, and endorsed by the Prime Minister at a great gathering in London attended by nearly the whole of the Cabinet, has taken the place of Home Rule as the topic of the hour. It was only the other day that the proposals were , set out, and there is no need to catalogue I them here in detail. The broad lines of the 1 DOUCT are the settins no of a new Ministrr of

div.head: NAVY AND ARMY.
div.p: NAVY AND ARMY.

The year has been one of great activity and development in naval., Military, and aerial affairs. It closes with the certainty of yet further increase of expenditure on the Navy in the year which lies ahead, and the call for a reduction in the burden of armaments grows steadily louder and mdre insistent. Fortu- nately no serious disaster has marred the work of the great Service this year. The Army story is less happy, containing as it does the record of the cutting up of the British Camel Corps in Somaliland by the followers of the "Mad" Mullah. At home, there is a welcome improvement in recruit- ing for the Tersitoxial :Army., and the.sympa- thetic reply of the Prime Minister to an influential deputation which waited upon him to urge the need for further encouragement for the Force suggests that the Secretary of State for War may have important announce- ments to make when he introduces his next Estimates.

Both in the Navy and the Army aviation has been developed with great zeal and cour- age throughout the year, and the airmen of the two Services have many of the best flying feats of recent times to their credit. The sen- sation of the year in avicition has, of course, been the "upside-down" and "looping the loop" feats of M. Pegoud and Mr. Hucks, and it is believed by the experts that their achievements may lead in the future to the prevention of many disasters in cases where a machine side-slips or overturns in the air. In cross-country or rather cross- sea. flying Mr. Hawker's magnificent attempt to win the £lO,OOO prize offered for a. flight round Britain and M. Brindejonc des Moulinais' great flight across Europe were the events a year of fine accomplishments.

LABOUR UNREST. Unrest has once again been the dominating note in the world of labour. Although no great upheaval comparable with the national coal strike of 1912 occurred to paralyse the trade of the country, strikes on a smaller scale affected almost every industry. The most important of them all was the revolt of the Dublin transport workers, which,.begin- ning in a small way, led to scenes and deve- lopments which excited the country from end to end. The rugged and dominating person- ality of James Larkin was over all, and it is long since the incidents of a strike confined to one city aroused such intense interest and feeling. The riots in the streets of Dublin, the allegations of brutality against the police, the dramatic arrest and imprisonment of the fiery strike leader and his -still more dra- matic release, the carrying of the fiery cross to England, and the repudiation of its Syn- dicalist creed by the responsible leaders of labour here, were all big moments in a drama which must be recognised as one of the most amazing and disturbing in the history of in,- dustrial warfare in Britain_

SOCIAL EVENTS. /n the social sphere one brilliant event fol- lowed another. .The King and Queen took a leading part in many of ,the great society functions, and " the season" was one of un- tiring activity. The wedding of Prince Arthur of Connaught and the Duchess of Fife was, of course, the event of the year at home, and the brilliant scenes which marked the happy day will not soon be forgotten by those who witnessed them. The King and Queen went to Berlin to attend another Royal wedding which aroused the greatest in- terest in this country—that of Princess 'Vic- toria Luise, the Kaiser's only daughter, and Prince Ernst of Cumberland; and yet another event which made the year a notable one in Royal circles was the wedding of ex-King Manuel of Portugal and Princess Augusta Victoria of Hohenzollern. The scenes which marked the visit of the President of France to London in the spring were proof of the steady strengthening of the bonds of friendship between ourselves and our neigh- bours across the Channel. SPORTING SENSATIONS.

Sensations nave been many in tne sphere of sport. The crushing defeat of Bombardier Wells in the great boxing match with Car- pentier, the French champion, caused acute disappointment to the admirers of the art of the Ring in this country. The Derby, which was won by Aboyeur, a rank outsider, pro- ..emost sensational race of recent years, and will be memorable for the stop- ping of the King's horse by a suffragette, who received fatal injuries. Titania!' Tiiptc,r, delighted the whole sporting world by once more challenging for the America Cup. Oxford again won the Boat Race.

div.head: MANY DISASTERS.
div.p: MANY DISASTERS.

The darker side of the story is told in the record of an appalling list, of tragedies in the air, on land and sea, and in the bowels of the earth. Supreme among the tragic dramas is that of the British Antarctic Expe- dition. Few tales of adventure and tragedy have stirred the imagination of the world more than that which was unfolded when the Terra Nova came into touch with civilisation again in the beginning of the year. The terrible fate of Captain Scott and his gallant comrades on their return journey from the Pole fired the imagination of everyone, and plunged the whole British nation into sorrow. The story of endurance and heroism is one which will live in the history of exploration through ages to come, and the sublime sacri- fice of Captain Oates, and the immortal mes- sage of Captain Scott, written .with dying fingers in the blizzard-bound tent far sway in the frozen solitudes, take their place among the' most precious relics of a year, of wonderful memories. The burning of the Volturno in mid-ocean was the outstanding drama among many thrilling stories of the sea; and the mine disaster at Senghenydd, with its terrible death-roll of over 400, will be remembered as the crowning catastrophe of a week of disasters almost unique in modern history- On the railways, also, one tragedy followed another in startling manner. No fewer than seven serious disasters occurred during the year, the worst of all of them being the collision at Aisgill, which re- sulted in the loss of sixteen lives and the Imaiming of many more passengers.

CRIMES AND LAW. Or memorable crimes, fortunately, mere were few. The assassination of King George of Greece, the attempt on the life of .King Alfonso, and the murder of ex-Preeident Madero of Mexico were big sensations. In the criminal courts of this country the great "pearl mystery" provided the most remark- able story of the year.; and the murder of Miss Bradfield, whose body was found in the canal at Liverpool, provided the closing sen- sation of 1913. In the civil courts the 6,F6 of outstanding interest were few and far be-

div.head: SOME FEARS AND DOUBTS.
div.p: SOME FEARS AND DOUBTS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held last week. Mr. A. J. Jolley, the?vice-chairman, presiding. The chief item for discussmn was tliat a•ising out of the Office, Sites and Building Committee's report to the effect that the buildings be pro- ceeded with on the site alrea4y hpproved by • the Local Government Board.

The site chosen is adjoining the present Board Room and Offices, and of the i.ther two sites which were considered one as adjacent to the Fever Hospital anu the other near the Railway Siding. The present building will be used for detention cases. Those who objected at the meeting to the chosen site mainly favoured the one near the Fever Hospital, but it was pointed out that if such a-site had been adopted it would have been almost impossible to utilise the present building for temporary cases. Mr. Mather opened the discussion. Ire said he did not want to oppose the minutes; he could :only express his sorrow and regret that they could not move the site to a place which would be much better.
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: You mean you want the buildings erected elsewhere%

Mr. Mather: Yes. Mr. Mitchell: You said move the site. (Laughter.) Miss Broadbent said the matter was a very important one. The buildings would be large, and they were not satisfied at all. She wished the question could be reconsidered. Once the buildings were erected they could not move them.

Garnett: Ur. Bent was going to mention the same thing if he had been here. In my opinion we are making two bites at a cherry. I would pull this place down and put the new buildings here. Mr. Mitchell: It would be cheaper if we could utilise this building. The Chairman: That was one of the strong arguments in favour of the present site. Mr. Dale: Yes. that these buildings were to be utilised in conjunction with the new building. The Chairman: Any attempt to change the site spoils it all. It is the inferior scheme, but it is the second best, and if we cannot have the best we must have this. Mr. Mather said.he thought they could get the sanction of the Local Government Board to move to another site. It would not delay the building very much to try. Miss Broadbent: Yes, I think so. The Chairman: I don't want disgraceful con- ditions, whieh have existed too long, to obtain any longer whilst Guardians argue which is the best site. I think we ought to accept the deci- sion of the Local Government Board, which, in any case, is an improvement. Mr. Mather: We cannot move it when once we have the buildings erected. Let us be like a man who says to his sweetheart, "Let bygones be bygones," and forget what has gone before. The Chairman: The Local Government Board left the question as to where the buildings should be with the Guardians. Mr. Mather: We were in favour of having it, and the Local Government Board raised an objection as to the railway. The Chairman: Mr. Lowrie said that if the Guardians pressed for this site the Local Gov- ernment Board would waive their objection. Mr. Brooks: Instead of 4:14,000 you would want ..t20,000. Mr. Mather: I think it would be less instead of more. After further discussion, Miss Broadbent said she would move that the site be reconsidered. The Chairman: You will have to move this minute be not approved. If anyone wishes to throw the whole thing back in the melting pot they can do so by having the minutes moved back. The minutes were approved.

A BREEZE. During the discussion Mr. Brooks had said the men were at work on the foundations the previous day; whereupon Mr. Mather looked out of the window and said: " I cannot see them." Mr. Brooks: I say I saw them yesterday digging a trench, and now Mr. Mather tries to make out that I am telling a lie. Mr. Mather: I can only see a few pegs and a spade. Mr. Brooks: I object to such observations. Mr. Mather: That is all I can see. The Local Government Board wrote sanction. ing the erection of the new buildings.

div.head: PUTTING THE MAN ON HIS METTLE.
div.p: PUTTING THE MAN ON HIS METTLE.

It was decided that Mr. J. R. Jones be ap- pointed a relieving officer for one year at a salary of £100; and if he proved satisfactory the Guar- dians to consider a future appointment. Mr. Mather said it was a good precautionary measure to take, and it put the officer on his mettle.

In answer to a question, the Clerk said he thought Mr. Jones would be willing to accept the appointment on those terms. Mr. McKinley thought they should thank the Clerk for his action in the matter. (Hear. hear.)

div.head: NEW ASSISTANT MASTER.
div.p: NEW ASSISTANT MASTER.
On the proposition of Mr. Brookes it was decided that Mr. T. P. Eccleston be appointed Assistant Master of the Workhouse, at a salary of £45 per annum, together with rations, resi- dence and washing.

div.head: COST OF RELIEF.
div.p: COST OF RELIEF.
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell raised a discussion on a report showing the expenditure upon in- maintenance and out-relief for the year ending March 31st, 1913.

The report showed that the average amount per year for 1908-12 for in-maintenance was .49,778, and for out-relief ..-0,549, whilst the figures for 1913 were £10,423 and ~t 5,965. For 1908 to 1912 the average cost per head for in- maintenance and out-relief was 2s. 81d., whilst the cost in 1913 was 2s. 101 d. Mr. Mitchell asked what was the reason for
the increase of 21d.? Was it the increased cost of food? The Chairman: Mainly. _
Mr. Garnett: It is the Christmas extras for

• outdoor relief. The Clerk: It is a Local Government Board return. I could not give'you the cause of the ,difference at present. I think you can put it down that you have given more to out-relief. Mr. Brooks The price of food has gone up. Mr. McKinley: Has Mr. Mitchell any remedy for this?: Mr. Mitchell: I have only asked for informa- tion. I have no remedy. We ought to know if we can what is the cause of the increase. Mr. Mather said the increase was due to in- creased cost of food, clothing, and officers' salaries.

Mr. Mitchell: They are not included. The Chairman: It is for maintenance only. Mr. Mitchell : Our out-relief is going up, whilst other Unions are having a decrease. Mr McKinley We look after them better. The Chairman said the expenditure varied in different towns, according to trade and circum- stances. Warrington was below the average for the county. He thought they were as careful as they could be without any real loss to the deserving poor. They were obliged to Mr. Mitchell for his remarks.

div.head: COMPLETE EXAMINER STORY,
div.p: COMPLETE EXAMINER STORY,

you could have asaed me. But to sceal the cheque out of the envelope I left in your charge—" Here Tiny uttered a sharp cry, threw her arms over her head, and turned away. "Go where you please," cried the lady, "and don't venture into my presence again till you come to confess." Tiny wheeled slowly round and fixed her eyes on the angry face of her benefactress. She tried to speak, but only gasped and de- sisted. _

Then she turned away again, and began running towards the entrance to the gardens where they were lost in a little wood. " Let her go there and reflect on her great fault," thought Cassandra. "It will do her good to lose her lunch. Oh, how little I thought when I was heaping my bounties on her that this was to be the result of it !" The lady then returned to her house, ate her lunch without appetite, blamed the ten- derness of her own heart and having become so fond of the girl, and spent the afternoon in thinking over the best measures to be taken for the reclaiming of the erring one. "The child has evidently been badly brought up," she reflect. " Oh, these schools! No individual training; no prudent punishments, no special treatment for warped and difficult characters. But it will be all the greater triumph for me if I can convert her. She will be feeling hungry by , this time and will be coming to look for her tea. I must make up my mind as to how I shall receive her."

But Tiny was not coming to look for her tea. She was wandering in the thickets of the wood like a hunted thing that knows not where to hide from its pursuers. It was not one horror alone that she was running from, and running towards, no matter where she turned, but a whole leash of them. There was, first, a hideous accusation that would brand her as a thief, second, the loss of the love and confidence of the benefactress she had adored, and after that friendless- ness, homelessness and destitution. Wherever she ran she could not escape these, they were like the wood itself, through which_ she did not know the way to any outlet. She was not a clever girl and -she did not sit down to think the matter out, and con- sider what she had better do. She just plunged on, not khowin,„cr where she was, gol mg, and not sane enough to reason about anything. Nobody had cared about her till Mrs. Stonehouse had taken her up. Nobody cared about her now,. So powerfully did the mind of the strong woman who had held her in hand dominate her imagination that she soon began to see herself in the light of a thief. Those ribbons and bits of lace, she had thought and bought th.qm with her own money, but now it seemed' they were evidence against her. Those vanities she had been taunted with, what had they to do with a cheque ? What was a cheque ? How could a bit of paper be worth fifty pounds? She had never seen paper money. The shillings in her purse had always been her own. But it did not matter how or where that extraordinary piece of paper had gone. She was accounted now a thief, for Mrs. Ston.ehouse had said it.

The sun went down -unobserved by her and dusk crept into the thicket. Soon it deepened to darkness, and Tiny did not dare plunge on any further. Creeping into the underwood sho tried to recall her school lessons, to as- sure herself that there were no wild beasts _ . _

left in the forests of England. If this was not a forest it answered for one to the terrified little girl, who in the midst of her forlorn anguish listened keenly for the roar of a pos- sible lion or tiger. At last, after hours of misery and terror, exhaustion came to the rescue and she fell asleep. In the faint dusk of dawn she woke and gathered herself to her feet, wondering that something had not devoured her in the dark- ness. But, alas, what premise from the light! Homeless, houseiess, friendless, without a character, where should she go? Who could be expected to take her in when her idolised benefactress had cast her out ? No one, no one, no one. _ .

The young vitality seemed quenched in her body which was weak and faint for want of foal and rest, and from the shuddering of nerves that were wrung by grief and fear. Not knoNving why or where she began to move forward, pushing her way among un- dergrowths and overhanging boughs until she saw at a little distance an opening among the trees, and a piece of smooth grey water not much larger than a village pond, a little lake looking like a mysterious mirror set there to catch the reflectidns of the retreat- ing- stars as one by one they withdrew into the secret heavens. Suddenly the idea rushed into her little half-crazed brain that there, under that sweet water she could find a refuge and a home. She could slip in there 'among the last of the stars and be at rest. Nobody could hol- der her, and no one could cry thief at her, after that. She would be sound asleep, and zhould not hear them if they did. She drew near the marge and stood in d looked down into the water. Then she dipped in one foot and withdrew it, and stared all round at the ghostly trees and wraith-like parting clouds in the death-like dawn, as they are before the birth of the light. All still, all dead, no point of hope, no ray of warmth, no eye of a friend anywhere. She would have. courage and try again. This time she would make a spring and have it over. And so she sprang; but a strong rough branch of a bush caught her by the skirts and chucked her back again. In her maddened state, she thought it was an arm that had pulled her back, and a reeollectien of something forgotten burst on her. " Mother!' she cried with a sob, falling on her knees and stretching up her arms. She thought she had heard her dead mother teaching her to say, "Our Father," her, a little child, now grown up to be a girl cap- able of suicide. She uttered the prayer aloud as if repeating it after another voice, and fell weeping in the grass. Then the vehemence of her passion of re- pentance struck her in the heart, and already weakened by hunger, cold and vigil, she rolled over by the water's side, unconscious. When she awoke again as if out of no- thingness, memory was for the moment a blank life an experience new and unknown. Out Of the clouds she thought s]ie saw a face looking down at her, and as heart and brain began struggling to work again the face came down nearer and nearer, till at last it was bending over her. By degrees it grew fa- miliar; where had she seen it before ? Ah, yes, it was not an angel come down from the heavens to pity and help her. It was the face that had sometimes looked at her through a rift in the hedge. " Are :you better ? Can you rise ? Let me help you. Lean on me." The young man whom Cassandra had care- fully blotted out by stopping the holes in the garden hedge raised up the trembling girl trunk. and placed her sitting on a fallen tree- Liftingcried out: her eyes to his pitiful face, Tiny "a "Do not speak t , Don't! I am a wick- ed girl. ' know you lri me God Not until after God terrible r:i ble:mete.mpltatiwoans. But, w You praying." kr::0 goi,n. to drown myself. But I did not steal w anything about the eh eque I'm sure you !" iditn.a'tp6poemtnleicodihi.g,o,hme Iwithdional'e and tell me what has li t Tiny stood up and tottered along beside leawncsiz m :a her friend, and they travelled away to the young man's house, a long journey as it seemed to Tiny, because she was so weak and had Meanwhile haill s 6 k at) a e Stoneliouse was hav- ing as bad a time as sh e deserved to have. For some hours after Tiny's dis bright sunny hours of daylight, azipearance, fumed and fretted, • railing to herseellfnerely and others about ingratitude and di h s onesty, keeping herself up to a white heat, lest , any of her just wrath should cool before the re- turn of the culprit, which was certain to oc- cur in the course of the afternoon or even- ing. But tea time came and no TinY . The sun went down behind the black yew trees and no Tiny. The flowers grew pale in the dusk, auct the peacock was at roost, and still there was no sight or sound of the little girl who had been driven out into the wilderness., Then the lady began to lie more fright- ened than 2.nzu, and to send soouta here and

div.head: ON THE THRESHOLD.
div.p: ON THE THRESHOLD.
. BY
LADY GILBERT [ROSA. MULHOLLAND.] (Author of "The Wild Birds of Killeevy," " A Fair Emigrant," " Hester's History," etc.).

Mrs. Cassandra Stonehouse, mistress of that beautiful place, the Deodars, was sit- ting in an arbour of flowering clematis look- ing out over gardens a-flush with the early glories of June. She had been reading her Bible, but put it aside when a letter was handed to her which caused her some surprise. Within the envel- ope was a cheque for a considerable sum, and a few words ,stating that it was remitted by the anonymous sender "in payment of an old debt.' The surprise was an extremely agreeable one, not that Cassandra was at alum want of money, but simply for the very general reason that much would have more. She put a mark in her book, left it on the seat, and. hastened to the house, calling to her secretary, a very young girl who shall be known to this narrative by the name of Tiny. The girl, a slight thing in a white frock sat at a desk and answered the morn- ing's letters for her mistress and friend, while Cassandra 'reflected on the particular purpose to which she would devote the pleas- ing windfall. Cassandra's parsimoniousness was not of the kind that stints the cook in butter and diminishes the staff of gardeners when in- come tax runs high. Her belief in her genius for the training of. character did not extend to the close examination of her own con- science, yet her paroxysms of acute suspici- ousness had not resulted in alienating from her a certain band, of old servants wno had learned to smile at her unequal humours and wait till the storm passed by. Tiny was the only member of the house- hold who had not belonged to it for a year. Coming from a cheap school, where her dead mother's relative had found her she was . .

_ still living in Elysium, adoring the flowers, trees, and animal pets, and reverencing the somewhat hard-faced lady who had wrought a miracle in her young life. Her child-like mind accepted all contra- dictions of its own theory of bountiful per- fection, and at one reconciled them with its own standard. When rebuked for frivolity she hung her head and wondered mutely, not knowing that Cassandra, almost convinced of the entire goodness of her protegee's nature, but still (on principle) suspicious of guile, was giving her a training such as had no clouot built up the character of that admir- able and strong-minded woman,. the ' much. respected mistress of the Deodars. 'mile girl triad to believe she had been guilty of vanity in purchasing by post, out of her scanty pocket money cheap new lace to improve her muslin frock, and that she wae wicked in feeling miserable because certain invitations to Meet other young people of the neighbourhood had been absolutely re- fused for her by Mrs. Stonehonse. But an hour in the air with the flowers, the birds and the dogs had hitherto always restored her to happiness and virtue. Her correspondence disposed of all but one letter to her bank which had been left open on the desk, Cassandra sauntered down the garden, viewing her successful flower- growths with all the pride of a creator, paus- ing at a spot where some time ago a hole had been mischievously opened in her perfect hedge of 3tew. On one occasion she had sur- prised a face at the other side of this open- ing, a masculine face, young and bold, and had been quick at guessing a romance alto- gether at variance with her well-developed theories of proper conduct. Thorough as was her appreciation of her own especial excellencies 'she never for a mo- ment supposed it was to admire her digni- fied movements that an cag,er face of youth with down on the lips had placed itself at • that green window in,geniously opened be- tween her gardens and the adjoining proper- ty. She looked carefully at the place in the yew hedge where -the hole had been, and saw that the gardener had closed it so well that she could scarcely perceive evidence of its having ever existed. Thus satisfied she wondered whether that girl had gone to the village /yet to post the letters, and she returned to the house and to the desk in her sanctum. Tiny was not there, and all the letters were gone, except one that lay open on the writ- ing table. It was a letter to the bank, en- closing the cheque that had arrived so unex- pectedly that morning. The letter was still open, and she took it out of the envelope to assure herself that no harm had resulted from her neglect to close and seal it. Then she saw at a glance that there was something wrong. The letter as dictated by herself, and written and addressed by Tiny was all right„ but the important enclosure placed in the envelope only an hour ago by herself,—the cheque was gone. Cassandra rang for a maid to go into all the corners of tile room to oee whether the breeze through the open window might not have carried it off the table. She was not sur- prised, however, that there was no result, as breeze would not filch it out of the envel- ope, and she knew that she had put it there. Ett last she sat clown and came to a necessary conclusion. Tiny, who had written the letter and seen her put in the cheque, must have yielded to temntation and extracted it. " Always a dangerous sign when a .girl is fond of laces and flowers and ribbons,- re- flected Cassandra in consternation: and the element of suspicion which of late had found nothing to work upon in a household of tried and trusty servants, now rose from its sleep, and like a starved monster sprang at once to make a hasty mouthful of a little girl's char- acter. If Cassandra had ordered Suspicion back to his lair and taken time to consider how much liberty she should allow him when setting him free, things might have turned out dif- ferently. But Cassandra was Cassandra, and she took her own way in a hurried descent on the beautiful summer gardens, with outraged benevolence on one side of her, and unre- strained anger on the other. And there was the culprit, practising curt- teys before an arrogant and astonished pea- coek, like a society debutante before rovalty, The lady's rusliing skirts made a °little Whirlwind in the summer air, and the pea seek spread his tail and strutted away haughtily, like many a flair-weather -Irina at the first,breath of a storm. "Come here this moment, Tiny! Stand be- fore me, and look me in the face, and answer me !" Tiny dropped her arms by her sides, opened her mouth, and stared with, round eyes at tier benefactress. "What have you done with the cheque that ,I left with you in an open letter on my desk an hour ago ?" A cheque!" "A cheque. Do you pretend that you don't know what a cheque is? A written paper to the bank, worth fifty pounds." To Tiny the sum mentioned might as well have been a million pounds as fifty. She was not clever, and much money was known to her only in shillings. " I did not see it," she said. " You told me not to c!ose that letter till you had looked at it again." " Oh, you deceitful little girl! Give me a direct answer or have done with you. The cheque was in the letter, and it is gone. No one was in the room, or has anything to do with my letters but yourself. Where have you got it Return it to me, and I shall have mercy on you, considering your youth. You must be very ignorant or you would know that I can prevent your getting the money. I snail write immediately to the bank to withhold payment." Tiny stood stiffing, as if stunned. " I have not got the cheque," she said after a moment of stupefaction. "I do not want the money. I am not a thief." " I could not have believed that you were. But I must aredit the evidence of my own senses. I have been more than good to you, you ungrateful little creature! I gave you pretty frocks, and nice things, enough to satiatv any girl's vaulty, If 30u wanted more

. . there to enquire if. the girl had found her I way to the nearest village, as any wanderer , wita common sense would do. So cunning a little person would be sure to know how to see her way about. Oh, the depravity of the youthful human heart! Who could have guessed it •to be hiding behind that simple- seeming child-like countenance. Midnight came with no tidings, j and Cas- sandra was sleepless. To do her justice she suffered as she deserved. By daylight she was out roaming in the Park, and denounc- ing the dilatoriness of the messengers she had sent far and near, and who were slow in returning. When the sun rose behind the trees she staggered into the summer-house, grey-faced and conscience stricken. It was the same summer-house in which she had sat yesterday morning, placidly and self-righteously confi- dent reading her Bible. There, indeed was the Bible still lying on the seat where she had left it. And there was the mark she had placed in it, a bit of white paper showing half an inch above the hastily-closed pages. • She took the volume up and opened it. Here she should find some consolation for the wrong that had been done her. What ? Gracious Heavens ! The paper that lay between the leaves of the Book as a mar- ker was the missing cheque! The stolen cheque, here! And Tiny, where ? Where ? Cassandra rushed from the summer-house and met one of her messengers returning. He had tidings of the young lady. She was at present at Greenrig's Nallon, hardly two miles away. Young Mr. Greenrig— " Tell everyone that I have wronged her," shouted Cassandra, "wronged her, -wronged her, I say! Order the carriage, at once. I will drive to Greenrig's Nallon.!" Young Mr. Greenrig and his mother were still at breakfast when Mrs. Cassandra Stone- house was announced. Mrs. Greenrig went to her immediately, receiving her with Ipoks of mild reproach which changed to sympathy when she saw the distracted appearance oi the conscience-stricken lady. " I wronged her," said Cassandra. "I know you did," said Mrs. Greenrig. " How could you ever suspect a face like that 1"' " Where is she ?" . •• At present she is , having a sound sleep in bed. The sound sleep of the innocent. She was in a deplorable state, poor chid. Only --- for my son-" "Ale! And I was rude to him for looking through the hedge—" " 171, ell, I may tell you that he hopes to look at her as much as he likes after this. We hope you will hot object. You have been very good to her. The child's greatest grief has been the loss of your good opinicint of ' your affection. For she has evidently loved you dearly." Cassandra had not shed tears for many a day. But Ow she wept. You nfeau that your son—" "I do. Young hearts are curious things, , - and he has been loving her through that hole in the hedge for don't know how long. His family and property are not despicable, Mrs. I ' Stonehouse. 1 hope you will give your consent to his wooing, and allow her to stay -with us for some time to give him opportunity. May I bring him to be introduced to you ?" But Jack Greeurig refused to be intro- duced on that occasion. " No, I will not see the monster," he said, "I could not behave to her like a gentle- However, net ion. afterwards he accom- panied Tiny to the Headers, a triumphal visit of two on tile trees, and none the less so because young persons happier than the birds their -happiness was based on something like a tragedy. For long Tiny could not bear to go near that little lake in the opening of the woods. But a time came when a dark memory faded, and she would stand and look at the sweet, smooth water, thinking of the moment when her mother's prayers'''. had saved her, and where the dawn of a great love had risen like the sun of a new day on her now happy life.
HOW I LOST A STONE OF FAT AND REGAINED MY GOOD FIGURE BY A SIMPLE RUBBING PROCESS.

Three weeks ago I read in the paper of a lady who found that a simple mixture of herbs could be rubbed on fleshy place* and that this would gradually dissolve excessiVe fat. I was sorely in I, need of just such advice, so I obtained from a chemist 1 dram of quassia chips and 3 ozs. of cirola bark extract. After taking them home I put the quassia chips in a basin and poured over them a teacupful of boiling water. When it had stood for about half:a-minute I strained it through a cloth and added the cirola bark ex- tract. Then I poured the mixture into a bottle and applied it freely every night and morning with my hands for about five minutes, using a circular movement. The fat just seemed to melt away each time that I rubbed it on, and I never dreamed it would be so easy to get slender. Friends are amazed at the improvement in my appearance, for I have reduced over II stone of fat. from my hips and abdomen, and I look 15 years younger. Now I feel just like stopping every fat woman I see and telling her how I did it. G.M.B.

div.head: FIRE PROTECTION OF CATHEDRALS AND
div.p: FIRE PROTECTION OF CATHEDRALS AND
HISTORIC BUILDINGS.

A scheme for improving the fire extinguishing arrangements at Ely Cathedral has been carried on by Messrs. Merryweather, and Sons, the well-known fire engiveers. It consists of provid- ing the building with a network of dry mains carried to different levels and fitted. with . hydrants fimed at all important points. The hydrants at the higher levels are a special design, in order to augment pressure and obtain ! the best advantage from the COuncirs service of water; but if necessary the outer end of the main can be connected with the local steam fire " engine. There is thus no need to lay out long lines of hose piping, and a full supply of water can quickly be brought to bear from the hydrants nearest the scene of outbreak. A similar dry main system has been recently installed by Messrs. Merryweather and Sons, at St. Paul's Cathedral, London, and it is being generally adopted as one of the most efficient safeguards for the protection of country man- sions and historic buildings. •

• EFFECTS OF BENEFICIAL EXERCISE. Exercise to be beneficial must do these things': 1. It must slightly increase the strength and force of the heart beat, so as to improve the circulation and do away with any tendency to sluggishness. 2. • It must slightly quicken and deepen the breathing rate so that more pure all is drawn into the lungs and less impure air is left behind. 3. It mijst stimulate into normal activity the myriads orglands in the skin whose duty it is to rid the body of a part of the poison- ous substances constantly being formed within us. 'Practically any exercise, if carried out with the correct degree of moderation, will accomplish these results and So deserves the term "beneficial exercise." The trouble is that indulged in Past moderation, almost every form of exercise can do more harm than good.
