div.head: No Honours for Those who by Law are not " Persons "
div.p: No Honours for Those who by Law are not " Persons "
TIRING OF THE SHAPELESS WAIST.

The Court is wearing mourning for two weeks for the Dowager Queen of Sweden, whose grandson Married Princess Margaret of Con- naught. Almost a life-long invalid, Queen Sophia was obliged to live much abroad. Bournemouth was her favourite watering-place, and she spent many winters there. ' She was a daughter of Duke William of Nassau, a half- sister of the Princess of Wied, and consequently related to Carmen Sylva, and the German Prince of Wied, who is to be the first King of Albania. Carmen Sylva has lust entered upon her seventy-first year. Known chiefly as a writer of verse and charthing stories, she is even more versatile in her accomplishments than .the German Emperor, and is a painter, architect, and scientist, as well as a great musician, needlewoman, arid an enthusiast in all kinds of philanthropic work.' She is aunt to both Prince William and his Wife, Sophia, Princess von Wied. The young couple are well-known in fashionable Berlin society, and are giving up their home there for the somewhat risky and thankless office of the newly-created Balkan kingship.

div.head: Women and Honours.
div.p: Women and Honours.

•Women who distinguish themselves in any public' field do not ekpect to find their names among the ,favoured, personages upon whom honours are bestowed. Consequently they are not disappointed when the New Year or Birth- day Honours List appears. There are ninny women who have won distinction for the3n- elves as travellers, scientists, and in the fields of drama, music medicine, literature, and art. Had they beep men,' some of them, at 'least, would have. found theniselves with handles to their names, but so long as the law, and the powers that be, hold that a \vornan is not a Person," so no doubt this one-sided state of

things will rot-din-no. There would certainly be one drawback to any far-reaching change. If the woman' was married it Would be awk- ward for' the husband to assume the role of Sir Nobody, because his wife had been created Lady Somebody. As things are, married women find no difficulty in basking in the reflected glory of their Ausbands' honours. It must have been pleastint for the bride' who became ,Mrs,. Ernest
, IL Larith one day, to find herself the next Lady Lamb, the wife of the newly-knighted Member of Parliament for Rochester.

A French Revolutionary Artist. ' Among, noted French artists is Madame Sorgue, the successor of Louise Michel, syndi- calist, communist, strike leader, and sabotense. She has a most picturesque personality and is El niarvellonsly convincing and fiery orator. At the invitation of the Cambridge branch of the Fabian Society she lately delivered a remarkable lecture on "The Revolution of the Mind." Her dress on. that occasion was black, relieved at the neck by a very big bow t)f scarlet ribbon. She has short, early and very thick black hair, and it was crowned by a wide black felt hat 6f the sombrero type, fastened by one large scarlet pin. Her appearance Was as striking as her ideas are revolutionary.

The Silhouette and a New Skirt. A new skirt that promises to have a vogue as long as the present silhouette remains in fashion is Very effective in fine cloth, charmeuse, or crepe do chine, has a seam in .front, two quite generous, flat pleats on either side, and gathers (rather 11.01) at the 'back. : The pleats give the fulness demanded on the hips ,and-quite a bustle- like' effect at the back and sides. Towards the feet the 'skirt narrows in order that the peg-top , silhouette may be maintained. Opinions are divided as to the style of the silhouette for/the new year. Some authorities confidently assert that the peg-top effect and • hunelfiness at the hips will entirely disappear, and that slimness and slenderness will -eturn; others are equally convinced that the tight skirt is doomed, and, as corroboration of their assertion, cite the new coiffure which shows the hair piled on the top of the head, a sure indication ;that the quaint and graceful Watteau fashions are to prevail. It must be admitted that many of the new and
I
most original of this season's evening dresses have a distinct 18th century quaintness, but ,whether this is a mere caprice of Dame Fashion or a portent of modes to conic, time alone will prove.

The Vogue of the Cape. Not only is the capelet of fur to the fore, but the prophets insist that the cape proper is to carry all before it next spring,. Those models that have been allowed to see the light are ex- tremely simple in make, and consist of a length of cloth, gathered into a square collar of fur, and falling in folds round the hips. These models were Without lining. The short coutee, despite the condemnation of the doctors, has established itself securely in the favour of 'designers who provide the outfit for thoSe- of their clientele wintering on the Riviera. Nearly all the so-called tailored suits are 'furnished with a short coatee, varying in shape and length, but always having .as its distinguishing feature a remarkable waistcoat of fur, velvet, or brOcade. Sometimes the Short bolero is of fur, Which the doctors consider a dangerous garment, for it provides too much warmth on the shoulders ,and not enough around and below the waist. There are slight but unmis- takeable signs that the waist line will in the spring be more defined, if Mot slightly com- pressed., and considerably higher than at pre- sent. Such a change would be pleasant, for most womdn are tiring of the low draped sash and the shapeless waist.

To Utilise old Fur Coats. Many wOmen have old-fahioned coats of various furs that are too shabby and out-61-date for this season's Wear. These may. be utilised for the smart little 'capes that just cover the shoulders, and when made of .one fur, and edged with another of contrasting colour, are very becoming, besides being qulckly thrown on and fastened. This capelet is very fascinat- ing ,in white coney, edged with skunk,, and is at its test When rucked around the upper part of the shoulders and neck to the ears, somewhat after the fashion of a shawl. It may be fastened in front with'. any handsome braid ornament, and from the, latter tassels should fall' to ,the Waist-line. The cape is not crossed in front, but whole skins of handsome peltry are draped round the shoulders and prossed after the manner of 'a hug-me-tight. Many people have an idea that a. cape must neces- sarily be dowdy in its effect, but this shoulder tippet-,as the little garment was called years ago—is altogether pleasing and graceful. Many wide stoles this season, both Of fur and material, are slightly shaped to simulate a cape , round the shoulders, as the fit is thereby much improved.

div.head: HEALTH AND MIND.
div.p: HEALTH AND MIND.
Rev. A. M. Mitchell Asks for Church Crusade Against Disease.
ANOINTING THE SICK.
TO THE EDITOR OF "THE EXAMINER."

Sir,—May I claim the hospitality of your columns for the Guild of Health, which has been in existence some nine years, and, quite lately, has been re-constituted and re-organised? The Guild has for its patrons the Bishops of .Winchester, Salisbury and Worcester, and is controlled by a London Committee of influential and cultured members, including clerics and medicos, under the chairmanship of the Rev. Dr. Percy Dearmer.

One of the most Scriptural and practical of present-day organisations—the mission, as it were, of a man's spirit to his body—the Guild of Health stands for that oneness of life in man which should manifest in spiritual, mental and physical health; in fact, it seeks to revive within the Church the long-neglected function of spiritual healing.
_ Health is very much in our own power; it is largely a matter of mental outlook and will control. The objects of the Guild are formally set forth as four in number, viz.:—
1. The study of the influence of spiritual upon Physical well-being. in complete loyalty to scientific principles and 2.. The exercise of healing by methods. spiritual means,

3. United prayer for the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in all efforts to heal the sick. (0 4. The cultivation through spiritual means of both individual and corporate health. With the concurrence of the London Com- mittee we are about to form a branch of the ' Guild for this district, to be called "The New- ton-le-Willows and District Branch," and I shall be very glad to receive the names of all who are interested in the great health movement, who believe in the power of iniMl and will over the body. and its infirmities—of mind and will in co-operation with the Divine Life. Membership of the Guild is not restricted to the Church of England; it is open to all who accept the Holy Scriptures as the Word of God, but members of committees must be communicants of that Church, or of Churches in communion with her. Subscriptions are entirely voluntary, the .amounts being left to the members themselves, but, naturally, it is expected that the amounts should boar some proportion to the subscribers' means.

It should he clearly understood that the Guild does not exist for grumblers, whiners and wailers, those, that is, who "enjoy bad health," who are never happy except when on the sick list, but for those who believe in good ) health as the Will of God for man, and as an essential part of the Gospel of Jesus Christ cwithout which, indeed, the Gospel is imperfect and incomplete, and who are content to livo hopefully and peacefully in God's hands, to seek health, and ensure it for themselves, whilst radiating it to others round and about them. • In the visitation of the sick the Guild resorts to the Scriptural and primitive practices of the laying on of hands and the anointing with conse- crated oil. The anointing is not as a prepara- tion for death, but as a means, under God, for 1 restoration to health and reqeival of earthly life This country lost much when the optional anointing of the sick member, was eliminated from the office for the Visitation of the Sick Such provision- was made in the 1549 Prayer - book (the first English I'rayer-book properly so- called), but in the second Prayer-book of Edward VI. (1552) its place could nowhere be found Since the withdrawal of this beautiful and merciful provision for bodily health we have travelled further and further on the down grade of materialism, , until to-day we find belief in Material remedies wholly dominant, whilst the influence of mind, will, spirit in the great work of healing is totally ignored, or almost so. ' The Guild of- Health, which, it will be gath- ered, signifies the resumption by the Church of o their ibiy, the fulness of mission, should be the means of bringing back to her numbers of lapsed members, those who have gone forth from her in search of what they should have found, but the et always eha but, ed p did not find within her borders—the grace and help of spiritual healing. Much injury has been done to earnest, but, maybe, misguided folk, who have expectationsave distorted and mischievous Preeentation of the fnda out- side Physical aspect of the Jesus Gospel. Sickness and disease are rampant; serums, antitoxins, with other curative "delights," are: being multiplied ad infinitum; we are afflicted with maladies which we should never have known, or which, having appeared generations back, should now be eatinct; the medical side of the Insurance Act is not calculated to im- prove the health of the People. Is not the hour with us when the Church Should lead the great crusade for health against 'disease? Can she engage in a war more holy? in a work more Christ-like? The vast import. ance of this question, the great opportunity it presents, must be my apology for writing at such length.

div.head: PETROLEUM VOGUE.
div.p: THE PETROLEUM VOGUE.
Much In Favour With Specialists.

A new medical treatment of -which much is heard nowadays a which seems greatly in favour with the leaders of the medical profession is the use of purified petroleum in bowel dis- orders, more especially in chronic constipation. nd ; This method of treatment is based upon the well-known fact that petroleum, unlike animal oils, enters the intestines unchanged, where it acts as a soothing lubricant and disinfectant. Doctors maintain that by the use of petroleum the intestinal organs• are kept lubricated, and thus enabled to perform their functions more , easily and naturally. Whether or not this is the correct explanation, it is certain that vcry good results have been obtained from the use of purified petroleum (generally in the form of Angier's Emulsion) for chronic bowel disorders. Angier's Emulsion has been advertised for many years not alone for digestive and bowel disorders, lint, if we are not mistaken, . even more as "invaluable for coughs and lung troubles." To the lay mind it may seem a little strange that a remedy for lung troubles should also be of value in digestive and intestinal disorders, but as a matter of fact, it is now 'generally recognised that petroleum has a soothing, healing effect upon both the respiratory and digestive organs.

div.head: GUTTER PIRATES.
div.p: GUTTER PIRATES.

There are on our city streets to be foundmany representatives of genuine poverty, but the* fol- lowing unhappy little story, which appear§, in 344,t. izity sparrows, conducted b Lady Cie.., mentine aring, gives one to think that too often behind the appeal for charity with.which we are met in our daily peregrinations there exists small cause for us to exercise our com- passion. Would ,we could but more truly dis- criminate between the humbug in the trappings of poverty ' and those who are genuinely in. want: "Jimmie," an enterprising but misguided six-year,old, was taken from the street to " the- Childrenis Shelter, Ilign-street, Edinburgh, which became his temporary home under the following circumstances. He had attracted the attentioni of the general secretary of the society by hanging about the street just outside the entrance to the head office of the society, look- ing dirty and very ragged, and evidently intent on extracting pennies from tender-hearted pas- sers-by: He was invited to come up to the general secretary's romp, and after a little per- suasion, did so. As- he could give no very in- telligible account of himself, except that he was' hungry; and did not get enough to eat at home, one of the society's inspectors was sent for, and he was taken to the .shelter, and there detained to enable- full inquiries to be made as to the condition of the home and the truth of the state: merits he had made. It was then ascertained that 'Jimmie' had already been , under the notice of the Edinburgh Committee, the police having noticed him begging in the streets, and having reported him at the shelter. The condi,. lion of his home was found not to be so un- satisfactory as 'Jimmie' had described it. He had not been starved there, but had taken up with other boys who frequented the streets for the purpose of begging, and who had induced him to engage in the same occupdion by glow- ing accounts of successful appeals for pennies to kind, but mistakenly generous, passers-by. The resttiV was 'Jimmie,' although he could have got quite enough food at home, rapidli acquired a taste for street-begging, and, besides forsak- ing his • home, became- .truant from school. After a few days at the shelter, during whith he soon learned to be ' tiity. and • clean; and was found to be a bright, well-behaved little chap, `Jimmie was sent back, to his hoe in the Cowgate; and he is now attending school regularly„ and it is hoped that he has given up all idea of going back to his former occupa- tion of 'street-trading.'

Sir,—We wish to express our extreme thank- fulness for the generous response to our appeal through the Press and in other ways, to relieve our work from a large burden of outstanding debt. Through the death and removal from the district many old subscribers are no longer with us, so we make an appeal for new sub- scribers in the current year, and we earnestly ask the charitably disposed in filling up their lists to give a kindly thought to the work of this society, which rescues little children, and gives them a fair chance in life. Every case is most carefully inquired into by a committee, which sits for that purpose, and no deserving case is refused, .but where,a' parent or guardian. is in a position to contribute towards the cost of maintenance the ease is only Accepted on these conditions. The results of the work are of a most encouraging nature, and the society is well worthy of support. GEORGE D. KILLEY, Chairman. G. BRADSTOCK LOCKETT, Hon. DiOc. Treas. GEORGE W. NORRIS, lion. Dioc. div.head: DISESTABLISHMENT AND DISENDOW-
div.p: DISESTABLISHMENT AND DISENDOW-

Sir,—Replying to Mr. Stidston-Broadbent's letter in your issue of January 3, I feel that I can only refeehim to my previous letter, which dealt . fully • with the position and was a state- ment of plain historical facts. These can be easily verified by any person of average intelli- gence who will refer to a good history of Eng- land. Mr. Broadbent's statement respecting Lord Halifax's position simply proves that Lord Halifax does not support the present Bill for the 'Disestablishment of the Church of England in Wales, because it does not carry out dises- tablishment thoroughly enough; and leaves the Church very largely under State control. I am prepared to accept half a loaf rather than no bread, and to hope for complete freedom in the future. If Mr. Stidston-Broadbent's idea of contro- versy is to assume that his opponent does not understand the meaning of the words 116 uses, then this correspondence had` better Close. It is a matter of historical knowledge that the Welsh bitterly opposed everything English Until their final subjugation by .Edward I. Mr. Stidston_Br _ oadbent has not controverted my statement that a branch of the ancient Irish Church existed in Wales previous to the intro- duction of Christianity in Southern England, as s_hown foundation of the bY the date of the "iocese of Bangor. My letter of December 15, if read carefully, shows quite clearly that I con- sider it a violation of the rights of conscience to force any man to contribute to the maintenance of ailY particular religion. If he really believes , • his religion he will make sacrifices to main- tain it without State interference. I have never advocated that endowments should be handed to the County Councils or the Welsh Libraries, but I would point out that what Parliament gave to the Church, Parliament can take away °gain, and as the Church of England at the Present day only holds her ancient endowments ' bY the good grace of the State, the latter can, Of course, decide to divert them as it thinks fit. If Henry assumption of the Papal authority, his Statute of the Six Articles of Religion, together with the illegal appointment of Cranmer as Archbishop of Canterbury, the seizing of the parish churches, monasteries, &c., did not mean the establishment and endow- ment of a church to suit his personal conveni- ence, then I must confess to not understand- ing history. My authorities are 1, The Zurich Letters; 2, Brewer's Letters and Papers; 3, Pocock's Records of the Reformation; 4, Green's History of the English People. With regard to moneys for the repose of the , souls of donors, one very plain case is Sir Richard Whittington, the notable Lord Mayor of London, who died 1425, leaving large sums for the founding of the Guildhall, Grey Friars Library,. and for masses for the repose of his soul, to be said at St. Bartholomew's. Other cases can be found in Manchester Cathedral en- dowments, Eccles Parish Church (1111 and there is one endowment at Warrin tot."' Parish Church, left by Thomas de Boteler for there of his soul. Church reform so-called is merely se " tinkering" with a disease which goes right; 'to the roots of the Church, the only remedl• fo which is a complete and ruthless re-orgiii'iisar- tion from top to bottom. With the Church Ills-Established we should have the right to manage our own affairs in our way, with the Power to say to all Parliaments, "Hands off," and to strive for uniformity of doctrine and government. . In conclusion may I point out to Mr. Stidstort- Broadbent that he is mistaken in thinking I express the views of the Liberal party. ,MY speech was delivered at the monthly meeting of the siLYruon of m Liberal Association, and was an ex- ores • . Personal opinion, as also are my letters.
Oak Le ,an a. Statham. " uav 6th, 1914.

SECTARIAN BIGOTRY IN IRELAND. Sir,—l shall not occupy your valuable space or4,weary the patience of your readers by going over the gross mis-statements of • your corre- spondent, G. W. S. Jarrett, but simply give a few facts and figures which shbuld clearly de- monstrate to any unprejudiced mind that there is not now, and never was, any such thing as intolerance on the part of Irish Catholics to- wards their Protestant fellow-countrymen. Prior to the coming into force of the Local Government Act of 1898, public appointments in Ireland were in the main in the hands of the Grand Juries, and the rule was that the officials chosen were Protestants. The spirit of ascend- ency was carried to such lengths indeed that even in the most strongly Catholic districts the public officials were Protestants. When the Act was passed the power of ap- pointment passed to the popularly elected bodies. The County Councils had power to dis- miss the existing officials. What happened? In hundreds of cases—in the vast majority, indeed —the officers were retained, and large numbers of them still continue to hold their appoint- ments.

The Catholic majority did not evince the least desire to interfere with the Protestant officials because they were Protestants. The following table will prove that Irish .Pro- testants fare infinitely better under a Catholic majority than Irish Catholics fare under a Pro- testant majority. The first four counties are in what is called Prbtestant Ulster, where there is a Protestant majority on the Councils, even though the majority of the population are not in all cases, Protestant. "Last week," he said, inci- dentally, " at the Poor Law elections in Cork, Miss Day, a Protestant, was returned at the head of the poll; in Bandon, the Earl of Ban- don, it Protestant, is chairman of the Town Commissiokers; in Kinsale, Mr. David Acton is chairman, and he also is ,a Protestant; while in Skiboreen, the same pleasant conditions exist, , the chairman, Mr. William Wolfe, being an- ther Protestant." As a matter of fact, the people who complain j loudest of the persecution of the Protestants in, the South and West are people who do not live there (like your correspondent Mr. G. W. S. 1 Jarrett), and whose occupation would be gone if they had the courage to admit the truth. No candidate, whether for Parliamentary, town, county, urban, or rural elections, enters the contest as a Catholic or a Protestant, but as Nationalists or Unionists, and if there are only 1 16 Unionists out of • 600, as Mr. Smith says, or 15 out of a total of 703 as G. W. S. Jarrett puts it, surely that is conclusive proof that the over- whelming majority of the people of Ireland con- sistently demand Home Rule. Is Mr. Jarrett aware that one-tenth of the Irish National Parliamentary party are Pro- testants, elected by solidly Catholic constituen- cies? I have tried to be very easy with Mr. Jarrett, because it is evident be is not at all acquainted with Irish affairs-he doesn't even know where the United. Irish League Rooms awe situated in Warrington! Well, our rooms are at 25, Winwick-street, two doors from Central Station ; if Mr. Jarrett cares to call there any evening I shall endeavour to give him a further lesson on Irish Catholic tol- erance. But I will not again take any part in trying to enlighten him through the columns of your valuable paper.

In answer to "Fair Rent," I have only to say that it gives me great pleasure to know that, even at this late date, he agrees with me. He says: It is to be regretted that I did not put forward the accountants' certificate before now." No one who read his letters would have thought a certificate was necessary to con- vince him. He debated as one who knew all about rating. After reading all his letters, I have come to the conclusion that a well-known writer cor- rectly said, "People leading lives that exercise their brains too much, and their muscles too little, commonly bring their strongest excite- ments forward towards the end of the day. But those whose lives conform best to the lines of health by exercising their muscles, exhibit early in the day a vivacity greater than they do towards the close."

"Fair Rent" suggests that something might be done to alter and improie the present sys- tem of rating. I hope so, and shall be pleased .to support any sensible and workable scheme that he may think out, even though it be sent anonymously. The Limes, Orford.
GEORGE SMITH.

div.head: nOW TO HAVE A HAPPY
div.p: nOW TO HAVE A HAPPY
HOLIDAY THOUGH MARRIED.

The man who convinces himself that a wife is an encumbrance on the journey of life, if he has married by mistake, thinks that it is better not to bring his wife with him when taking a summer holiday. For myself I of life and a holiday trip are improved by a wife. True,' y„believe that both the journey cannot fold her up small and pack her in anywhere especially if she has many hat boxes, but if she be the right sort of woman she will go anywhere that it is wise for you to go. When the Sultan of Tur- key was deposed and sent to Salonica he brought eleven wives with him; why should I go on a journey without in3l one and only wife?

After telling hie son that honesty is the beet policy a xna,n added, "I have tried both.' In this matter of bringing a wife on a holiday and of not doing so I have tried both and can say from experience that an ac- companied holiday, so to speak, is sweeter than a solo.

THE WISDOM OF WIVES. The first great advantage of bringing a wife with you on a holiday is that you are saved from anxiety about her. You see her w tion not to get letters from her you have not theel lndtroubleh aPPY—then, though it is a depriva- tion o f writing news about yourself to her. a Women are now becoming nomadic and make capital travellers. They easily form acquaintances and they get information and privileges that do not come to men travelling alone. When I see how much it costs some bachel- ors to live at home and the extravagant way they travel, I wonder how they can afford not to be married or to take tours without wives as managing directors. The travelling expenses of wife and hus- band are not nearly double what the man w if short sighted selfishness induced. him topgae alone. The saying that what will keep one will keep two is often misleading, but there- is great economy when two people, on a trip share rooms, carriages, portions at restaurants And such things. So serpentine is the wisdom of some wives their way when on that they can almost paY a tour. They make better bargains for rooms than men do--they give " tips " with more judgment and better grace, and there- fore more economically. If a husband leave the entire tipping and lArgaining business to his wife he will save, far more than thQ Twice of her tickets. _

div.head: INDIAN TEA.
div.p: INDIAN TEA.

It is interesting to note how the consumption of Indian tea is increasing through the world as people come more completely to realise its many virtues. Indian tea is justly famous, not I only on account of its high quality and purity, but also because of the delicacy of its flavour, and the great tea-drinking public now know that teas which yield delicate, light brews are •just as much Indian as those which give a fuller flavoured infusion. It is, we confess, pleasant to know that the British Empire stands supreme so far as this most popular of all beverages is concerned, for both the labour and capital involved are British, and the process of preparation is under the supervision of English expq,rts.

div.head: SUGGESTION TO THE TARIFF REFORM
div.p: A SUGGESTION TO THE TARIFF REFORM
PARTY.

Sir,—One cannot help feeling sympathy with the Unionist party in connection with the mess into which the leaders have landed the Tariff Reform question. Might a humble individual be allowed to make•a suggestion? It is clear, if things are left as they are, there will be large deflections from the support the Unionist candidates 'will receive at the next election in agricultural districts. The position will be a , very serious one if some definite action is not at once taken to rescue the party from its pre- sent muddle. My proposal is that, presuming a Unionist majority be returned at next election, an Act should be passed putting a tax on manufa,c- tured imports, but this Act should not he put in force unless, and until the electors at the second election vote for taxes on food. An Act would then be passed putting taxes on food imports, and the two Acts be brought into operation at the same time. I submit that such a course would de away with the legitimate fears of the agriculturists that they would have to pay more for what they buy and get no compensation in the rise of price of the food they sell. A. 13.

div.head: ALCOHOL AND " LIBERTY."
div.p: ALCOHOL AND " LIBERTY."

Sir,—Mr. G. E. Holme, in your issue of Nov- ember 29th, -asked "Would local veto be use- less?" I would have liked him' to say, in his next letter, what value he placed upon the Parliamentary return of New Zealand, which tells us that under "No licence" drinking per head does decrease. Instead of this he falls ,into the rut of personal liberty. I read in the same "Examiner" in which his letter was pub- lished, a report of a case upon which I would like to ask Mr. Holnie, or any other defender of the drink traffic, a question. It was "A sad case of neglect," which was before our Mayor and other magistrates. These are some of the items reported: "The husband gave the wife £1 2s. 6d. out of over .415; he had lately drawn in wages . . . . he had been employed at very good wages. . . . There were five children. When the baby was born he left his wife, and she had to provide money to keep the home The Mayor asked if prisoner was out of work entirely through his own fault, and the Inspector replied, 'lt was through drink.'" This, Mr. Editor, is a typical case of many, and not even so bad as some you sometimes report, and my question is this: Where should we put our energy and our influence? To per- petuate the traffic which in the case mentioned has not only been a curse to the man who had the liberty ( !) to please himself, but a blight to the home? Or to shield the women and the helpless children, who, through • the present licensing laws, have no remedy for damages against this cruel monster—alcohol? If on no other or higher plane than that of true patriot- ism, I think all who have a spark of human feeling in them will answer for the sake of the weak, "Let us . who are streng, because not contaminated with this vile, insidious foe to mankind, put all our strength forth, so that we may conquer it and lay it low, bruised even to extinction." January Bth, 1914.
BENJ. P. PARKES.

div.head: INCREASING RENTS.
div.p: INCREASING RENTS.

Sir,—lt is with mingled feelings.' I "tilt and slash" these further lines. It requires no keen observation to perceive, especially after reading Mr. Rathbone's last letter, that he is ill-beset. I never dreamed, when I wended my "tortuous" way through the last "epistle" to the tax evaders that I, by the plain state- ment of a few simple facts, was capable of dis- turbing the placid temperament of my oppon- ent, and rousing him to a state of high fever. Alas ! the limpid stream has become a rushing, seething mass, a regular "Bouillabaisse—a sort of soup, a broth, or brew." I accept the full responsibility for my inconsiderate actions, and continue this debate with a feeling of deep obligation to my opponent for the "diffidence" shown to me. I feel that, some compensation •is due to him for the "Don Quixote" -like man- ner in which I "slashed" his arguments to pieces; and though he has written two-thirds of a • column of what he must consider solid argument, but which, if written by an oppon- ent, he would describe us " packing rhetoric abuse and insinuations," I will again show him why the owner of property should have five per cent. on an improvement costing £lB. The builder erects houses for a profit, and when the houses are completed he asks for a rental that will return a fair dividend on the amount expended. When the paving is conv pleted, which often takes place many years after the erection of the houses, the builder raises the rent to recoup himself for the addi- tional outlay. If he sold the houses he would expect the cost of the erection, plus the cost of the, paving. Why Mr. Rathbone should expect the landlord to accept half-the latter cost, I do not know. The house was erected in the hope of getting a fair return for the capital expended, and the street-making is just as necessary for the health and convenience of, the tenant as the paving- in the backyard, and if Mr. Rathbone's suggestion is logical, why not halve the • cost of paving the backyard? In fact, go a step further—why not halve the cost of the house? The next subject Mr. Rathbone touches upon -is his desire to procure a post for me. He suggests that I am grieved that I have been overlooked in the selection. ,He should save his tears; for (lid not our now quiescent friend, "Trade Unionist," infer that I lived \in a lavish and extravagant state? Did not Mr. Rathbone' say: "I am not so fortunate as Mr. Smith to possess balance sheets, hrttises and land." Surely a little attention to his own advancement appears more necessary than the attention he bestows upon my affairs. He ought to be more consistent in his statements. I do possess balance sheets and bense property: Balance sheets that have caused me to say that there are works in Warrington that are under- rated; works that have trebled their output, if the balance sheet and statement can be relied upon, and pay little or no additional rates for the privilege. Mr. Rathbone asks How? 11 aee r i balanceo; When? Who are they? Let him look round for himself; it is not for me to specify any parti- entfeiltay t keep aier r.firm. But there are works which now t one machineryhund goseisleeotn. o .R running ' nearer one ed nd sixtye hours dd - rsper Te. This s week than the fifty to Sixty y f treble than double and somewhat sup- ports the the name of :tlieexcCulsieanhceimlloslf f Chancellor, atoidr he would have me believe that it' was men- tioned to ease my troubled mind, and as a panacea for all the builders' late troubles. His explanation must, of course, be accepted, but having regard to the calamitous way In the builders have been affected by the Chancel- lor's actions, it is not to be expected that they look towards the politician for any "rays of hope" or with feelings of gratitude. We ought never to-he expected to appreciate the policy of punishing the legitimate acquirer of property in order to make the man, who, through con- quest and violence, became a plutocrat, dis- gorge a portion of his holding for the benefit of , the State. Finally, Mr. Rathbone invites me to deal with the grabbers of the £70,000 of property, and suggests that these should be made to foot the bill for the increased rent. Mr. Rathbone should re-read my first article with care and without bias. In it he will find matters that he has quite overlooked or evaded. Increased cost of materials, dear money, paring and exacting by-laws were all quoted as conducing to increased rents; and it was to justify the latter that I set out on this campaign. He need not think that we are "whining" because our profits are less than the manufac- turers'. div.head: AN OIL FIRE AT WIDNES.
div.p: AN OIL FIRE AT WIDNES.

At the London and North-Western locomotive depot at Witbies on Monday evening an out- break of fire occurred in a shed in which a large quantity of oils was stored. It is thought that the room became filled with vapours owing to a leakage from one of the barrels and that these vapours were ignited by a lighted torch which a workman was carrying. The fire was not extinguished until much damage had been done.

div.head: "BRUTAL FRANKNESS."
div.p: "BRUTAL FRANKNESS."
No Food Taxes "Means" "Manufac-
turers First."

- The National Farmers' Union and the Farmers' Tariff Union are up in arms against the Bonar Law policy of putting food taxes in the background of his fiscal programme. Many Unionist newspapers have closed their columns ' against the discussion of Tariff Reform, as we pointed out in a leader a few weeks ago, because. such discussion was calculated to damage the -prospects of the Party ! E But Unionist Tariff Reformers" who are opposed to the "Edinburgh Compromise," and are not permitted to voice their discontent in the Unionist Press, have found "another channel" for the expression of their. view's—the "Westminster Gazette," one of the leading Liberal organs in the country.
An Open Letter to Mr. Bonar Law.

Mr. Bernard Gilbert, the honorary secretary of the Farmers' Union, writing this week to the 'Westminster Gazette," addresses the following "open letter" to Mr. Bonar Law, Leader of the Opposition : Sir,—You will ask why a body of Conservative farmers approaches you in this manner. Although agriculture is our oldest and most 'important industry, although not less than 85 per cent. of our farmers are Conservatives of the staunchest type, and although their livelihood is being threatened, the whole Unionist Press is closed against them in an iron boycott. When you lowered your flag at Ashton, and threw agriculture overboard, not a voice was raised in its behalf. The National Farmers' Union rose in revolt, backed -up by Mr. Henry Chaplin; but lie was unable to secure a seconder amongst , all the agricultural Unionist M.P.'s, Who stood with folded , arms whilst their con- stituents were sacrificed. Alarmed by the revolt, you offer 4 at Edin- burgh last spring, certain alternative offers, to make good the loss imposed upon farmers by the new fiscal policy. The only one of value, relief of rating, is ;long promised by both parties, and long over- due; the remainder cause a smile amongst practical farmers, and are, in the words of the Chairman of the Lincolnshire Farmers' Union, "purely imaginarY and ncithing decisive." "Justice demands," he went on, "that all should be treated alike . .or we had better remain under Free Trade." Our position cannot be better stated. Your offer was confirmed at Norwich last October; the revolt of agriculture was unmen- tioned by the Press, the two wings of the Unionist party seemed to be content with the and apparently all was well. But compromise, all is not well.

div.head: "A Fiery Cross."
div.p: "A Fiery Cross."

The resolution of the National Farmers' Union, " That we will be no party to ally change in our fiscal policy that excludes agri- culture from its benefits," passed around the country like a fiery cross, and has been carried by nearly every County Executive, by the National Executive, and by a great number of local branches of the Farmers' "Union. From ! them it has spread to other organisations, farmers' clubs, agricultural societies, he., and it is still travelling. The "Farmers' Tariff Union" has been formed, with a committee of Conservative farmers ONLY, to carry on this campaign. As its secretary, I have received thousands of letters from sympathisers, and it is clear that the farmers of England are deter- mined to fight the matter to a finish. But, despite the adoption of the "resolution" by one body of Conservative farmers after an- other, the officials of the party remain obdurate and the Press silent. The Tariff Reform League wavers. so rigorously boycotted by the Unionist Press, will you allow me to assure Mr. Humphry Oldcastle that the severance of my connection with the Unionist party was no hasty action taken in a moment of pique? Two colossal blunders by Mr. Donar Law had already set me seriously thinking of the step, and only "party loyalty" held me back. There was, in the first place, the betray-al of the farmers, as finally sealed by the Edinburgh speech: and, secondly, there was the making of Unionist support for Ulster contingent on the result of a General Election—a notoriously inadequate method of finding out the will of the people on any particular question. And now on the top of all comes a great conspiracy of silence on the part of the Unionist Press, acting no doubt in concert with the party leaders; and those Unionists who dare to think for themselves and to have consciences of their own are to be forbidden that freedom of speech which the Press pro- fessedly exists to uphold! When freedom of thought and speech is again permitted in the Unionist party, I may rejoin it, but not before; and so far from regretting the step which I have taken, I, trust that the 'same step will be taken by many more, and that no false conception of party loyalty will be allowed to stand in the way of a fearless assertion of one's political creed.—Your obedient and obliged servant, IMMO S. div.head: MERRY, JOVIAL THRONG.
div.p: A MERRY, JOVIAL THRONG.

Over 30,000 years! This represented the aggregate number of eventful years that had been lived by the • guests at this year's old people's treats, held at the Parr Hall on Thurs- day. There were 600 men at the dinner and 800 women at the tea. All were merry and bright, and the Mayor and Mayoress, Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., and Miss Furneaux, and others did all they could to make the entertainment as enjoy- able as possible. The oldest present at the dinner was Mr. Isaac Johnson, of 60, Allen-street, 86 years of age, and at the tea Mrs. Helen Shaw, of 10, ScLatfl- street, Latchford, 93" years of age. The former seconded a vote of thanks 'to the President. When Alderman Smethurst took the chair at the conclusion of the dinner he was greeted with a hearty round of applause. He said the earliest record he could find of those treats was in 1860, but there had been old men and women's treats , before that year. Alderman Smethurst was a great favourite with the ladies when he commenced to speak prior to the entertainment. The Mayor, seconding a vote of thanks to the subscribers, proposed by Alderman Smethurst, said he was pleased to see that the working men in Warrington were rallying round this insti- tution, and that they were giving more year after year. A pleasing entertainment was given in the evening by artistes from the different theatres and local talent.
MUD-SPLASHING MOTOR 'BUSES.

div.head: Tradesmen's Petition to the Town
div.p: Tradesmen's Petition to the Town
Council.
With the return of the wet weather, corn- plaints are again made in regard to the
Laud

splashing of shop windows by the Corporation motor 'buses. A special article appeared in The Examiner" of October 11th on the sub- ject- The writer was then informed that the Corporation were going to take steps in the matter, but nothing has been done, and we print below a petition to the Tramways Committee from Horsemarket-street tradesmen, who suffer considerably. In our article reference was made to two protective arrangements, one being the patent splashboards fitted by Messrs. Tilling, the makers of the Warrington 'buses, and the other being a capital device in the nature of a large rubber ring, which will entirely cover Vie outer edge of the tyre and overlap sufficiently as to catch the mud or throw it in a straight ' spurt behind, into the ordinary semi-circular guard. This disc is fastened to the rim of the wheel, and will be very durable. It is to be , hoped that the Corporation will act in the matter at once, for great inconvenience is caused to pedestrians as well as tradesmen. The following is the text of the petition : Horsemarket-street, Warrington, January 6, 1914. To the Chairman and Committee, Warrington Corporation Tramways. Gentlemen, We, the undersigned, wish to dratv your attention to the nuisance, viz., the splashing of mud from the wheels of the motor 'buses over the shop fronts and plate-glass windows as the motor 'buses pass up and down Horsemarket- street during wet weather. We request that a splash guard be fixed on the wheels of the motor 'buses in such manner as to prevent a continuance of this nuisance. We feel you will admit we have great cause for complaint, not only through the unnecessary labour caused,-but also through the unsightly and dirty condition of the shop fronts, princi- pally at week-ends. Thanking you in anticipation of .yoar prompt action in this matter, We are gentlemen, Yours faithfully, Donegal Tweed Co. (J. R. Adamson), W. and It. Fletcher, Ltd. (W. Brown); (Mrs.) S. J. Toft, Jacksons Ltd. (F. Vickerstaff), Lancashire and Cheshire Rubber Co. (G. B. Carr), C. Moun- field. Thomas Bayley, Manchester Clothing Dept. (H. Eglin), William Almond (W. Wilkin- son), Meadow Dairy Co. (W. Dodgson), Redmans Ltd. (R. Boyle), Shepherds Dairies, Ltd. (J. J. Flannery), J. W. Hall, E. L. Brown, Sterlings Ltd. (Thomas Day), Arthur Clowes, Suits Ltd. (G. P. div.p: EDUCATION .AN INDUSTRIAL ASSET. The late DUKE of DEVONSIiIRE once let fall the
obiter dictum, while giving over his onerous
duties as virtual Minister of Education, that
the British public hates the subject of educa-
Lion. The utterance was, perhaps, character-

" safe " politician was ever at any altz...r time

div.head: But it is true the British public
div.p: But it is true the British public
guilty of.
is too apathetic on this vital problem.
The
meeting at the Mansion House, in support of the London Continuation Schools, brought out
a great defect in our system of national eduea-
lion. In the last recorded year, so the Chair-
man of the Education Committee of the London
County Council pointed out, out of 216,000 young persons, less than 50,000 enrolled them- selves as students in the evening schools. The
evening school system is breaking down.
There are industrial centres where the London
record is bettered; there are others in which
it is not even equalled.
The Government's
hope to make a great advance • in. improving our educational system, so that this wastage
Of latent ability may be checked, depends on
the British public being brought to see thal
education is a great industrial asset-
Mr. PEASE, in a. notable speech at the Mansion House Meeting, appealed for a strong effort to
_ be made to stop this wastage of latent ability.

T)le most promising line of solution was, he 'declared, through a system under which employers will make arrangements, in regard at any rate to employes between the ages of fourteen and sixteen, for time- to be given Off, without deduction, of wages, for attendances at day continuation classes. Under this scheme, employers will not find the 'supply of labour diminished, and there will be no reduction Of the family income. The reforrn which Mr. Pmsn advocates would affect about one million
and a half of the youth of the country. Only by Some such measure can this country hope to hold its own in competition with other counteies which are devoting more attention
to continuous education. It is to be hoped that the nation will respond with alacrity to
Mr. PEASE'S patriotic appeal.

LITTLE BY LITTLE. LEON HERBERT. Little by little the time goes by,— Short if you sing through it, long if you sigh; Little by little, an hour a day, Gone with the years that have vanished away: Little by little the race is run, Trouble, and waiting, and toil are done.

Little by little the skies grow clear; Little by little the sun comes near; Little by little the days smile out Gladder and brighter on pain and doubt; Little by little the seeds we sow Into a beautiful yield will grow.

Little by little the world grows strong Fighting the battle of Right and Wrong; Little by little the Wrong gives way, Little by little the Right has sway; Little by little all longing souls Struggle up nearer the shining goals.

Little by little the good in men Blossoms to beauty for human ken; Little by little the angels see Prophecies better of good to be; Little by little the God of all Lifts the world nearer the pleading call.

FOOTBALLERS' STRIKE
The Warrington Players Refuse to Make Journey to Hull.
GRIEVANCE OVER BONUS.
Special Interviews with Players.

A great sensation was caused in Warrington football circles last night by a strike on the part of the players of the Warrington N.U. Club. As a consequence, the first team will not make the expected trip to Hull to-day, where they should have played Hull Kingston Hovers in the N.U. League. A meeting of the Warrington Club Com- mittee was called, and the attitude of the players was so determined that the committee decided to wire to the Hull Kingston Hovers Committee declaring the match arranged to-day off. Thus a most peculiar situation, seldom, if ever, equalled in the history of football, is created.

"The Examiner" representative was in- formed Officially last night, by Mr. T. P. Brad- shaw, the secretary of the club, that it was correct the players had gone on strike, and that the Hull match had been cancelled, but beyond that he had no further information to give. Although there is absolute silence in official quarters, no doubt the committee have their side of the case, which will, we should say, be placed before a general meeting of the club.
The incident naturally caused much corn- ment amongst the supporters of the club, who got to know of it last evening. The players also discussed the matter amongst themselves.
THE BONUS TROUBLE.

"The Examiner" representative interviewed a number of the players, and they were agreed that the whole trouble arose over the bonus question. " We have had a lot of trouble," said one player, and the others confirmed his 'statement, "over the bonus question during the holiday matches. We think we have been unfairly dealt with in respect to the bonus matter. "When Huddersfield came to Wilderspool last Saturday, they were promised a bonus of XI per head if they managed to defeat War- rington. Instead we beat Huddersfield, and we got no bonus, although we thought we were entitled to one.
"Last Wednesday we offered to meet the com- mittee to discuss the question; but they refused, and this has made our grievance still more acute.

"We waited until now, but as the committee had not met us we decided to .come out, And there will be no match at Hull. We are unani- mous in the matter and are determined in our action." It will be interesting to learn how this action will affect the chances of selections for Austra- lia ,coming Warrington way.

div.head: PASSING WEEK.
div.p: THE PASSING WEEK.

QUITE ENGLISH! , Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., who this week has brought his future wife to Warrington, to intro- duce her to his constituents, has, unfortunately, made it impossible for us to record the fact in a way we should have been pleased to adopt. At a public meeting held in Hamilton-street Schoolroom on Wednesday, he made use of the following sentence, which, in anyone else, would have been deemed most extraordinary: "She asks," he said, " noticing better than that you may say of her, in spite of faults which I must confess I have not detected, that she came an English girl into an English constituency, and that she honestly and seriously strived (and succeeded) not only to win her way into the hearts of the Warrington people," and so ori. As the Member for Warrington has deemed it necessary to put in the foreground the fact that he is bringing an "English" girl to an English constituency, we feel impelled to question whether what we have witnessed this week is altogether according to English ideas. Of course, times are changing rapidly, and old- fashioned customs are giving way to new; but we think it is setting -up a precedent to have the arrival of a bride that is to •be in eight months photographed for reproduction on the cinematograph, and the lady made the centre of a torchlightprocesSion and the fearfiil atten- tions .of that :organisation, the Tariff Reform Bugle Band. The English way up to now. has been to reserve such demonstrations till the 'great 'day. MU perhaps time presses. Mr. Harold Smith may think—without cause, we , can assure hitn--Ithat the longed-for dissolution of Parliament may come this year, and it will be better to get the adVertisement in now. We are, not much concerned with this. We our- selves believe most thoroughly in advertising, and we think it a healthy state of affairs that a man in this country is free to. advertise as he likes, just as he may marry whom he likes—so long as he keeps within the taw. What we •resent, and what the town will resent if we know anything of the town, is that the re- mark about the. "English" girl should have been uside in the, connection and the circum- stances in which it Was made. Names ending in "eaux " are not convincingly English, but, fortunately, there will be no doubt about Miss Furneaux's name being English when it is Mrs. Smith. •

ANOTHER STAGE. But, as Mr. Smith told his audiences, he has reached another stage—the stupid stage. That may account for the manner in which he has missed fire to a great extent in the speeches he has made during his latest visit. 'fines, as we have said, are changing. It is a sign of Tory decadence, we think, when a Member Of PalH liament can soar no higher than to compare the Government of his country to a Co-operative Stores that ,is giving the Empire away with: a pound of tea. Our reporter says there was laughter at' this sally—if there had not been considerable laughter the audience would have been .sadly,neglecting, its duty. But this levity and recklessness conies of the undoubted fact that Mr. Smith belongs to a party that is politic- ally bankrupt and hopelessly outcast—it may be for forty years, as their cheerful leader warns them. It is this hapless plight that causes the plunging we witness. from day to day. Mr. Smith's assertion this week that Mr. Crosfiefil knows "nothing about Ulster or any political question," is :the Tory way—just to say their opponents know nothing and that is an end of .the matter. Assuming that people know noth- ing, they try to delude themselves into the belief that they can say what is the exact opposite of the truth and contentedly await the hazard of an- other election. For instance, Mr. Smith said at Latchford, on Thursday night, that Mr. Lloyd George had never carried out one promise he , had, made. The truth is, of course, that the Tory party have nearly lost their senses because ,Mr. Lloyd George has carried out his promises. If he had failed to do so they would be smiling at him now instead of reviling him. Similarly, they say the Home Rule Bill is an unconstitu- tional measure, when, as a matter of fact, it is demanded, and has been demanded in the only way known to the constitution for a quarter of :a Century by three-fourths of the country con- cerned. It is the "bloody, civil war," which Mr. .Barold Smith foretells if Home Buie be- comes law, that is unconstitutional, even in the threat. But it is patronised for political pur- poses by Mr. Smith's party, and therefore it is right. The sentence quoted is one that does not come trippingly from the tongue; it has a nasty sticking effect about it. That may account for the funereal air which pervaded St. James' Schoolroom on Thursday night, to cast an air of depression over the gathering. It was too bad, so near C- hristmas, but it had to be.

CHEERFULNESS IN ADVERSITY. On the other hand, we learnt from Mr. Smith that the Women's Tariff.fleform. League, which it appears is still the most wonderful body of its kind in the kingdom, have been holding tea meetings during the wrek. It is well They can drink tea ..at. a time when the "great cause " for which they are banded together is having the rough passage it is experiencing. We pub- lish on another page some details of a revolt by the deceived farmers of the country, that is well calculated to make even Warrington Women Tariff Reformers abstain for the time being from tea drinking. The "first constructive plank " of the Unionist party was broken in two by Mr. Bonar Law at Edinburgh, and, one of the pieces stowed away in the party- lumber room. ,During the last few weeks a large section of the party, backed by the farmers, is demand- ing that the two parts of the constructive plank should be brought together and spliced. Naturally the agriculturists are at the front in this demand. They, have no intention of being left .out in the cold when the spoils are distributed: • They have little confidence that the British electorate will ever submit to food taxes, and see that the only chance is to get them through along With taxes for manufac- tured articles. In any case, they have quite made up their minds they will not have what they buy taxed, unless there is a correspond- ing tax on what they sell. They will not put their trust in the electors Voting for a tax on food on its merits. We sham their mistrust..

div.head: Qua GREAT TRADE RECORD.
div.p: Qua GREAT TRADE RECORD.

Not only the farmers, but the 'trade returns are up in. arms against this benighted Opposi- tion. The official figures' for our oversee trade', which are now available for last year for the United Kingdom, show that our imports were £769,033,959, and the exports £525,461,416, an increase of £24.393,328 and £38,237,077 respec- tively over 1912. This is, of course, a record year. The second quarter of the year was the period of greatest activity. The rate ,of pro- gress has somewhat slackened in the last half- ,

year, especially during the last quarter. In -this the ex' ports are only two millions over the correspending .quarter of the previous year, while the imports. have decreased by four millions. • 'lt is, however, impossible ,to form an accurate conception cif the tendency of trade on values only. No doubt the shrinkage in value of imports is in part attributable to change in values:

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL.
The proceedings at the Town Council on Tuesday were not very dignified, taken as a whole. There was four hours' talk, a great deal of which was superfluous. Some impor- tant issues were at stake.

Councillor Pemberton succeeded in getting a committee appointed to take the question of the Bridge in hand, and, if possible, to expedite matters. As there is so keen a division of opinion as to the real facts of the case, the appointment of a committee was a very wise decisiok.
Howard Place was doomed to a fate it does not deserve.

The question as to whether drunkenness pre- vails in the streets was discussed briefly, but with some feeling; and the production of the first District Auditor's report caused a little display of old-time feeling. market Gate im- provements were once more passed in review, and it looks as though the Council were going at last to hustle in view of the injustice that is being done to Buttermarket-street,

div.head: COUNCILLOR OSBOKNE AND COKE.
div.p: COUNCILLOR OSBOKNE AND COKE.

It will be remembered that, at the meeting of the Town Council held last month, Coun- cillor Osborne drew the attention of the mem- bers to a minute of the Gas Committee, having reference to the sale of the surplus stock of coke; and suggested that the best way of accomplishing that object was to offer greater facilities to the ratepayers to get it. At that time a person could not Purchase less than five cwt.—and had to make provision for his own carting at that. Councillor Osborne pointed out that a less quantity should be supplied, and other facilities granted to the ratepayers. The committee have no* decided to retail coke in half-cwt. lots. So far so good. T appears to be in tile question dirnionofeudile.l niver°vi‘ ng, and the suggestion of Councillor Osborne on Tuesday evening was that instead of putting people who live so far away from the source of supply, viz., Longford Gas Works. to such gretit inconvenience by having to go or send for it there, depots should be opened in different parts of the town. We must confess we cannot understand why they committee have not seen their wa_, earlier to make some such provision. This is provided for by every up-to-date distributing agency throughout the country, and might, fit, he undertaken, at an early date, by the Warrington' Corporation. We are quite certain that it would meet the wishes of the ratepayers. with pro-

Brown, a well, ta: and traveller. He died Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, on Sunday, at the comparatively early age of 57 years. He had been in failing health for some time, but his illness took a turn for the worse on Saturday. For close upon 40 years lieliad been connected with the firm of Messrs. He was well known through- out the greater part of Lancashire. Mr Brow was one of the pioneers of short- hand in the district, and for a time taught the system at the evening classes of the Warring- ton Technical School. div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY,
. - affection -entertained towards I 'Thursday.: ,val it may be mentioned that skill., was go in: - -
the St. Helens Mothers' Meeting pays him an annual visit.
Came to Warrington.

- In October, 1892, the benefice of St. Peter's: became vacant and was offered to Mr. Percival by the Rev. H. V. Pigot, now of Grappenhall, but then of St. Paul's, Warrington, and an alternate patron of the living. The offer was accepted, and in December of the same year he was instituted at the Palace, Liverpool, conse- quent upon the late Bishop Ryle being afraid to hold a public institution in Warrington on account of a severe smallpox epidemic from which the town was just recovering. Mr. Per- cival entered upon his work with determination and a grit that has ever since characterised his movements. At his first service it is interesting to observe the collections only amounted to lie. 6d., whilst at the present time that amount is more than doubled, which is very good, con- sidering that it is chiefly a working-class parish. For the first six months he was witliotui any assistance, as there were no funds with which to pay a curate. The work of the parish was in a very backward condition, and there were serious matters to be dealt with at the Sunday School, where there was but a very poor attend- ance, only part of the large room being used. Now, after much sacrifice, there are about 800 children on the books.

The Growth of the Church. The church attendance has grown enormously and the number of communicants, compared with 1892, is three or four fold. ilaving ol- tamed the assistance of a curate, the Men's Bible Class was formed, and has pToved a great success. At the time Mr. Percival came to Warrington the clubroom, in John-street was in the hands of the Corporation, who let the pre- mises to anybody who required them, but, through the kind offices of Mrs. Beamont, it was transferred to St. Peter's Church, Lord Newton kindly giving the freehold to the Vicar and Chum hwardells their successors. A i Mission was mmediately established' under a Church Army officer, where meetings are still held, regularly, and the building has also proved of great use for Sunday School and other Church purposes.

In the first year following Mr. Percival's arrival the Vicarage was built, at a total cost of a little over ,t 1,600. Most of the monaY was in hand for the purpose, but the Vicar raised about £320. He has, through the kindness of friends, been able to inetease his living. During his 21 years' service a new organ has been built in the church at a cost of .t 240 and a church boundary wall, costing a little over £2lO, has been erected.

Exodus to the Suburbs. In the course of an interview with "The Examiner" representative, Mr. Percival .re. marked that as people in his parish improved their status, they' left the district to live in the suburbs, and to keep in touch with them meant a good deal of work. When questioned about church attendance, he said that the increase in the communicants was a great encouragement, and regarding the 'poor attendance on Sunday mornings he said that there were a good many people who had to work late on Saturday nights, and it would be out of all reason to expect them to attend the Sunday morning service. From what he had seen of the churches in Warrington, steady progress had been made, and they had maintained that progress. Mr. Percival was very strong in favour of em- ploying laymen in the Church, and he added that if it was not for help received from this source he would scarcely know what to do.

Friendly Nonconformists. A query as to his general opinion of War- rington elicited the reply that on the whole it was satisfactory. Ile had always looked upon the town as in a fairly satisfactory condition. There was no great antagonism between the various creeds, as was noticeable in other towns, and the political parties were exceptionally clean in the fights. If a speaker on any subject got on a platform he was assured of a good hearing. which certainly was not granted in some other places. Speaking from a very personal point of view, Mr. Percival emphasised the value of/persever- ance in all walks of life. Of course, he said,
(Continued in next column.)

div.head: VICAR'S "COMING OF AGE"—continued.
div.p: VICAR'S "COMING OF AGE"—continued.

there is such a thing as talent, .but the greatest talent of all is perseverance. lie had had to fight his way, but no great obstacles had ever been placed in his path, and this proved one of the foundations upon which his undoubted love for the Church rested. If the Church will so help a poor lad, is it not worth while defending? he queried Bishop's Wife As Organist. He was married in 1881 at Holy Trinity, Cam- bridge, by the Rev. J. Barton, who was assisted by Dr. Maule, the present Bishop of Durliam,i whilst Mrs. Maule, then Miss Elliot, played the Wedding March. It is an interesting fact that this Miss Elliot was a niece of the Miss Elliot who composed the well-known hymn, "Just as I am, without one plea." Mr. Percival has had very serious illnesses, and during one of these the church was man- aged by the Rev. W. Bracecamp, who was at that time the curate at this church. Mr. Per- cival is quite unostentatious, but is deeply devoted to his parishioners, who return their appreciation of his labours. THE ANNIVERSARY SERMON. preaching at his 21st anniversary on Sunday, the Rev. B. Percival took for his text, Ist Epistle to Corinthians xvi. 13, "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be stron..." He said that they stood on the threshold of another year, and all thinking men looked back upon the last year and reviewed it. They took an account of events that had passed, and consid- ered how best to prepare for the future. The government of a country, the management of a business, or the upkeep of a society, could not be succeSsfully carried on without this, and what was applicable to society at large was appli- cable to churches. Having taken that account their motto was in short striking sentences, urging them to "watch, stand fast; to quit themselves like men, and to be strong." A well-known statesman had said the other day that they could not open their papers with- out finding signs of unrest in various walks of life. There could be little doubt that they were living in stirring times, and that there was , great need for watchfulness, constancy, and strength. They might be on the point of a great upheaval, the far-reaching consequences of which no man could foresee, so that there was - much need for prayer. The Church was in danger; there was discredit and, derision within and enemies outside, so that they all needed to stand fast in the faith. Responsibility Realised.

I have been with you 21 years, he proceeded, and I can honestly say I have tried to realise my responsibility. There is no more important office than this of a minister of the gospel, and no man should take upon himself the office unless it is a call from God. During these 21 years I have had much kindness shown towards me on many occasions, and although there have been failures and discouragements, they have been far exceeded by your kindnesses. I can sincerely and honestly say that I have always sought to know the truth and place it before you. Oh! how I have longed to see you grasp it! What joy it has been to me to see the change —the results of your endeavours to walk as ! children of (loch! I thank most heartily all who have very willingly helped me in the various organisations of the church. What could I have done without the assistance of the church ' helpers, Sunday School teachers, district visitors and the Mission workers? I only ask for a con- tinuance of it, and our Motto points out the way in which it should be done:

- . A quick-change taste of weather was experi- enced in Warrington and district early on Tues- day morning. It started with a gale and hail, then came a momentary lull, to be followed by three vivid lightning flashes and two loud thun- der peals. Next it snowed and within another five minutes the moon came out brilliantly. The quick-change trick lasted about 13 minutes. After that there was more snow and wind.

policeman Seeks Damages. ' P.C. Smith, Rixton, at Warrington County Court on •Thursday, claimed ..t.51) as damages for personal injuries he sustained through the alleged negligence of W. Rogerson, horse dealer, Ship-yard Inn, Warrington, or his ser- vants. The officer was cycling between Rixton and Warrington, when, he alleged, he met some loose horses, owned by defendant. While avoiding them, the constable averred, he was knocked down by a Dilator cycle. There would have been no accident, he alleged, but for the presence of the horses. The case was adjourned.

The Fatal Billet. Mr. I. A. Jones, the deputy coroner, aeld an inquiry on Wednesday on John Woolley '35), of 1, Margaret-street, and who was employed by Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. The evidence showed that deceased, during the absence of other workmen, attempted to lift up a t-teel billet. One end of the billet, however, ,Aus locked by other billets resting ,upon it, and when deceased let go, after it haa overpowered him, it sprung back and caught him in the stomach.—The medical evidence showed that death was due to toxic poisoning and gangrene of the intestines, following upon strangulated hernia, and that death was accelerated by the accident.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: Undertaker's Death.
div.p: Undertaker's Death.

Mr. George Platt, who is well known in the Howley district as a boat owner and undertaker, passed away at his residence, Howley-lane, on Sunday morning at the age of 55 years. He leaves a widow and one son. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Thursday.

div.head: St. Barnabas' Church.
div.p: St. Barnabas' Church.

A service, dedicating the beautiful carved oak font cover, presented to St. Barnabas' Church in memory of the late Mrs. Hollingworth, mother of the Vicar, was held on Sunday after- noon. The cover, which is the gift of the Bible Classes and Sunday School scholars, cost £33.

div.head: Warrington Musical Society.
div.p: Warrington Musical Society.

The Warrington Musical Society will give the second subscription concert in the Parr Hall on 29th January. The public ought to give great patronage to the concert, for an excellent pro- gramme is promised. The artistes will be Miss Nellie Anderton, vocalist; Miss Clarice Newall, solo pianist; Mr. Vincent Needham, solo flautist, and there will be a chorus and orchestra of over 200.

div.head: British Women's Temperance Association.
div.p: British Women's Temperance Association.

At the usual monthly meeting of the 8.W.T.A., at Bold-street on Wednesday, Mrs. Owen presiding, the following officers were re- elected: President, Mrs. Owen; vice-presidents, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mrs. Harvey Cooke, Mrs. Moore, Mrs. Moreland, Mrs. Whitmore; treasurer, Mrs. Richard Tanner; corresponding secretary, Mrs. Simpson; recording secretary, Mrs. Clatwoithy. Arrangements were made for a social.

div.head: Indian Mutiny Veteran's Death..
div.p: Indian Mutiny Veteran's Death..

An Indian mutiny 'veteran's funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday, when the late Quartermaster-Sergeant George Knott, of 158, Orford-lane, was laid to rest. He served through the Indian Mutiny as an apprentice apothecary in the Indian Medical Department, and afterwards in the native labour department at Calcutta and Mauritius. Enlisting in the 37th Regiment (now the Ist Battalion of the Hampshires), he transferred later to the per- manent staff of the third Battalion King's Liver- pool, and retired on a pension in 1889. He was 71 years of age. The funeral was of a semi- military character.

div.head: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.
div.p: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

On Thursday the usual monthly special ser- vices were held in the above place of worship. In the afternoon a sermon was preached by Mr. Shimmin, of Manchester, who officiated in tile unavoidable absence of his father, through indisposition. At the close of the service a goodly number sat down to tea, which was kindly given by Mrs. Mills. Later Mr. Shim mm delivered a most interesting address on the work of the Church in the uplifting of the masses. The Rev. A. J. Chessum also spoke on the same subject. Both services were very enjoyable, and were attended by fair congrega- tions. The chair was taken by Mr. B. Bridge, senior chapel steward.

Warrington Photographic Society. A good muster ,of members is always assured on the evening when the A.P. and P.N. prize slides are shown, and Tuesday's meeting proved no exception. Three things contribute in making this exhibition thoroughly pleasing and instructive to experienced workers, as well as beginners—the excellence of the selection, the editorial comments, and the sound condi- tion of the slides. Five were cracked, only slightly, out of 125, a notable state of things when one considers the thousands of miles of "railway polish" they have had, a state worth contrasting with another set shown some weeks ago, where 37 were cracked or wholly smashed out of 100. This is entirely due to difference of packing. The sets of pictures most appre- ciated were those earning the silver plaque for portraiture, the flower studies, and some of the half-dozen by Mr. Hill, of Leek, dealing %%Oh rural scenes. The splendid lamp own,ed by this society scored when the dense olour slides I were thrown, and everyone agreed that the A.P. and P.N. competition. shows no sign of falling off this year.

div.head: Warrington Ragged School and Mission.
div.p: Warrington Ragged School and Mission.

It is gratifying to know that, during the festive season, the poorest children of the town have not -been forgotten, and that various agencies have been at work in endeavours •to make many little hearts happy. Councillor Skelland and his co-workers at the Ragged School have had a very busy time, and their efforts to provide suitable entertainment for the poor children have met with a very generous response. On Boxing Day over 800 children were invited to tea, and, afterwards were given toys and fruit, kindly supplied by the Mayoress, Mrs. James Dodds (the president), "The Daily News and Leader," and others, whose names will appear in the annual report. On Sunday Mrs. Edmund Osborne, in the unavoidable absence of Mrs. Dodds, whcg had generously given shawls and scarves for the children, attended the Mission and gave a very appro- ,priate address. She urged the children to begin the New Year well, and to be honest, truthful and kind. Robert Louis Stevenson put the matter in a nutshell when he said, in " A Christmas Sermon "—a letter he wrote home to his mother—" To be honest, to be kind, to earn a little, and to spend a little less.". She hoped that after making good resolutions they would all do their utmost to carry them out. She afterwards presented the gifts, and the teachers assisted in the distribution to the iCnogu nto cill or children, who showed their appreciation by cheers and clappii", of hands.
