div.head: MILITARY MUSIC.
div.p: MILITARY MUSIC.
Pleasing Visit of the Talented End South
Lancashire Band,
CONCERT TO AID INFIRMARY.

The visit to Warrington of the well-known 1, Band of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, arranged by Major Green, was sig- nalised by a most successful concert in the Hippodrome on Sunday evening, for the benefit of the Infirmary. The enterprising manage- ment of that deserving institution, having enlisted Major Green's help, found ready sup- porters of the idea of an Infirmary concert in Mr. Turpin, the manager of the Hippodrome, through whose kindly offices not only was the , building lent free of charge, but Mr. Turpin's courteous services, and those of his well-con- ducted staff, were placed at the gratis disposal of the organisers of the entertainment. It is gratifying to record that a large audience filled every seat in the building. Although the Military Band's performances may be regarded as the feature of the concert, most welcome variety was given to the pro- gramme by songs, contributed by Miss Marie Houghton, and by the violin solos of Senor Angel Blanco. The fine body of instrumen- talists constituting the hand played four big items with great energy and a display of taste and finish which, if not always irreproachable, served to carry through all concerned with fly- ing colours. The familiar and brilliant "Wil- liam Tell" overture whetted the appetite for the more substantial dishes, ,which took the form of the "Samson and Delilah" fantasia, and the "Peer Gynt" suite, in both of which the various sections of players in turn distin- guished themselves in crisp attack, fine grada- tion of tone volume, and the intelligent phras- ing of passages which might otherwise have been obscure. But the climax of the bands- men's playing was reached in Tschaikowsky's now well-known "1812 Overture," in which, as can well be imagined, executive difficulties are paralleled only by the sheer physical strain involved in getting through this gigantic work. That a fine, and, in many respects, adequate interpretation of it was given, must be frankly admitted, and great credit is incidentally due to Mr. R. E. Cahill, the conductor of the band, for the masterly way in which he pioneered all concerned through the intricacies of the score. The ensemble of the overture was, of course, stupendously resonant, but whether it gained by the bringing in of Such realistic detail as the letting off of firearms is questionable. Tschaikowsky's inclusion in the score of a carillon must be regarded as fully satisfying ' his ideas on the subject. Of Miss Marie Houghton's songs, the one which unquestionably gave most pleasure was • the very appropriate "Nearer, my God, to Thee," which she vocalised with the ease and • grace properly belonging to an artiste trained

under a famous tutor. - Encores being plenti- fully lavished upon the performers during the evening, Miss Houghton had later an oppor- tunity of singing as an "extra" the good old Scotch ballad, "Annie Laurie "—a song which 8116 has recently made her own in the sense that she is frequently associated with it in quite a successful way. The violin solos of Senor Angel Blanco came as an astonishing revelation of finished technique and artistic powers, for which one was scarcely prepared, and, in ex- pressing the unalloyed pleasure with which we listened to Senor Blanco's playing, we may be pardoned expressing the hope of finding further opportunities of confirming the best of opinions we have formed in regard to it. None of Senor Blanco's solos were set down in the programme, so, recognising them as best we may, his " Zigeunerweisen" may he instanced as a splen- did demonstration of this virtuoso's complete command of his instrument, and of his soulful insight into the deepest meanings of the com- posers whose works he essayed. In Senor Blanco's'solos, and in the songs of Miss Hough- ton, Messrs. Osborne and Foster were severally concerned in playing the pianoforte parts, which they did with tasteful restraint, and therefore with good effect. At an interval, Mr. F. A. Frost tendered thanks on behalf of the Infirmary.

div.p: The Late Mrs. Winifred Lawton.

The funeral of Mrs. Winifred Lawton, wife of 11,Ir. Jacob Lawton, saddler, 54, Sankey- street, took place on Wednesday, at the Ceme- tery. She had been in failing health for sev- eral years, and her condition became so serious on Boxing Day that she never recovered, pas- sing away on Sunday morning.

To-morrow at Parish Church: South Lancs. Band to Accompany Service. The fine Band of the South Lancashire Regi- ment will accompany the morning service at the Parish Church to-morrow, Sunday, 10.30. Members of the congregation are requested to be seated early.

The clever pupils of the People's College are to repeat the Concert which was such a success last December in the parr Hall on 29th Janu- ary, in aid of the Infirmary and Nursing Asso- ciation. The annual ball in aid of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children takes place in the Parr Hall on Tuesday, and a brilliant function it promises to prove. Tickets should be secured immediately.

Police Swimming Club Supper. The second annual supper of the Warrington Police Swimming Club was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday evening. The dial]: was occupied by the Chief Constable (Mr. Nicholls). The Chairman said the men were exceedingly zealous in the work, and they had been exceptionally fortunate in gaining a thor- ough knowledge of life-saving methods, whilst a number of them had obtained the proficiency certificate. This year they had done better than ever, and he believed the whole of the men who entered for the examination had Passed, with one exception. The Watch Com- mittee had not yet made it compulsory for the men to learn swimming, but the men had vol- untarily gone in for it with good results. In a town like Warrington, where they had numer- ous waterways, it was really essential that a Police officer should be able to swim. It was impossible to expect the older members.. of the Force to learn, but it was necessary /or all young men to have some knowledge of the i natatory art. It was a great credit to the Force to have achieved such satisfEctory re- sults. (Applause.) The Deputy Mayor (Coun- cillor Dr. Joseph) presented the swimming and other awards as follows Life-saving Society's bronze medallion, Superintendent Wil- liamson, Sergeant Woollacott, and Constables Corbett, Bowles, Morland, Andrews, Skelton and Grubb; medallion and proficiency certifi- cate, Constables Willis and Adcock; honorary instructor's certificate, Sergeant Woodland; proficiency certificate, Constables Bromwich and Cameron: silver medals for recruits' race—

Ist P.C. Ballard, 2nd P.C. Moody, 3rd P.C. Tay- lor. Constable Moody was also presented with a silver medal for best breast stroke in swim- ming. Constable Manson was presented with the Hippodrome Silver Cup for weight-putting, whigh now becomes his absolute property, he having won it three times in succession. Prizes were also presented to the following officers, who recently took part in an ambulance com- petition, held at the Police Station: Ist P.C. Bromwich, 2nd P.C. Rowles, 3111 P.C. Cutler. The Mayor, who arrived late, owing to another appointment, responded to a .toast of his health, proposed by Alderman Bolton, and said that anything in connection with the Police Force in Warrington was most important to him. If there was a department in the Cor- poration in which he took a deep interest it was the work of the Police Force, and he hoped at all times lie would be able to do his duty towards them. Songs were rendered dur- in,, the evening by Sergeant Woodland and P.C. Gibson, wtilst Mr. H. M. Ashton and P.C. Wood contributed humorous items, which were much appreciated. Mr. J. Gibson ably acted as accompanist, and also gave two songs.

div.head: ROUGHING IT IN CANADA.
div.p: ROUGHING IT IN CANADA.
Warringtonlan Wishes He Was
Home Again.
VIVID BUT DISMAL PICTURE.
The following are extracts from a remarkable letter recently received from British Columbia by a Warringtonian from a friend who journeyed to Canada in the early Spring to better himself :
Vancouver, 8.C., December 9th, 1913.

My Dear Friends,—l am certainly a long time in replying to your letter, which, by the way, 1 was glad of. By this reaches you Christmas will be with you. I have no doubt that will recall some pleasant memories. lam not likely to forget the pleasant times We had together, and wish to goodness I was going to have the same this time.

Since writing last I have gone through all kinds of trials and tribulations. For a long time I was out of work and nearly at the end of my tether, when I got a job as grocer's assistant, but "chucked" it up, because it was only 12 dollars a week. I have had reason to regret that many times. Instead of using my own judgment I listened to the advice of so- called friends, with the result that I was soon on the "bum," as they call it here. got a temporary job ultimately as spare polic—nan on the C.P.R. wharves and depots. After that I took charge of about 50 labourers, and escorted them to a railroad construction camp about 750 miles away in Alberta. These men sign a contract with an agent of a Labour , Bureau to work on a camp on the terms of free fare to destination and back at the end of job. With a view to getting free transportation to another province your average labourer takes on the job and clears off at the end of the journey or somewhere en route to a more congenial job or better terms. I don't blame him for that after my experience of railroad camps. But it was my job as " bobby " to try and prevent them going. Well, when. we got there I asked the boss for a job with them, and I worked for a month on the wild prairie and lived in a camp with Russians, Dagos, GaletianS, Germans, and French; in fact, all kinds of nationalities. As for getting their pass back again, it is never the intention of these bosses to give them one; when they get what they want out of them they are fired. As it is impossi,ble to live on the prairie in winter there is no work, and, some- times 60 below zero, these men are soon up against it, and have to go back to the coast as best theY can.

You will have heard of the "Hobo." This is the country where he is manufactured. My brother was fired because he was ill, so he, with severat more Britishers, beat it back to the coast, jumping freight trains and walking some 00 miles. They ultimately arrived here, foot- sore and weary, sometimes lying all night in the rain in a bush with no shelter, or waking next morning with their clothes covered with hoar frost. I was able to get a free pass back, because I demanded it as escort.

div.head: EXERTION TO MAKE HEART AND BRAIN
div.p: EXERTION TO MAKE HEART AND BRAIN
BURST.

What a 11— of a country it is. Believe me, I could write a big book on it, and I am only a greenhorn. That month's work in the camp was not very good. I was given work that nearly made my heart and brain burst through exertion. Then the cold snaps came on in the nights and mornings. We were laying 40 miles of new railroad, following the Pioneer, an in- vention of the Devil that lays the track and runs over it. They speed the thing up to the top limit of men's strength; consequently wen are dropping out or getting fired every day. The prairie is monotonous, grand and inter- esting all in a day. The sunrises and sunsets are a thing to wonder at. The Rocky Moun- tains were about 90 miles from us and did not look more than five miles would look in Eng- land. Most of them are covered with snow even in summer; in the autumn it is a beautiful sight to see the migration of wild geese going south for the winter. At night time you hear the blood-curdling howls of ,the coyoote. I saw several; they are much like a collie dog. Since getting back to the coast I have not done badly. I went to another construction camp, across the water this time, and worked on the sea coast. We got wet through every day here, so had to quit it. I then got a week or two's work as bobby," and since have had casual work at the docks as longshoreman. This is a well-paid job, but you can only get one or two days occasionally. I got six dollars for 13 hours' work last Saturday. I next got a job looking after a train to Calvary, Alberta, taking care of some stoves in the cars so that the com- modities would not get frozen. I was away a week, and what sleep I got was inside a con- ductor's van or caboose; so I did not get to bed for a week. Anyhow, I got 25 dollars for that, and this was some consolation. It is very cold in the mountains. I got my nose and ears nipped many times on the jour- ney. To see the mountains from a caboose is a sight never to be forgotten. The engine seeto to wind in and out like a huge snake going down and up a winding staircase. I should think there is no sight in the world to equal a train ride through the Rockies. This is my fifth time through them.

NOT BRITISH, BUT ASIATIC COLUMBIA. Vancouver is an exceedingly wet place in win h- ter. It is worse than Manchester. It is, ow- to get out several times. I ever, a beautiful place in summer a er job as Ihavetried gordinary i tow aChina,get tutt ten dollars foundth aat,mboeni being " 1 aseagmreaen to sail less than the others, so I says Nothing doing passage to Australia, I have but tried e do t thaoa dw‘ak chal my chance yet,ha t butth sI will countryd o s if I ,a I m convinced s , absolutely no good. I have been a trier all the time and have done 1 jobs that I could not have (treamed of doing in the Old Country. I have worked alongside the scum of the earth, desperate men that think nothing of a man's life. The distress is terrible and y-ou can see men of fine physique glad to beg five cents; see them as I saw them on the journey to Alberta, hundreds, not ones, making their- way back to the coast, absolutely up against it, tramping hundreds of miles. I cannot see that I shall ever want to bring my dear wife and children here, so intend to get all I can, and get back at somebody's ex- pense; that is, if my health keeps good, which, I am thankful to say, up to now it has. It is not British Columbia at all; Asiatic. Columbia would be a more appropriate name. Vancouver has its China town, Jap town, and Itindoo district. Dagos there are in thousands, and many of all nationalities; as a matter of fact, an Englishman is very unpopular. I don't know why. I can tell you for a fact of dwells of cases where men have been refused jobs because they were Englishmen. Tell my respected friend, Hit. that I have made a virtue of necessity and have become a total abstainer, at the same time my best wishes. Tell , him this is a Godless country, too licked even for an Atheist. It makes my heart ache when think of the good, civilised people in the Old Country. and contrast them with the types of this, and when I think of you going to refresh with good, honest, English cheer. Well, goodbye, owd for, I won't come back beaten. "A merry Christmas and a happy New Year" is the sincere wish to you and all in Warrington.
[We publish a letter from a Lymm man in Toronto under our Lymm heading.—Enrroz4

div.head: STRIKES AND POLITICS.
div.p: STRIKES AND POLITICS.
"Labor Omnla Vinclt " and Mr. Chas. Dikes.
LABOUR CANDIDATE QUESTION.
TO THE EDITOR OF " THE lISAMINFAt."_

Sir,—Perhaps your readers are thankful to Mr. Dukes for having made known the fact that I am "troubled with a bad liver," that I make "concealed thrusts," that I have my "back scratched by men of avowed opposition to the workers," that I "lack that ultra-necessary quality known as bowels—some persons term this thick-skinned—and that it is as "well that we reflect on the interests for which he is pros- tituting his pen, &c. Lc. And he also does not forget to slip in a good word or two for himself whilst on the job. All that may be interesting, but it is quite beside the mark. The value of this controversy does not rely upon my qualities or otherwise, but upon Mr. Dukes. lam unlike Mr. Dukes. I happen to be an ordinary nonentity, as the comedian would say, "one of the lads." Therefore 'Mr. Dukes displays a fatal lack of sagacity by wasting at least two- thirds of his space upon dressing me—that is nothing—down. Does Mr. Dukes really appre- ciate the fact that I am not responsible to any- one, not even the back scratchers, and that he holds a very important position, and no amount of attack upon myself alters the case? But recognising the interests that I serve, I will deal with something more substantial. I believe that Mr. Dukes' utterances are the re- sult of his own circumstances, rather than the circumstances of the working class; and Mr. Dukes knows that I am not the only one who shares that belief. _ _ _ _

I put it to Mr. Dukes and ask him what would be think if our positions were reversed: If I had been mainly instrumental in persuad- ing a flourishing organisation to change its name and constitution as a protest against the in- activities of the Labour party in the House of Commons. Will lie deny that he was mainly instrumental in getting the old I.L.P. to secede from the national body as a protest against the, as Mr. Dukes then put it, job-conscious Labour Member of Parliament? Was he not sent as a delegate to Manchester to represent some of the local Socialists at the inauguration of the Brit- ish Socialist party, which party was a strictly anti-Labour party? AT what would Mr. Dukes think of me had I stood at street corners by the hundred and on platforms by the score, with the "Syndicalist" contents bill displayed on many occasions, and gathered working men into the Gasworkers and General Labourers' Union by the thousand with the strike gospel? Certainly in these days of Liberalism and Toryism he has not got them in by preaching political action. Will Mr. Dukes deny that his favourite shib- boleths used to be, " That we must knock h—l out of capitalism by wrecking the capitalist state with strikes as big as we could get them," and also "It was ridiculous to go to Parliament for better conditions of labour, for—mark this— the wages question was in the workshop, and would have to be fought out there"? I know there are scores of persons who got utterly sick of hearing Mr. Dukes use this phrase, who can substantiate what I say as the truth. Was not his chief contention during our con- troversy some fteen months ago the proposition that Labour could be monopolised. and that my alternative proposal was that it was the ownership of the source of wealth that mattered and not the monopolisation of Labour power? I remember deliberately attacking strikes pur- posely to bring Mr. Dukes out in public con- troversy upon that particular subject. Cer- tainly the argumentative point was not political action, which Mr. Dukes now tries to make as believe lie never opposed. These statements are upon a level with what Mr. Dukes has to say about my gross perver- sions of his speech at the Freedom and Fellow- ship Rooms. Perhaps alongside this letter I will manage to get some kind of substantiation or otherwise of my report of Mr. Dukes' speech from that source'. His statement that he did not say strikes had failed, or words to that effect, is like his assertion that he never opposed political action. I put it to Mr. Dukes again that if he never opposed political action, and does not now say that strikes have failed, why did he not then make it perfectly clear there when one of the speakers, who knows him per- fectly well, said he could hardly believe it was Mr. Dukes that was talking? If there was not any change of opinion why such a drastic re- mark?

Upon the public platform or in "The Examiner" Mr. Dukes tells us that he does not believe in hero worship, and then in private conversation says something different. Does Mr. Dukes re- member the time and place that he furtively whispered into my simple ear that he had begun to believe there was "something in" the "big man" theory.

If these inverted statements are correct—and I ask Mr. Dukes to believe these are the impres- sions he has given to me and many others— what conclusion can we come to other than that Mr. Dukes is more influenced by his own cir- cumstances than the general circumstances of the whole of the working class? It is quite natural. Three years ago Mr. Dukes started upon the very difficult task of organising the lowest strata in society, the unskilled labour. What is more natural than for anyone to choose their choicest arguments for that purpose? How many times have I heard Mr. Dukes tell the crowd that Labour was the only source of wealth and that the reason why the workers did not get their fair share of the wealth was because the workers had not sufficient sense to organise their labour power? Now Mr. Dukes has got the men into his union he has no need for those specious arguments, and is advocating a fresh line of business. I am going to ask Mr. Dukes a very delicate question. Has he never been approached with the proposition that he should stand as Labour candidate? If Mr. Dukes can bring evidence to prove that my surmise is wrong I will withdra4 my impu- tation and apologise. L certainly think that through Mr. Dukes' letter he owes me an apology.

LABOR OIENIA VINCIT. P.S.—As Mr. Dukes said my first letter was a " perversion:* I have written to the authprities of the meeting to which I referred, and hold a letter saying in reply that my version of what Mr. Dukes said is "substantially correct."

Warrington A.C. had a nice pack running over seven miles of mixed country. Hanson moved grandly and led the way home, with Vose in attendance; then came Boltonaollowed by Jep- son and Shadwell. Gregson, who started several minutes after the pack, came through at a nice pace.

div.head: New Type of Insurance Card.
div.p: A New Type of Insurance Card.

Councillor Dr. -Josepl. presided at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Insurance Com- mittee on Thursday evening. Referring to a conference in London which he and the Clerk attended, the Chairman said that a scheme was 'considered for simplifying the administration of medical benefit. It was decided to distri- bute a new form of card.—The Clerk said that the cards would be posted to each insured per- son in 14 days.—The new' card will take the place of the old .red medical ticket It will enable insured persons to get a doctor in any town, without any trouble. It would do away with the old temporary green voucher. The benefit of the new cards will be felt more so by those removing from town to town.

Death of Viscount Cross. Lord Cross, who was chiefly famed because he was the man who defeated Gladstone in South-West Lancashire, and which result had a good deal to do with him being later elevated to the peerage, died on Thursday. He had at one time a close connection with Warrington, and in 1852 married Georgiana, daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Lyon, of Appleton Hall. He was, in his early day?. einployed at the Old Bank, Warrington, under Kr. Barn It nas .he who opened the Infirmary in 1877. He is. ' succeeded by the Hon. J. E. Cross, of nigh Legh, and another son is the Hon. and Her. C. F. Cross, Vicar of Stratton.

STOeKTON HEATH.
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.
There are careless "Heathens." They litter the streets with paper. Fried fish consumers are said To be the worst class of offenders. Councillor Westbrook has a very drastic cure.

He would make the people eat the paper Along with the fish and chips bought. In the olden days there was a fool Called "The Lord of Misrule," who Made a tax collector eat the parchment Upon which the taxes were set forth. The Heath evidently wants such a person To niake fish and .chippers eat the paper. The Heath seems very, healthy just now. The disinfectors have not had to wGrk For well over two months—soft job. This means the absence of infectious disease. If we could keep that away it would pay "Heathens" to pension the disinfecting man. A new terror is threatened the Heath. „A threat is"made that meetings should be held In 'Victoria-square to stir up an agitation To force the Parish Council to provide allot- ments. Politics are bad enough, but Alexandra-road is to get two new lamps. So the Parochial Committee have generously 'decided. Is it because the Parish Meeting is coming near?
Which clock keeps the accurate time In the Heath? • The Square timepiece, the tramway clock, and The Church clock disagree by five minutes. Greenwich time is pvidently quite unknown.
A Light Subjeot.—On the recoMmemlation of the Lighting Committee of the Parish Council, two new lamps are to be erected in Alexandra- road and one in Orchard-street.
The Healthy Village.—At the Parochial Com- mittee on Tuesday it was stated that no disin- fection had been required in the village since October last.
Late Mr. G. Brown.—We regret to announce the death of Mr. George J. Brown, a well-known resident. An appreciation and account of the funeral will be found on another page.

Liberal M eet i ng.—Liberals are showing much activity in the district, and part of their cam- paign includes a mass meeting, to be held in the Hall Cafe on Tuesday evening at 7.45. The chief speaker will be Sir W. P. Ryles, M.P., who will have something interesting to say. Mr. P. M. Oliver Will also speak, and Councillor H. Roberts will be chairman.
"Quite Time."—Councillor Dukes was rather indignant over Derby-road alterations at the

‘. _ . Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday. lie thought if the work was not got on with, they .'"?-••`-'•.',:,!,•• ought to withdraw the contract. The Chair- -4 - man said the matter would be seen to, where- upon Councillor Dukes retorted "It is quite •,,ii: time." ,

Medicine Depot Wanted.—At the Parish Coun- cil meeting on •Tuesday the question of Dr: Barr, of Stretton, having a surgery in the vil- lage was discussed, the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians having written about such a concession. It was explained that it was not so much as a surgery that was needed, but somewhere where medicine could be left, and it was ,decided to write to the Guardians to that effect.

Light That Failed.—lt was stated at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday that there had been an improvement in the regular lighting of the street lamps, although it was stated that the lamps were lighted early enough but the light was blown out many times. One member said th6t the lights in some lamps had been out most of the night, and this was a serious loss.

Untidy " Heathens."—Why don't " Heathens" use the waste paper receptacles placed on the lamp-posts? Careless people are vexing the members of the Parochial Committee, and on Tuesday it was suggested that some public re- quest be made to the people to use the baskets.— Councillor Westbrook said that fried fish eaters who threw the paper about the streets should he made to consume the paper with their fish.

Had Enough of the Village.—ln regard to the proposal to erect a public convenience in West- avenue, the Clerk reported at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday that Mr. George Norman had intimated that the tenants would object to a public convenience being placed near Victoria-square. He was unable to assist the Committee in the matter.—Councillor Pearson, chairman of the Sanitary Committee, said he had seen several of the tenants, and at the Bon Marche he was told it would be very objection- able to have their back premises used in the way suggested. The adjoining shop, where the Parr's Bank used to be, was shut up, and Mr. Shaw, the butcher, said it did not matter to him whether the Council did it or not, as he was leaving Stockton Heath, because he had had enough of it." The tenants seemed unanimous that they did not want the convenience there.— The matter was referred'back to the Sanitary Works Committee, for them to see if any other site could be found.
ot

The Bridge Again.—The Swing Bridge delays were again Tnentioned at the Parochial Com- mittee meeting on Tuesday. The Clerk said that the Ship Canal Company had acknowledged the Committee's resolution, but he did not know whether they had acted on it or not.— Councillor Clarke: I think not.—The Clerk: They simply acknowledge the letter and say the matter will have attention.—Councillor Clarke: If we don't get a proper reply in a reasonable course of time, say, before the next meeting, we should press the matter. I don't think Stock-. ton Heath and Cheshire people should be kept waiting for an unreasonable length of time. How a man can tell, in the dark, whether the bridge is a 32nd of an inch out of place I don't know, but that is what they seem to be endeav- ouring to do.—The Chairman': The Clerk 'rill Probably hear something before the next meet- ing.

COUNCIL OF MANY SUBJECTS.
Result—A Long Discussion and Nothing Definitely Decided.

div.head: INQUIRY COMMITTEES APPOINTED.
div.p: INQUIRY COMMITTEES APPOINTED.

Councillor Whitley presided at the Parish Council meeting on Tuesday. Several matters of importance were discussed, but nothing definitely was decided in regard to recreation grounds, allotments, or the library, except that committees were appointed.
RECREATION GROUNDS AND ALLOT-

div.head: MEN TS.
div.p: MEN TS.
The first resolution discussed was that apper- taining to the question of recreation grounds and allotments.

Councillor Dukes said he thought the feeling of a previous meeting was that the matter should be gone into fully. He thought a com- mittee ought to be appointed to seek Suitable Sites and report. They could then discuss the matter with more certainty. - Councillor Westbrook: We were prepared to entertain applications from ratepayers for allot- ments, but none came. No one wanted allot- ments in Stockton Heath. Councillor Dukes: We are here to create a desire. Councillor Westbrook : Not that. Councillor hose: To satisfy a demand. Councillor Dukes: I say to create a desire.

div.head: " Tactics of a Quack Doctor."
div.p: " Tactics of a Quack Doctor."
Councillor Westbrook: I object to that. It is the tactics of a quack doctor, who makes you think you ail from something of which you do not know. Councillor Dukes: We know there is an ail- ment. .

Councillor Westbrook: No. You are appoint- ing-a committee to inquire. I say there is un demand for allotments. Councillor McDermid : If we find 'it demand we are bound to proceed with the matter. Councillor Westbrook : I don't _think it is within our province to tell a man he ought to have an allotment. We are here to supply a demand, but the demand must make itself felt, and be a natural one.. I think it is a waste of time, and I refuse to serve on any committee with regard to allotments. The Chairman: Applicants could apply to the Parish Council.

To Agitate. Councillor Dukes: But a lot of people don't understand they can obtain these things. If someone were to get in the Square and tell them what they could have, people would object to them asking for what they were entitled to get. If it were made known that allotments could be had at a certain rental we should have plenty of applicaions. Let them know the full de- tails. The only allotment gardens in the village had gone. Councillor Westbrook: Where were they? Councillor Dukes: The square behind Old London-road or Chapel-lane. The Chairman: Are you aware they are giving them up, because they are worked at a loss? Councillor Dukes: If we cannot have them one way we will have them another way. Councillor Rose: Do you -Mean agitate? Councillor Dukes: Yes; if we have to have an agitation before we get them. Councillor Rose: You would create a demand? Councillor Dukes: Yes, if necessary. Councillor Rose: You had better ask the Village if they want a demand creating. Councillor Dukes: Why not? . •

- Councillor McDermid agreed to the appoint- ment of a committee. Why not meet the de- mand if there was one. The committee could supply all information to applicants. Councillor Dukes: That is all I have asked for. I do hot ask the Council to commit them-
selves. Councillor Rose _wished there was a demand
for allotments, and healthy exercise and recrea- tion. If anyone created an artificial demand,

it would be a great mistake, for it would cause considerable trouble, instead of giving an advan- tage to the people. Councillor Hallows was of the opinion that they should get to know who wanted allotments. He would like to see men working more in their ,gardens. Councillor I.lcDermid: The absence of appli- cants is due to lack of information . The committee appointed was: Councillors McDermid, Dukes, Bose and Pearson, with the Chairman.

div.head: PARISH COUNCIL OR PAROCHIAL
div.p: PARISH COUNCIL OR PAROCHIAL
COMMITTEE?

A discussion then took place on the idea raised by Councillor Bottomley at the Parish Meeting that the Parish Council ought to deal with such matters as they were competent to deal with by law, instead of by the Parochial Committee. Councillor Pearson said it was like Tweedle- dum and Tweedledee, for there seemed no differ- ence in i,t. The Parochial Committee had worked well since 1895, when he first became a member. There would be no advantage in Councillor Bottomley's suggestion. The Clerk (Mr. Bradshaw) said the resolution was: " That a committee of the Parish Council be appointed to deal with such matters for which the Council have authority, instead of delegating their powers to the Parochial Com- mittee. Councillor Westbrook pointed out the incon- veniences of such a step. They Nvo-ald not be able to deal with streets and sanitary matters. The advantages of the Parochial Committee were many. The idea would he a retrograde movement instead of one of progress. He moved that the resolution be not entertained. Councillor Clarke seconded. This was agreed to, and it was also decided that Mr. Bradshaw, the Clerk to the Parish Council, attend the Parochial Committee meet- ings. Councillor Bottoniley was absent.

LIBRARY AND NEWSROOM. The provision of a Library and Newsroom was next discuss(xl. The Clerk explained that the Council had power to adopt the Public Libraries Act and expend one penny in the Councillor Rose: £7O per year. Councillor Dukes: This is another matter for a Committee. • Councillor Rose said he would object to the cost of the newsroom and the providing of fic- tion. News was cheap, and fiction was too cheap. It was the really good books that were wanted. He would advocate that if they got a Library and Newsroom the people should be provided with a study ticket for the Warrington Library. He was of the opinion that they did not want a newsroom. It was suggested that a cottage could he used for a newsroom, and also that a room in the schoolawould be useful. Councillor Westbrook referred to the recreation grounds, and asked why could not the children play in the playgrounds of the schools, although tliat would not do for the youths who wished to play cricket and football. Councillor /Dukes agreed with that idea. Councillor Westbrook agreed to the appoint- ment of a committee to go into the question of Library and Newsroom.
The Committee appointed was: Councillors Whitley, Mclntyre, C. Hallows, Rose and Bottomley.

div.head: COTTAGES FOR THE WORKERS.
div.p: COTTAGES FOR THE WORKERS.
An Investigation to be Made as to the
Need.

div.head: DUTY OF PUBLIC BODIES.
div.p: DUTY OF PUBLIC BODIES.

The question of the provision, of working men's dwellings was raised by Councillor Dukes at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday. Councillor Dukes said he did riot know of any empty houses in the Village, but •Councilloi Whitley said there were 19. At the conclusion of a lengthy discussion it was decided that full investigation be made by the Clerk and the Staveyor. Councillor G. Pilling presided and there were also present Councillors Westbrook, Whitley, Dukes, McDermid, Warburton, J. Hallows, C. Hallows, Pearson, Mclntyre, and F. Rose; with Mr. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. S. Wright (sur- vey:or). /

The resolution proposed by Councillor Dukes was: ",That, owing to the scarcity of cottage property, the parish should seek powers to erect a number of workmen's dwellings." ' Councillor Dukes said that in bringing that matter before the Council he thought they would agree with him that they appeared to have reached a stage where eyery public body would be compelled to consider the housing question, and he thought, without going into statistics or anything of that kind, it was com- mon knowledge that desirable tenants in Stock- tot Heath were unable to obtain houses or move out of those they occupied to seek places where they could have better accommodation, and which would be more suitable to :their rtwire- ments. He thought it was true to say that there could not be any empty houses in Stockton Heath.

div.head: UNIQUE. _OPPORTUNITY.
div.p: A UNIQUE. _OPPORTUNITY.

There might possibly be an odd one, but he did not know of any, and Ile had had a look round. From the standpoint of necessity the subject needed little or no argument that there was a need for working men's dwellings. When he said that, he did not of necessity mean the kind of dwelling usually put up at the lowest possible rental, or the least provision of accom- modation, but on the semi-detached principle. He thought tlieY had a 'unique-opportunity at the moment—seeing that the Speculative builder seemed to have left that field of speculation, owing to causes with which, he thought, they were all conversant. The builders said they could not obtain a return on 'capital, and, on the other hand, they said it was reasonable in remuneration, but there was an uncertainty as to whether they would be interfered with at a later date. . -

The cominittee did not approach subjects of that kind from the Standpoint of the specula- tive builder, or the private property owner. They were confronted with a different problem altogether. They were met with the difficulty that there were requirements, and they had powers to meet those requirements, and whether it be. remunerative or otherwise,- they were, in duty bound, compelled to make the necessary provision.

TO SET AN EXAMPLE. Whether it be profitable or not, he did not want to argue, but they stood in a different posi- tion to those public, authorities where in• many cases they were compelled to deal with slum areas, and of necessity had to take on expensive schemes lor removing property. They- Isere in a position to undertake the provision of houses Stockton. Heath in the best way which wotild set an example for buihhrs to take, after their venture. There were opportunities in the village for the acquirement of lam!, whiich would ^mable them to build an ideal cottage, and be said advisedly that the time had passed to leate the matter to speculative enterprise. Whether bqilders had designedly ceased building or not—true it was that they had not made the necessary pro- vision they had in the past—he did not think that should stand in the way of public bodies malting more adequate provision for the inhabi- tants.

In Stockton heath i there were many desirable people who would be prepared to pay a reason- able rental—which would be sufficient to com- pensate the committee for their capital outlay— and who were only too anxious to take advantage of reasonable cottage dwellings built on semi- detached principles. Ile• was not merely ad•.-o- eating the scheme from the standpoint of build- ing long rows of houses as in the past. •

div.head: PROVIDE DESIRABLE DWELLINGS.
div.p: PROVIDE DESIRABLE DWELLINGS.

_ —.....--_ Tie thought Parish and Urban District Coun- cils should take the opportunity-, for they had not the difficulties to contend with as others had in congested areas. Ile would rather they main- tained an open mind on the question and re- quest that they should be provided with infor- mation as td the 'cost of providing desirable dwellings on the lines he had hinted, and that they should have a statement from the architect as to a probable rental, and what provision they could make. After that they-could show that there were sufficient people, prepared to take the places as tenants, and they would have a sure ground on which to base their scheme. div.head: LATE REV. T. S. TOFTS.
div.p: THE LATE REV. T. S. TOFTS.
Funeral at St. Thomas's Church.
LATE VICAR LAID TO REST.

The funeral of the late Rev. Thomas Sinclair Tofts, whose death was reported in last Satur- day's "Examiner," took place at St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday. The reverend gentleman was formerly Vicar of St. Thomas's, but at the time of his death he was living with his sister at 3, Barrfield-road, Pendleton, Manchester. Ho was 64 years of age, and death was due to pneumonia. The coffin was borne from Manchester in a motor hearse, and the mourners also came in motors. A service in the Church was conducted by the Revs. F. Molyneux (amber Bridge), J. H. Collins, H. V. Pigott and E. W. Clarke, and the hymn "On the Resurrection morning" was sung by the full choir and congregation. Mr. F. Rose was at the organ. The chief mourners were: Miss Tofts (sister), Dr. Snape, Mr. J. Hall and Mr. G. Shaw (Pen- dleton), Mr. and Mrs. Hulme, Mrs. Ward and Mr. J. Warburton (Manchester).

, Amongst those present in the church and at the graveside were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. H. I. Wynne Jones, Mr. Henry Greensll, Mr. V. B. Davies, Alr, L. G. Davies, Mr. W. Mclntyre, Mr. A. Down, Mr. J. J. Whitley, Mr. J. Hallows, Mr. J. Whitley, Mr. W. Seward, Mr. C. 11. Hughes, Mr. William Speed, Mr. J. 'Tobin, Mr. F. Tim- Perley, Mr. H. Johnson.

div.p: Floral Tributes.

Wood (Irlam-o'-tle-Heights), "Sally and Nellie," and Arthur Jes Sop.

div.head: INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHOIR Carry Away the Chief Trophy From Manchester Eisteddfod'.
div.p: INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHOIR Carry Away the Chief Trophy From Manchester Eisteddfod'.

As briefly announced in our last issue, the choir of the Independent Methodist Church, of Stockton Heath, returned from the Manchester Eisteddfod on New Year's Day, jubilant at hay- ing won the chief trophy. To win a prize for choral singing among a people so famous for harmony as are the Welsh, is no small achieve- ment, and the choir have received many con- gratulations.
We are able to give a picture of the trophy, which bears the inscription, "Manchester Eis- teddfod, Fischer Challenge Cup."

The occasion was a happy one, and was adorned -by the presence of the Lord Mayor of Manchester'. The adjudicator;'Mr.'T. Carring- ton, in giving the award, spoke in very con- gratulatory terms of the winning choir. They were commended for good attack and fine ;lend- ing. Undoubtedly, said Mr. Carrington, they had won the prize, and their singing had been. most pleasant to listen to. Other points of corn-, mendation were the fine control in which the voices were held, and correct reading. Special praise was given to the perfect blending of voices, a quartet effect being perfectly attained. A prize of .k.. 5 accompanied the challenge cup. A Kindly Act.—There was a good attendance on Thursday evening at St.. Thomas' Band of Hope, ,when a very interesting address was given on "Missions " by Mr. Whiteman. During the evening the secretary. Mr: Starmard. read letter i received from the Children's Dome at Dutton, in response to Christmas cards and letters' sent by the members directed personally to each boy anal e4,d en Chri.tnips Day. Many of the letters" received from Detton, were very, well, written and most interesting, and all ex- pressed thanks for the letters and cards.—Mr, Hallows said the sending of those cards and letters to cheer their little ftiords or CltriQtme morning made the-, missimmyios for God and followers in part of those ',011,. men and women who, as Mr. Whiteman had told them, left home and comforts for others.

div.head: 'HIGH LEG H.
div.p: 'HIGH LEG H.

The Presents Ship.—The High Legh Schenb: room was prettily decorated on Saturday on the occasion of Colonel Legh's annual treat to the scholars of both the day and the Sunday schools. The conventional Christmas tree was suPerseded, and in its place stood a large deco- rated ship with a cargo of presents. An excel- lent tea was served, after which 'Colonel Legh distributed his prizes to the winners of the educational examination, which was held last month. The following were the successful scholars :—Best in the school: 1, •Alice Bernd; 2, George Bend. Best girl: 1, Alice Cooper; Myrtle Atkinson. Best boy: 1. Harold Porter; 2, John Wardell. The Colonel spoke in high terms of the ,excellence of the papers, and urged the losers to persevere. The Rev. E. 11. Edwards then distributed the presents from the ship to the scholars.

div.p: RISLEY.

Mr. George Holmes occupied the chair. Mr. William Hughes gave a helqui ad- dress. Miss Gertie Hughes presided .at the piano.

div.head: I_AYMM.
div.p: I_AYMM.
LIRERAL PARTY POLICY.
Air. ()User Expounds the Four Great Principles.
W EAK NESS OF PREFERENCE.

There was much enthusiasm amongst the audience assembled in the Eagle Brow Primi- tive Methodist Schools, Lymm, on Tuesday even- ing, to hear an address upon- "Liberal Princi- ples." by Mr. P. M. Oliver, the prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division. Mr. D. Daniels, vice-chairman of the Lymin Liberal A ssociation, presided.

_ Mr. Opyxa said that such a subject as he pro- posed to take could only be dealt with in a cur- sory manner, for it would take a very long tiuli to go into detail. His idea was to take some of the main principles of Liberalism, and then apply them to certain modern day topics, and to do so he would :take the four great phases of Imperial, foreign, constitutional and social politics. It was said that .Imperial politics should be aboVe party, politics. He really did not believe that anything could be above party politics, if politics were not looked upon as a. game. Liberals must try to secure an Empire on lines of absolute self-control; they had tried and had done that with considerable success in South Africa, and they intended to do very much the: same thing in regard to Rome Rule. They believed that the principle they were applying to South Africa would be equally efficacious if applied to Ireland. It would be the remedy for the religious bigotry that existed in Ireland, as it would turn people's attention to problems nearer home. THE QUESTION OF PREFERENCE.

They found the Conservatives advocating a system of Imperial preference—a preference to Canada, Australia, . New Zealand and South Africa. This was a system :that would only benefit certain sections in those colonies, and would perhaps set up jealousy. They would establish vested interests in the Empire, a thing Liberals had fought, and were still fighting against. They were finding it hard, enough to put down vested interests in England. and it would be a-greater danger if they allowed them to grow up within the Empire. The Liberal had a great ideal to stand for, and they ought to pay it a little more attention than they seemed to do. The foreign policy of tlit Liberals should be that Englishmen should re- tain their nationality and live at peace with all men. -

England being an island State, needed a very much larger navy than any other Power, and they had set down a limit of a 60 percent. super- iority. ..They must have an all-efficient navy to protect them, but further than that, they did not wish to go. We had vested interests in war a nil peace on account of the armament firms beingnot only national but international con- cerns. and the evil being infbrnational, the remedy also should be international. He sug- gested a naval holiday to he arranged between England and Germany, and it would then be an easy mattter to arange a naval holiday amongst the other great Powers.

FOR POPULAR GOVERNMENT. • s, With regard to the Liberal Constitutional policy, they had always stood for popular gov- ernment. It was the Liberals, or rather their predecessors, the Whigs, who really got through he Reform Bill of l8:12, and now the Liberals. if they followed their principles, would' extend the suffrage to both men and women. This was bound to 'Come soemer or later. The plural voter was going, and so was the House of Lords before, very long, and it was rather important it this time that they should ..consider what they were going to do with the Second Chamber. It was very easy to criticise the House of Lords, but to reconstruct it was rather more difficult. The Second Chamber as it at present existed was an altogether impossible institn- i4scili told lotitothe needs of the country. Mr. them that any reform of the Second Chamber would be a democratic reform. that .would be established ,On a ,popular basis. What was the popular basis to be? There was one suggestion of larger constituencies .for the election of the revising Chamber, but be thought the :most effective would be the scheme of a Second Chamber Chosen from such societies as trade unions, employers' federations, friendly societies, scientific societies chambers of com- merce. rural district councils, &c., &c 4 How- ever. whatever was decided upon, the Liberals would not be satisfied unless there was direct representation from the workers.., THE SOCIAL POLICY. Then there was the social policy of their Parl)". They were trying to set up a minimum standard among the people, a standard of health, of housing, and in some trades of wages. and here were some people who faltered by the wayside, and who said the Liberals were de- parting from their old traditions. But Liberals must move on, if they did'n't they would be no better than the Conservatives. lie maintained that the traditions of Liberalism were being carried on effectively.

div.head: LINES FROM LYMM.
div.p: LINES FROM LYMM.

Politics have been in the air., The Liberals are going strong. Two meetings within eight days Is a prOly fair record., Seasonable festivities linger on. The "I:nuts" are busy at dances, The a liddle-aged at whist, The aged are enjoying themselves all round. The lirobell clanged on Wednesday. Folk rushed to "the blazes." , They were disappointed, pe'rhaps pleasantly. There was no conflagration at all. The bell rang to test the efficiency Of, the liremen—they were all right.

Death of Mr. Frederick Holt.—Wo regret to announce the death of Mr. Frederick Holt, which occurred at his residence in Pepper- street, Lymni, on Thursday. He was the owner of a considerable amount of property in the district, and was a well-known personality in the village. Testing Firemen.—The ringing of the firebell shortly after seven o'clock on Wednesday even- ing was productive of the usual excitement that attends such occasions, but investigation elicited the. fact that it was only a .false alarm to test the efficiency of the, brigade. The engine was promptly taken out and a practice held at Camsley.

Lymm Liberals.—.A meeting of Liberals will be held ,on Tuesday in Hirst's Pavilion at 8.15 t't:c elect representatives to the 'Central Council. Still Festive.—The festivities are dying hard, as is evinced by the parties, of both a public and private nature,, being held in the locality, :ind generous hosts are putting forth their best endeavours to give guests a happy time. On Tuesday evening Mr. and Mrs. W. G. Groves -ntertained the members of the Newfield Girls' Sewing 'Class. Free Church Services.---The annual series of levOtional services held under the auspices of the Lymm Free. Church Council have, taken dace at the Primitive Methodist Church during this week. On Sunday night a united com- munion service was conducted by the Rev. R. W. Ferguson. The Rev. J. A. Penaliggon should have given an address, but was unfortunately unable to attend through sickness. The meeting .on Monday evening was taken charge of by Mr. 13. Smith, in the absence of the Rev. R. W. • Ferguson, who became serieuSly indisposed shortly before the time for commencing the ser- vice. Mr. Smith has markedly advanced as a public speaker, and was heard at his hest from the text "Abhor that which is evil; 'cleave to ,that which is good." This advice, in the' opinion of the speaker, appeared to be superfluous until we recognised the illusive and attractive guise ander which evil too often presented itself; .while goodness frequently demanded self- abnegation and toilsome duties. The Rev. E. liorgan, of Padgate, was the preacher on Tues- day, when he gave a vivid description of an Eastern wedding, drawing from-it a parallel in the second coming of Christ. The preacher said that death to the Christian should not, be a time of fear, but one of rejoicing, for the bridegroom brings joy, not retribution. "The glory and responsibility of human life," as tank by the parable of the rich glutton and 11.e?,arus the hag. gar, was' the subject dealt with J the Rey. L. E. Lovell on ,Wednesday evening. The preacher said that the 'wonders of thehomits iivelrus, c in e tend to _) exalt I:he greatness of Man, iv tion of God's works, and that all other creations wetil to have, been made for 'humanity. Man's :responsibility was in helping sotherie to find salvation as well as himself. Thursday's ser- vice was conducted by Mr. W. Mort, who took for his text John x. 10. Mr. Mort said 'that Christ "Ned such pointed parables as that in the text to enable the disciples to grasp the meaning of :His mission. Speaking of Christ as "The Bringer of Life," the congregation were told the true meaning of life, and of the glorious possibilities that await the faithful. Mr. El' Brown's Ilness.--4`he news cif-the sud- den illness of Mr. Edwin Brown caused a pain- fed surprise in the district last week, but we are pleased to learn that he Successfully underwent an operation at the Manchester Royal infirmary on Tuegday, and is as well as can be expected.

- - POVERTY AND TRUSTS. The following' are extracts from a letter re- ceiver! from. Mr. Arthur Burdett, a Lynau man in Toronto This is my seventh home in Toronto, and flit, although it costs a little to be always on the t, , I believe a change is as good as a holiday- What did you say? How art' oldtnheess knowslahoicoluhydeitioaniseairmodunednoyuoguii; co here. The estimate 'of unemployed in Toronto at' the present time is 20,000 men out of a perm_ lation of 500,000 people-4 Per rent. For although there are hundreds (literally) of banks in this -city, yet the money is not really the There are a dozen millionaires here who could tie up the city's progress by refusing finaneiill aid to big manufacturing concerns, . who find it hard' work to supply demand. Of ,mirse, these firms are large employers of labour of all kinds, arid the demand for goods is great chiefly on account of increased population and to heavy immigration. Then, having their best securities turned down, the firms' finances dwindle, ifor, in my judgment, oftener than not cc huge enterprise flourishes on intangible assets. What is the result of the firms' inability to raise funds? Why, the men are put on shoxt time—probably dismissed—and who suffers? The working man! I am no longer an out-and-out Tory, 1)4 that •I ever was, but having been, as it were, face to face with these problems, meet- ing men every day of the week and hearing dis- cussions by competent men in charge of the dis- t ribution of labour, I cannot feel but " Socialis- tic " inclined. I am most decidedly Opposed to trusts, monopolies, combines and coalitions. American prices are ,vut up every year, whether conditions warrant °V not, and who pays?' The• middle man doesn't make much in this game, the public pay every time—and dearly, too. Public ownership is my platform where the .voter directly elects men to represent him as a Joint owner. When you write again let me know something of your politics. lam just get- ting interested again, after nearly three years' rest from the arena.

div.head: CONCERNING GHOSTS.
div.p: CONCERNING GHOSTS.
Their Eccentricities and Unaccountable Habits.

div.head: AN EXCURSION INTO GHOSTDOM.
div.p: AN EXCURSION INTO GHOSTDOM.
BY ARTHUR

Christmas and the ghost story have been in- separable through the ages. The yule log and the awesome tale crackled cheerily together for ages; and together they have gone out. No wonder that weird stories filled the yule air. Superstition. is always hungry, and if Christmas be the season for taking one's fill,' the hunger of the mind must be met, as well as the hunger of the body. Of course there are no 'ghosts now. Twenty years of the Pyschic Research Society has laid the very last of them. Nothing remains but to discuss the ghost as he was, to label him and to describe the doings that we cannot explain.

THE TEHHOR-BOUND PAST. It is difficult to get back to the mental atti- tude of our ancestors in lids matter of super- stitions. We have to remember that the most enlightened people in earlier days inherited a mass of notions and teachings which were com- municated to them with an awe and reverence that bordered upon the religious. They heard of various omens, that announced, tn 9 deaths of former menibers of their family; a catalogue of things lucky , and unlucky; a variety of _charms to warts, toothache and cramp, with .spcculations ,as to the causes, of shiverings, burning of the ears and cheeks, and itchings of the eyes and elbows. , Along with these Milder beliefs went whole- sale terrors cennected with death. The room in which a; father or mother had died was left for a long time uninhabited by the family. If the person were one who had been supposed to hold strange religious opinions or had been re- garded as an infidel, the house would be ' avoided for months, and might stand empty until it fell to ruin. In the case of a suicide, ; matters were worse, and to take up residence in , a suicide's-house would haye beeh counted not • an action' of courage, but a very tempting of . the Furies. The room in which any such tragedy had taken place was nailed up and • rendered for ever after uninhabitable,

TERRORS Ol INDOOR. or . , , If a druacn Inr6b°rll ANokehits neck when Fe- turning from town upon a dark night that spot - f was haunted. Brave travellers might pass it : after dark, but only got safely away by repeat- ing secret spells and involving the aid of saints and angels. Almost every byway had its ghost who glared over gateways or stiles with saucer eyes, or appeared in the :form: of a headless cow or horse. And xis they buried suicides and murderers at cross roads, the .erossings had their peculiar terrors. Then, worst of all, mur- derers were hanged in gibbets by the roadside, and such places were next to impassable after sunset.

A sensational murder left results that lasted for generations. Ghosts who had left the flesh under painful circumstances came back with peculiar accompaniments. Those of superior rank rode in coaches drawn by six headless black horses and driven by a headless coach- man and postillion. .The manor houses were all haunted. In every old house some former mistress or master walked abroad either to inspect the scene of , their own murder, or perhaps to reveal the hiding place of ancient treasure. A churcri yard was the most populous and lively place in the parish after dark, where no one but a sexton could ever raise courage to walk. These beliefs were so general that to doubt them would have been regarded as little less than atheism. They added cruel and needless terrors to life, yet they held their own through long ages, and have only been laid to rest since the ,days of our grandparents. Floppy is the people that has no ghosts and that can make excursions into ghostdom, as we are about to do now, for sheer fun and fancy.

div.head: AN ACCOUNT OF 6110STDOM.
div.p: AN ACCOUNT OF 6110STDOM.

A ghost, as most people know, as supposed to be the spirit of a deceas person N the earth in various forms and guises, walked the and for divers reasons. He might becad injustice to be ustoicre he a restless spirit because of s , crime which waited to be redressed! might have to " walk " upon some ci errand, 'such as the discovery of a murder, or to point someone to the hiding place f 0 money or papers. Another common idea was that murdered per- sons whose bodies had been, secretly 'buried, could not be at ease until their bones had been taken hp and laid in consecrated ground and with Christian burial. The belief is 'a very old one indeed. The ancients had it that Charon was not permitted to ferry the ghosts of un- buried persons, but that they wandered up and' down the banks of the river Styx for a hundred years, after which they were mercifully allowed to cross the river to the land beyond. nut English'readers won't feel n very keen interest in the ghosts that wandered lonesome by the Styx. They would rather know some- thing of the flimsy ligiires their fathers met at the dross roads or that cast woe-begone looks over a hedgeroW.

GLANVILL'S BOOK ON GHOSTS. We need a trusty guide in this unfamiliar realm -of ghostdom, and so we will enlist the :trn,oit'yviao tsiele „ grave services of loseph Glonvill. Of credulous B e t y still o oa ft h h Abe visited b ey C northern aisle:' GI liu Church the of Bath, was a scholar of Ox- foi,d, born in 1636, and ,buried in 1680. Against Ox- the gross Puritans, who would listen to no non- sense 'about ghosts he compiled a massive and still a classic treatise full of 'the , most , convincing evidence, w ject. e should say, on the sub- The Absurd Churchyard Ghost It is refreshing arid rather surprisi frojn this volume that churchyard Jose; earn such silly creatures as to be hardly worth.rnaerne tioning. Certainly nobody but a child would be afraid of them. Alone among the ghost tribes they adopt the absurd fashion of appearing in white, presumably to scare people from tread- ing,on their graves. It is suggested that they may, in their day, have done good by frighten- ing drunkards into sobriety, and that they may, according to their own • stupid idcaS,• be striv- ing after the public good. But the suggestion is evidently due to the author's charity. We .hardly, need to read between the lines to, learn That they are silly creatures, whom nobody . I ought to have taken any notice of. It was not'so with the real ghost. With him there Was no baby play of white sheets. He or she always- appeared in the clothes worn dur- ing life. Never except in a.churchyard did any- one ever seen a white ghost. They might appear without heads or arms, but Me flum- mery of white sheets was left to the graveyard wanderers, who never did anything greater than assist .the village policeman. Ghosts with a Mission. • The ghost with a mission was a creature to be reckoned with. His coming was announced in dramatic style and in a variety of ways. Chiefly it was noises that preceded, him, all of Ahem Ominous and dreadful. Sometimes there ,Would be a rattle in an old hall as of a coach 'and six, or as the rumbling of cannon balls down a. deep staircase. It was univei:sally noticed that a ghost alwn.ys made a point of seeking his victith when he was safely tucked away •in bed, an ingenious little plan, doubtless, for taking him I in fits moment of greatest helplesSness. • The door would fly open as by magic. and .between an opening in the curtains of the bed. the trembling -victim would behold his visitdrit.

div.head: NIOUNFIELD.
div.p: NIOUNFIELD.

Upon the next point of interest, we had better quote Glanvill's own words, as the intorfion will prove important to any who may chance to have to interview a spirit. "It is necessary to observe that it has been -universally found by •experience, as well as affirmed by divers ap- paritions themselves, that a ghost has not the power to speak till it has been first spoken to ; so that notwithstanding the urgency of the business on which it may come, everything must stand still till the Person visited can find sufficient courage to speak to it; an event that sometimes does not take place for many years." ' The thought of a ghost wandering for );ears with something upon its mind, all because some cringing mortal found his teeth chattering every time, is pitiful in the extreme. "It has not been found," adds our author drily, ''that female ghosts are more loquacious than those of the male sex, both being equallY. restrained by '1.71-il5 law."
How to Handle a Ghost. The mode of addressing a ghost was to de- mand in the name of the Three Persons of the
Trinity that it should tell you who it was and . .
what was its business. It might not answer
the first time, but if the demand • were made
three times over, it could not fail to give a full
response. In a low and hollow voice It would

declare its satisfaction at being spoken to, and , would desire the person between the sheets not to be afraid. After this assurance we are told that tile ghost woulddaunch out upon its narrative, which being completed, and its command's'. or requests given, with injunctions that they be immediately executed, it would vanish, often in a flash. Thoughtful ghosts used to anticipate a shock froth this flash of light, and advise the closing of the eyes as a protection. So at least says the well-informed Prebendary
Glanvill, and plain folks cannot talk back to a
specialist
Sometimes a considerate ghost went further, and would make amends for any mental suffer- ing he had caused by gliding away to slow and
peaceful music.
The Etiquette of the Occasion. Very emphatic advice is given as to the de- portment of the listener. On no account would _ . . _ _ .
a ghost consent to be interrupted in his story. A question was, an impertinence, and the ex- pression of a doubt raised a situation of grave
hanger, but any ghost would listen to a question
after its tale was done.
Of peculiar offensiveness were any questions respecting the state of the ghost or the state of any other inhabitant of the spirit world. Such questions were so seldom answered thak it was
inferred that all spirits were, restrained from divulging the secrets of their priSon house.
Some Peculiarities of Ghosts.

We have made a very serious effort, by the aid of Glanvill, to understand the ghost, yet feel obliged to say that, however good in his intentions, he is peculiarly stupid in his methods. • This opinion may be due, of course, to our not having sufficient synipathy, or not under- standing his difficulties. At the risk of being shaken up at midnight and left without even the solace of soft music, Vve say it; a ghost's

business methods were abominably bad. In cases of murder, a ghost has never been known to go to a Justice of the Peace or a policeman and file his evidence. Instead, he appears month after month to some poor -

labourer, who knows none of the persons con- cerned, or draws the curtains from the bed ,of some old woina'n five nfile away. Or he May hover round the place where his body was hid- den and scare everybody except the murderer. The same shocking want of judgment is seen whenever there is ,a case of injustice to the widow or orphan. Assuming that Ire does not }mow the address of a Justice Of the Peace, one Would think that the shortest and surest plan would be to haunt the \evildoer until he made restitution. But this is the one thing that never seemed to happen. Nor were the pointing out of hiding-places managed with better business skill. It was not to a lawyer or a detective that the place was revealed, but to some person ignorant of the whole affair, who was generally too much scared to want to dig the ground or search in hollow trees, and who often was too timid to tell anybody.

When Ghosts Got Angry. In such cases we learn that a ghost would drop All show of friendliness and begin to make it awkward for the person t who had not handed on the information: ',There would be a series of fresh appearings ; at first a discon- tented, then an angry look ; then a furious Countenance; then a threat to. blight the cattle or tear the poor, quaking creature to pieces if he did not tell the proper person. If threats were not effective the next thing would be violence; and some night the hapless man would encounter what seemed a fierce beast in the road, and receive a blow that would lame him for life. • Did no one ever suggest to a ghost that a five Minutes' visit to a lawyeç would save months of this sort of trouble? . It is pleasing to be told that a ghost always seemed gratified when he found a willing accomplice. Upon a business being completed Glanvill assures us that he would always pay a final visit with a cheerful face, saying that he could now rest for ever, and, by way of thanks, .would communicate something which no one was ever known to reveal.. - The Ghost Cantankerous., -

The ghost with a:mission was a very mild fellow compared with the ghost cantankerous. These were clearly the black sheep of the spirit world. They disturbed .houses without giving the least reason for doing'so. They gave signs and potents innumerable; invisible cannon balls rolled down the stairways, and invisible weights fell wilt shivering shocks upon floors; but nobody could get an answer to a question. They were common disturbers. ,Olanvill assures us that there was no other common be in them. forw n remedy eon mu term t t om F than- to exorcise and eject them; in the o ghost. ltahni spaugre, pose two or three clergymen were needed. The vi othi °err g u struck terror to a capai e clergymen (such as the reverend author himself) could lay a ghost for any length of time up a hundred years. I ded years. They could, by the magic of theilru r Latin shut him up in solid oak or in 9/ barrel o f 4beer. If he were an esquire it would be a barrel of wine. But the most severe punishment for the ghost cantankerous was to banish him to the Bed Sea. Of all places he liked it least. We are told that ghosts have pleaded with clergymen during the service of exorcism to give them any fate rather than that. But wise clergymen (such as our penetrating author) knew that to be with Pharaoh and his host on the sultry banks of the Bed Sea was the securest prison, and that no ghost .had ever been ingenious enough to get away before his time as up. Some Smaller Details. That our readers may be informed yet a little further, we will hand on U few more details. The true and usual time for ghostly visits was( always midnight/. though ghosts were not always punctual. The only occasions when daylight manifestations have heen known have been in the cases of ghosts, whose time at the Bed Sea has expired and who have come back more audacious than before. In the old days, when compulsory vaccina- tion first began, the Japanese vaccinated every- body on the tip of the nose. Why? Well, because it was a good place, where there's no movement to rub off the scab. And also be- Cause a. vaccination scar on the nose was easily\ identified by the medical officers of the govern- ment. knowledge fiat English ghosts never dritgged chains. Ghosts Of any other nations paraded their manillOns or dungeons in this degrading WaY. Not so on English soil. Persons born on Christ- mas are happy in being unable to ever see or hear one. • • This Mention of Christmas Eve reminds us 'that ghosts never walked on Christmas Eve, a belief which Shak.espeare refers to in "Hamlet." They were all kept in bondage, that the world might have a good time. Happy rushes, who could travel to the festive board without the dread of fiery eyes or sepulchral voices! The day of the ghost is over. Anything that hears a semblance of him is handed to Sir Oliver Lodge, and the Society of Psychic Research, with a little awe, as if it were the handing of a tramp to the policeman. To be dragged vip on a charge of loitering is too much. No self-respecting ghost will stand it. And so he makes the best of it by the Red Spa, or wanders wearily, with disconsolate eyes, on the i banks of the Styx.

div.head: WqRLD
div.p: THE WqRLD
New Books.
lodern Parliamentary Eloquence. By Earl Curzon of Kedleston. London: Macmillan and Co., Ltd. 2s. 6d. , net.

In this book Lord Curzon has expanded the Bede Lecture which he delivered before the University of Cambridge in November last, and, as it now stands, it forms, as he says in an in- troductory note, "a more comprehensive study of the question than coqld be inferred from the condensed reports that appeared in the Press." Lord Curzon is himself a speaker of no mean repute, and tins lends an additional interest to his judgments on the orators whom he passes in review and his general observations on the development of modern. public-speaking. Defining eloquence as "the power of moving men by speech," Lord Curzon rightly insists that the test of eloquence is the effect of a speech on the audience that hears it, and in support of this view he quotes an interesting passage from Mr. Balfour's eulogy on Glad- stone' in the House of Commons on the latter's death. "It is .not," says Mr. Balfour, "the speeches which read best which are the great- est speeches. Posterity cannot possibly •judge of their Merit by a mere study of the words used. They must see the man, feel the mag- netism of his presence, see his gestures, the Hash of his eyes. . . . The test of a speaker is the audience he addresses. There is no other judge; from that court there is no appeal." , It follows from this that a man whose speecheS read well is not necessarily a great orator, but`the converse does not certainly fol- lON-V. John Bright was in every sense of the word an orator, but his speeches are yet fine reading none the less. Macaulay's speeches are splendid specimens 'of , literary art, but Macaulay was not an orator. He did not Move men by his speeches as John Bright did., Glad- stone was an example of the orator who de- pends on many things besides words to move an audience. His speeches do not give one who did not hear him anything like the impression created in those who listened to his .magnifl- cent voice, and, who therefore came under Cie influence of his extraordinary personality. Lord Curzon gives an interesting account of the change that has Aaken placeduring the last hundred years in the .conditions of speech-mak- ing. The changes in the Cohstitution, the change in Parliament, the rise of reporting and the sketch," the development of platform speakin, and the quite modern praCtice of ex-, ,telnpore'speaking, all these have had 'a profound effect on eloquence. The difference may be measured by the fact that eighteenth century oratory "was the art of an aristocratic society, practised under aristocratic conditions, in an ,aristocratic age.' The aristocratic age has passed away. We live in a democratic age, and , oratory, to influencr the modern audience of either Parliament or the public .meeting, must be attuned to modern democratic conditions. And democracy, it seems to Lord Curzon, "will I produce an eloquence, perhaps even an oratory,

. • of: its oWn.' I Lord Curzon's observations on the various orators whose merits and demerits he appraises are always interesting and often extremely apt. 1 The range iS 'very wale, all the"welbknowW speakers of the present day and many others of the modern period, being noticed. It is im- possible in a; short revieW to quote. any of his judgments on thou, interesting as they are. • We may .remark,, however, that id one instance, Lord Curzon appears, possibly quite unconsciously, to have allowed political prejudice to influence turn. He says (p. 15): " Mr. Lloyd George reserves the Master-pieces of his peculiar .style for Limehouse, Newcastle, arab Swindon." We think that such a remark

is entirely out ,of place in a Work of this kind. The writer may, perhaps, have no greater par- tiality than Lord Curzon himself for some of the peculiarities of Mr. Lloyd George's, public utterances, but if eloquence is to be judged on the conditions laid down by Lord Curzon (and we- are quite in agreement with him as to those conditions), we think that it cannot be [ questioned that Mr. Lloyd George is one of the master orators of our time, for no speaker, in otir experience, at any rate, has had a more electrifying effect on his audiences, not except- ing Mr. Gladstone himself, and this would seem to be the supreme acnievement of oratory. It it triie—and it is only right to say-c--that in another part of his book (p. 23) Lord Curzon appears to have some kind of discernment of this fact, but this does not, in our opinion, exelige the earlier sentence, which somewhat mdfs the otherWiSe excellent impartiality of the book, nod we think that on reflection Lord [C4Zon, Wirl perceive it.
