div.p: OP LETTERS.
Literary Gleanings.

ULSTER FOLK LORE. For nearly twenty years Miss Elizabeth An- drews has been collecting stories of Irish fairies and other legendary tales of Celtic mythology, and here is the result, in a pleasant little vol- ume. Miss Andrews finds, from her inquiries among the peasant folk, that they do not imagine the fairies as tiny beings that shelter under mushrooms and gambol upon gossamer, but as a much larger race, about the size of children of four or five years old. From this fact, Miss Andrews adduces the theory that 'fairy lore does not owe its origin to ancestor i worship, but rather to the vague traditions of history. She believes that the various small races which appear in Celtic lore are attribut- able to primitive races of mankind, and that the frequent legends of children being carried off by fairies can be traced back to retords of raids in time of war, when captives were removed into caves by means of subterranean passages. Some peasants .describe the fairies as about the size of monkeys; others picture them as clad in red jackets and wearing red hair and manes like hOrses. They are attended by the sound of music in the night, and indulge in fierce battles, of which living people have been eyewitnesses. In some regions salt is put on children's heads I) protect them from the malign influence of the "wee folk," who are supposed to be power- ful on Ilallciw-e'en ; in other places St. Ilridgefs Eve is the time when crosses of reeds are made as amulets of the home.

div.head: "11E111.%.01115.'
div.p: The lore and legends of the Maoris were in danger of passing into oblivion, for the Maori had no written records, and all tradition and ancient teaching had to be passed on by word of mouth, by trained teachers, to propel* pupils in the " Whare-kura." This danger was (averted by the Governor of New Zealand, Sir George grey, gaining the confidence of the Maori chiefs and acting as the recorder of their ancient wisdoni. This was done in 1855, kinu the second edition appeared in 1885. As it is now difficult to procure either edition a new edition has been issued by the Government of New Zealand, having been compiiled by Mr. Jarnes 17ett. Maori lore was handed down orally, by the teachers in the " Whare-kura," sacTe& college, esoteric school, masonic lodge, or whzdever it may be likened to. The "Whore- ' kura " ta New Zealand was no doubt a faithful copy of the " Whare-kura" in the old home, Flawa.iki. The manner of building and dedicat- ing it was somewhat as follows. The priests built it of materials given by the people. Dur- ing the thillding the priests abstained from food each day until the work was finished, so that the " Whare-kura " might be "unstained by any exhibition of mere animal grossness." At each stage of the building sanetificatory rites were ! performed; and when Completed, a sacrifice in (rout of the building was offered. While this was being offered outside the building "a I sacred lire and arllflli oven) had been lighted I within the building. At the close of day an- other fire was lighted in the courtyard, where food was cooked and eaten by tiie sacred men." The " Whare•kura " being now readY, the can, didates had to be made reddy also.. Twenty or 'thirty youths of the highest rank were chosen and led to, a stream or lake near by. While the youths stood in the water the priests dropped some water into their ears front a stalk of toe-toe. Then the priests entered the water themselves; ladled it several .limes rover the candidates, and repealed the proper incan- tations. This will at once remind one of the ancient rite of baptism. Water represents truth, as we read: "Sanctify them in the truth; thy word is truth" ; and, "Now ye are clean, through the word which I have spoken unto you." The touching of the ears with a little water was no doubt symbolical of opening the mind to understand knowledge. All the other parts of the ceremony were also full of mean- ing, to those who undefstood. One of the strangest parts of this ceremony of initiation was the use of fresh sea-weed which priests and candidates took, and having re- peated over it incantations, threw it from them as they came out of the water, and proceeded to the " Whare-kura." This is thought to have some reference to a " flood " legend which was thus kept alive in the memory of Maoridom. It may have been so, or it may have been a symbolical representation of something else, for the Maori has several " flood " legends which appear to stand out apart from this initiation ceremony.—" Theosophical Path."

div.head: ROUMANIAN LADIES.
div.p: ROUMANIAN LADIES.

A writer in a German paper describes the women of Roumanian cities as more elegant, but more artificial, than the Parisians. They spend more money, she declares, over their toilettes, and devote more time to the cultiva- tion of theif personal charms than do the French women. The daughter's of the better- class families see nothing of the hard lot of the toilers on the land. They are never permitted to g 0 out unaccompanied, they are watched incessantly, whether they are occupied or idle. It is rarely the mother who exercises this super- Vision; it is the duty of the governess or of, the duenna attached to the boarding school. The young girl is taught to make the most of her personal appearance; she is encouraged to believe that during her school days and in later life she cannot use her time better than in en.- deavouring to render herself pleasing and at- traptive to men. She learns that when she goes into society her. whale life .depends as much upon the impression she makes as on her father's wealth. The Eastern love of luxury is stilhin her blood; according to Dr. Horwitz she is listless, indifferent, selfish, and she hates anything that approaches discomfort. The rich woman is as idle as the peasant is industrious; she is all curves, while the other is slim and muscular. The former shows her love of decoration in the profusion of rich cloth- ing and jewellery she wears, but not in her home surroundings, while the woman of the people is simple in her tastes and has few needs. The woman of the upper classes leaves all work and duties to her husband and to paid strangers, while the toil•er on the land is unceas- ing in her devotion to her husband and chil- dren, labouring always to make the best of her , home and its occupants. . Naturally some form of amusement is neces- sary for women who spend their days in idle ' luxury, and so Roumanians play cards all day long, and with more zest than any others in the world. There is, indeed, one Woman in the country who gets up at four of a morning to do her work, and who sits over her books late into the night. She holds a more exalted position than any other, but, she is no Rouma- nian, Carmen Sylva, the poet Queen, organ ised the Institute for the Blind by her own N•- free earn et rce efforts; through her energy schools for teach- ing handicrafts ‘vere established. All the rights for which the women of the West have striven so long are in the hands of the Roumanians. Though they are too luxury- lovingl,3, m uacV, theyto o idle a e v° o eliving themselves h by anigyheprroefdeusseiaotnionatlite oyr geaanreisattioon a ee rri their exercise. their disposal; the universities , are open, and their choice of a career is not, dependent on the caprice of any professor. They are at liberty to practise as doctors or lawyers, they may he chemists or dispen;->ers Ifie.\ • • may hold official appointments, and married .a nd single alike are eligible for posts as teachers in schools.

AT SCHOOL AGAIN!
My dear Children,—

"It's a bother !" didn't some of you say on Monday? It was a "bother," wasn't it, to have to return to school after all the fun of the holidays? I should not think it a bother to go to school again, and I do not think your fathers or mothers.would eithe'r. • _ .

To we older folk who can look back over the years the school time seems the happiest we have over spent. I hope therefore none of my nephews and nieces think school a "bother." I ain certain you all like school, and are trying to learn as much as you can. If the holidays are past never mind—Easter is coming. Long before Easter, however, I hope to have several compftitions. I shall announce a new one next week, so look out. With holidays over I hope you will do a little work for this column, which is all your own.
I want you to try and get as many new members as you ctn. I know you will tty. Your loving t_i_NiCLE JACK.
DOWN IN TUE MINE.

About five o'clOck in the =mine the miner leaves his cosy bed and dons his working clothes, usually a flannel shirt, moleskin trousers, jacket and vest. After refreshing himself with a cup of lta, he takes his "piece," and makes his way to the pithead, to wait his turn to descend the shaft. _ .

At the pit-bottom the miner lights his tallow lamp, and, getting a report from the inspector or fireman, who has examined the "places," he makes his way along a series of roads to "the face." Removing his jacket and vest, ha toils with pick and shovel at bringing down the coal, and filling it into hutches, to which he attaches his " pins. ' At nine o'clock an interval of half an hour is given, during which the " piece " is taken, and then work is resumed. Two o'clock brings great relief to the weary worker, for now his work is done, and he makes his way once more to the pit-bottom. Imagine yourself for eight hours every day of a week hacking With a pick at coal which seems un- breakable! It is no joke, but a grim, grimy reality, and therefore the miner's gratification at turning his back on the pit for one day even Is fully justified.

The working of a colliery is also interesting. When a tub or hutch is filled with coal it is conveyed by a " drawer " to the main road. ith several others it passes over " braes " (if any) by means of mechanical haulage, whereby the full tubs descending the incline draw a similar weight of empty ones to the top of the brae. They are then drawn liy rt pony to the pit-bottom, where they are heisted up the pit shaft.

On the pithead girls are employed to remove the pins from the hutches. These pins are usually little bits of tin or iron stamped with a number, and by their means thp number of tubs filled by each man is known at the pithead. By an ingenious method, known as the 'tumblers," the coal is transferred into wag- gons, after which it is taken by train to t/19 nearest port.

MY FANOURITE PET. I am sure that my favourite pet is a bird. You cannot help but love one of these little creatures. Some time ago I had a male canary who was exceedingly tame. In fact, he was so tame that if I called to him he would come flying to my shoulder. I used to let him out of his cage whenever I went into the room where he was kept, and many were the fine times we had together. I crocheted a little chain of pink wool, and with this I taught him to skip. I used to place him on my lap, and while I turned the chain he leapt over it as it came down. He did it beautifully, too, never leaping before the time, nor omitting it altogether. I do not think most little Lards con do that. He had a magnificent voice, and it WAS pos"H!va.* as good as going to a concert to hear him, lie used to love to hide himself in somebody's hair; and once he got entangled it was hard to get rid of him. One day, however, we let him out of his cage, not noticing that the window was open. Of course, out he flew, and we lost him entirely. I have a bird for a pet now, but though it is a dear little thing it is not so tame as the other was. It is a female and cannot sing much either. I think I love little birds the best of all pets. They have such soft, warm

little bodies and beautiful dark bead-like eyes. Then they are so defenceless and timid that no- body could have the heart to be unkind to them. If one has a tame bird it is quite as good as a companion, for will it not sit on your finger and talk to you in its own little way? And then you cannot be gloomy long if you listen to its sweet song, which is truly beautiful. There are many other animals I like, but none so much as a bird, which is one of the smallest of God's creatures.

div.head: ATE ENEMIES TO GAIN STRENGTH.
div.p: ATE ENEMIES TO GAIN STRENGTH.

" Soul-stuff" is what primitive man called any- thing mystic or beyond his understanding. This quaint yet expressive belief was touched upon in an excElent lecture delivered by Professor G. Currie Martin, at the Adult School, Academy-street, Warrington, on Monday even- ing. It was the first of the four on " The Les- sons of the Great Religions" delivered in connec- tion with the Adult School movement, and the first theme was "Religion of the primitive races —Fear." MA J. A. Ransome pfesided.

div.head: MOST VITAL SUBJECT.
div.p: THE MOST VITAL SUBJECT.

The subject of religion, said the Professor, was really the most vital subject there was to tackle. There was nothing that mattered so much as religion; it was not only Christian men who said that, but men of .other faiths. It used to be said that there were heaps of people in the world who .had no religion. but was re- ligion really confined to certain races? There was, with only a few exceptions, no race which was without it, so that it was practically a uni- versal thing. A religion was "a consciousness or sense of dependence upon powers greater than ourselves.
Beginning and End orLife....,

Primitive -man, in sortie ways, was like chil- dren—everything had got to live: Watch a child at play. Everything it played with was alive, according to the child's idea; so primitive man regarded the universe as alive. Everything led nim to think so. lie looked at the suw and found, for example, that it gave the heat that rna de him comfortable. Later he discovered that it helped the trees to grow, so he looked upon the sun as having being. The things that had to do with the beginnings of life or the end of it, were the things primitive-lElin looked upon as of the greatest significance. It meant that his idea of the universe was that it was something alive, for all around him was the manifestation of life. That was termed animism Or "soul-stuff." When he went to sleep he dreamt, as they did, but the primitive could not understand how he could "see" people and scenes Miles away, while he was in his hut. Then it dawned upon him that it was his "soul. that went away. and if it could not be caught he would never waken up again, lie t notco‘geil:assal conversation -had fought with the next village and had killed one man. Perhaps that night be.would dream that he.wasiti with talgteaidneartlaemlisaend, and he could that it !vas his "soul-stuff," and that if it was to do him no har m lie must do something to keep the animism of the dead e . nemv sweet to- wards him Perhaps it would like to be nicely buried, and so I dead, and that et the idea of honouring the the elaborate alsofune explained the reason of • ral ceremonies. That was the beginning of ancestral worship. .

Cannibalism. Then there was cannibalism. It was believed original man loathed the taste of human flesh. but why did he and his followers practise it?' The idea was that when a man was killed, espe- cially a strong man, if they ate Part of his body some of the "soul-staff " would go to them and make them stronger. That was the philoso- phy of ,cannibalism. Another side to primitive man's religion was that the "soul-stuff" could be governed and used for their,own ends; and that vi-as done by ' employing a "fetish." This could be any- thing so long as it had been- "dedicated." One way of dedicating the "let was by going to a new grave and watching for the first sign of life—a spider, a. fly, or anything, that moved over the grave. The insect. was placed on the article .to become a fetish, and it was believed that the "soul-stuff " of the departed had passed through the. insect and into the piece of wood, ite. which was now dedicated. This was a
charm. and the power of a man depended upon the strength of the fetish.
Fear of Spirits.

Sacrifices were originally offerings by primi- tive man to pleape the spirits. Thus it could be seen even early man observed that spirit was greater than matter, ami he had fear of spirits. It was, however, ,evident early man believed there was a Supreme Being who even eontrolled the spirits, of which he was afraid, but that Supreme Being was supposed to be too far away to take any notice of him, therefore all his mind was concentrated upon the spirits he be- ilieved were uear

The Public Auditor's First Report
on Finances.
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND THE PAST,

There was some material in the minutes of the Finance and Estate Committee submitted to the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening which might have proved the fostering bed of Ei pretty little squabble, but the anticipated row did not develop, although there was a sharp, though brief, passage-at-arros between Councillor Wilkinson, chairman of the committee, and Councillor Pemberton.

The matter arose out of the report of Mr, F. Lambert Stevens, district auditor, who made the first report upon the accounts of the borough since they were placed under Government audit. The report, which is a detailed one, stated :

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

"Gentlemen,—ln pursuance of the provisions of Section 247 of the Public Health Act, 1875, as applied to your accounts by the :Warrington Corporation Act, 1911, I have to report that I have audited your accounts and those of your officers, for the year ',ended 31st March, 1913. "The statutory financial statement, which I have, certified, contains particulars of the re- ceipts and expenditure during the year under the prescribed heads, from which it will be seen that. excluding transfers, the receipts amounted to £366,679 Os. 104., and the expenditure to ..t.362,197 15s. scl.

"The net balance in hand at the end of the year amounted to .189,428 6s. lkl., which sum includes £643 Bs. Bd. uninvested sinking funds, £7,590 3s. lid. uninvested reserve funds, and £4,976 ss. 6d. unexpended loans.
"The total amount of loans and capitalised value of annuities outstanding at 31st March, 1913, was .4,277,493 Is. Id.

"The securities relating to the investment of the Police Superannuation Fund, the Gas, Water; Electricity " and Trtimways Reserve Funds, and the Gas Works Sinking Fund were produced to me, and detailed inventories of stores in hand at the end of the year were sub- mitted, upon which values have been placed as follows, viz.:—

Borough Surveyor's Dept. .22,995 0 11 Gas Department ... ... 5,992 19 Water Department ... ... 4,104 811 Electricity Department ... 2,548 6 9 Tramways Department ••. 967 18 8 "An improvement in the method of keeping the records of receipt and issue of sundry stores of fittings in respect of the Gas, Water and Electricity Departments, and miscellaneous articles in the Tramways Department is desir- able. The system adopted in the Electricity De- partment during the current year appears to meet the-case. "I have found the accounts well kept, and arranged so as to accurately show the financial condition of each department. "The only matter to which I think it neces- sary to specially call your attention is your practice of paying travelling and hotel expenses to members and officers attending conferences, or engaged on other business of the Corporation, in London, on the basis of a resolution passed in 1897, fixing the allowance at 30s. per day, and first class railway fare. This, I consider, should be amended so as to be in agreement with the regulation made by the Lords of the Committee of the Privy Council on Education, under the School Board Conferences Act, 1897, that is to say, that the maximum allowances should be the actual travelling expenses, and is. per diem when absent from home at night, and 10s. 6d. per diem when not absent from home at night. "I have to acknowledge the ready assistance 'rendered by your officials throughout the audit."

The financial . position of the town is sound, as I have said on a previous occasion, and the business of the town is carried on in an efficient manner. At the same time it is very possible that in the first report we have got, one's mind should go back to the days —(A Member: "Evil days ")—when certain statements were made. It is very gratifying to me, and, I think, to the whole Council, to see this report stamps out all the mis-statements that have been made in years gone by. (A Voice: "No.")

div.head: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S RETORT.
div.p: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S RETORT.

- - - Councillor PEMBERTON : I did not intend to say anything, but I cannot allow the remarks of the Chairman of the Finance Committee to pass. The statements made in the days past were true, without a doubt, and were called for. This certificate is only for the past twelve months, and you have had two years' notice that he was to come, and you would have been foolish if you had not been prepared, and they had found anything. After the tremendous slating you got, in the House of Commons, and the strong ' things said by the ChairmAn of the House of Commons' Committee about you. reported in all the papers in the country at the time. I am simply astounded that Councillor Wilkinson should have introduced the matter at all; be- cause it is beyond question that then the Coun- cil was found to be in a deplorable state. Money had been spent improperly and •wrongfully as the Rouse of Commons' Committee reported, and now to bring up this matter here is quite wrong.

The- MAYOR: It is quite wrong. I agree. Councillor PEMBERTON: Yes, it is out of order for Councillor Wilkinson to say these frliingB' but if they kick I shall kick back every time. The minutes were finally approved. .

DAHLIAS. ' Dahlias cannot be classed with slich popular flowers as chrysanthemums and carnations. They are popular only amongst. the growers, tieing by no means a ladies flower on account of the peculiar odour. In some districts dahlias are grown extensively and are looked upon as " the" flower. In spite of its unpopularity with the-fair sex, the dahlia is a magnificent autumn flower. Few gardens give it the prominence it deserves---it is generally planted in en out-of- the-way place where its beauty is spoiled. • There i no liner sight in the- world of flowers than a mass of dahlias in a range of colours. !. The most glorious display the writer ever saw was in a cottage garden which siope gently from the cottage to the. roadway. Grouped in colours, it was a sight long to be remembered, the scores 01-varieties and Colours making a glorious picture in front -of the creeper-covered cottage.. The dahlia is a plant which responds to good -culture. The' old show and fancy varieties have now given way to singles, the cactus:the collarette, and the peony-flowered.

div.head: SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
div.p: SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
ALDERMAN SMETHURST v. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON.

The controversy over the completion of War- rington .Bridge produced another full-dress debate in the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday. The result was that a committee was appointed to consider the question. The debate was opened by Councillor PEMBER" TON, who moved: "That a cominittee of the Council consisting of seven members be now ap- pointed to inquire into and report at an early date upon the delay which has occurted in the construction of the new Warringtori Bridge, and that such committee be empowered to obtain any expert advice or assistance they may con- sider necessary and to recommend what steps should be taken to expedite the work."

posed by Councillor Pemberton. . He strongly objected to calling in more expert ,advice. They already had an expert the person of the engineer, and if they wanted ex-1 pert evidence, why not avail themselves of that for which they were already paying? He be- lieved ,it was a fact that, while the engineer regularly reported on the progress of the work, he had not been before the committee for 12 months. He would go all the way with any reasonable proposal to facilitate the completion of the bridge, and to remove what was a source of great inconvenience, if not of danger,. but he difl not think 'the resolution Of Councillor Pem- berton was the proper •way to attain that end. .Councillor BROADHMIST said as long as work at the bridge went on, so long would payment be made, and it was time that the members of the Council, as the representatives of the rate- payers, stepped in, -

• ALLOWANCE FOR DIFFICULTIES. Alderman BENNETT said while they were anxious to see the work conipleted, lie thought the Council had not made due allowance for the difficulties encountered by the contractors. Work was being done which was not apparent. He had been on every portion of the bridge day after day and had watched every detail, and anyone who had seen what he had seen would form a different opinion from that which had been expressed as to the manner in which. Mr. Thorne was doing his work. It was being done with great care and every possible precaution was being used.

THE CHAIRMAN'S QUESTIONS. Alderman SMETHERST said he would like to-ask if Councillor Pemberton was aware that the contract time was for the original design and not for the modified design? Would he specify) definitely the nature of the delay to which he referred, and say when lie visited the site, and what he saw to establish his charge of delay? Was/ Councillor Pemberton aware of the in- creased difficulty of the work in the abutments in the modified design, compared with the original design, and .that reinforced, concrete bridge work was not like dock work, where the more men that could be put on the sooner the work was finished?, Reinforced concrete work was special work, and the number of men cap- able of being put on was limited. On an aver- age 38 men were daily at work. THE SUB-COMMITTEE'S OBJECT. Councillor OSBORNE said what he was most concerned about was that the work ought to have been completed in 20 months. That time had expired and the work was not nearly com- plete. He thought that if a sub-committee was appointed it would be beneficial to the contrac- tors and the ratepayers. What was everyone's business was no one's, and the suggestion to have expert advice did not bar out Mr. Webster:. If the committee. thought Mr. Webster was the best expert they ought naturally to appeal to him. It Was not necessary to introduce any personal feeling in the matter, as the proposi- tion which .Councillor Pemberton made was a business one, and he should support it. Every- one admitted that there. had been unnecessary delay; even Alderman Smethurst admitted it. It was for the sub-committee to find out the cause of the 'delay.

THE QUESTIONS ANSWERED. Councillor PEMBERTO, answering Alderman Smethurst's queries, said the strengthening of the structure, according to the modified design, was no ground for extending the period of the contract to any great extent. As to the request for a more definite complaint, he alleged that the contractors had not had sufficient plant or men on the work. -On the first part a the bridge they could have worked on both sides at once. As to the increased difficulties said to arise from the modification of the design, he was totally ignorant of them. A bridge could not be done quite as quickly as dock work, but his conten- tion was that the present contract could have been carried out m ii more rapidly. Tie re- gretted that there had been unpleasantness over the bridge, but he thought it was time some protest should be made, and the matter brought to a head. They had delayed far too long.

Much Unpleasantness. Ther6 had been much unpleasantness about the bridge. Certain members of the committee had been very energetic in protesting, but they had been over-ruled every time. Why? Because when the engineer was called in to give an opinion, the laymen on the committee felt help- less. If the special committee were appointed on the lines he proposed, they could call the engineer before them, and, if they wanted an- other expert opinion, they would be able to obtain it. He had tried to be scrupulously fair and to gime the contractors credit fcrr every- thing that had been done. They had, however, only to compare what had already been done with the work that lay ahead to realise the posi- tion.

There were hundreds of concrete bridges in the world. Was there any special reason why the contractors should be allowed to dilly-dally on thia undertaking? None, except that they were allowed to dilly-dally on every Corporation job. Look at the baths and at the Lawson con- tract ! A committee of inquiry was appointed with reference to the latter, and they had .C 42,000 knocked off a claim of X 72,000. Alder- man Smethurst said there might he a lawsuit about the bridge. The Corporation went to law about the Lawson contract and they won. They had also been successful in several arbitrations since then. The MAYOR: We are talking about the bridge. The DRPrTY MAYOR: It was not because of your committee.
Councilor PEMBERTON' Any way, I received the unanimous thanks of the Council for what I then did.
HOW MEMBERS VOTED.
The division then took place and there voted: For the Resolution—The Mayor, Councillor Skelland, Osborne, Cunnington, Shaw, Broad- -liur4t, Gough, Lashford, Chrinies, Halliwell and Pemberton-11. •

Against—The Deputy 'Mayor, Aldermen Tinnion, John Evans, Smethurst, Bennett and Burton, Councillors Jenkins and Wilkinson..-8. The Sub-committee appointed was: Aldermen Forshaw and Tinnion, Councillors Locker, Osborne, Pemberton, Broadhurst and Cunning. ton.
—Alderman Tinnion intimated that he declined to serve.

div.head: REASON FOR THE MOTION.
div.p: THE REASON FOR THE MOTION.

Councillor Pemberton said the reason for his motion was the exceptional length of time which the contract was taking to complete. It was causing enormous public inconv,mience, and was going to be very expensive to the ratepayers unless the' Council took some very energetic steps. The old bridge had not been entirely taken down; how long that work was going to occupy lie did not know. The foundations of e the outside part had been Put in, and they were preparing thcentres to carry' the structure. If it had taken two years to do what had been accomplished, and the work was to continue at the same speed and with the same plant, it ras evident another two ye.ars would be required to complete it.
/ ...... The Time Limit.

The Council had been assured that the work was being Carried on as speedily as possible. A man did not need to be an engineer or to have any practical knowledge to see what was going on. What did he see when be passed? Perhaps two or three youths at a crane and a man here and there. He saw' the old bridge left for days without a single stone being removed. The original contract stiPulatea that the work should be done in 20 months. Of course, they knew that, with regard to the price, that con- tract was not being carried out, as the work was now being done according to a schedule bf prices. The ultimate cost was uncertain.

He understood, however, that the contract, outside the given sum, was valid. He might be wrong, but if it were S. why was the job being allowed to drag in such a manner? , The original contract was let for £14,310, and there were mqdifications of the design involving an additional 1'2,300. At the time the modifica- tions were sanctioned Mr. Webster reported chat the alteration in the cost did not in any way affect the contract, and that there was no question of breaking the contract. If that were ..o, the work ought to have been completed in 'le specified time.

A PICTURESQUE PERSONALITY.

div.head: Touching References to the Death
div.p: Touching References to the Death
of Mr. Birtles
COUNCIL'S TRIBUTE.

Seldom have more toliching references to a departed colleague been made in the Warring- ton Council Chamber than . those paid to the memory of the late Councillor Thomas Birtles at the Council meeting on Tuesday night. The MAYOR moved a resolution expressing regret at the loss sustained by the town and con- dolence with the relatives, requesting the Town Clerk to forward to them a resolution of sym- pathy.

During the last year, said the Mayor, Coun- cillor Birtles' record of attendances at the meetings of the Town Council and the commit- tees was the highest, with the exception of the Deputy Mayor. He was also a regular attender at the Education Committee and the sub-com- mittees. Mr. Birtles had also taken a keen interest in the Art Gallery and Museum, and, although he was a member of the Council for only six years, the esteem in which the Cor- poration held him was very great. He had visited Mr. Birtles during his illness, - the last occasion being only about a meek before he died, and Mr. Birtles was very keen about everything that, was going on in the town. He referred to the time when the old Town Hall was in the Market Place, and was particularly anxious that the Council should look ahead, and by looking' back see what they could do for the future. At the last meeting of the Council he attended, Councillor Birtles told him (the Mayor) that he had kept away from seeing a specialist until he had seen him elected to that chair. He took that as a great compliment. " Picturesque Personality.': The DEPUTY MAYOR (Dr. Joseph) seconding, said a local newspaper had referred to Coun- cillor Birtles as a "picturesque personality." That was a particularly appropriate term a- applied not only to his appearance, which picturesque and distinguished, but described his character to a certain extent, which was very much in keeping with his appearance. He was a Man of culture and of high ideals, and he possessed such sound common sense that they toned down the ideals and brought them within the scope of practical measures. It was Coun- cillor Birtles who some time ago brought before him the practicability of enlarging the Council Chamber. He did not know any man who had died so justly revered and I.y his family and the public.

Shadow of Bereavements. Aide/man BENNETT said at the close of the tune of festivity they met under the shadow of many bereavements, and he could not remember a time when they had to mourn so many departed friends at one time. He wished to lay emphasis on the great interest Councillor Birtles had taken in the work of the Museum Committee, especially on the artistic side. Councillor Birtles had the honour of being a fellow-student of Mr. Harry Woods and Mr. Luke Fildes. His et mind often reverted to the old days, and h referred to them with pardonable pride. There was no doubt he had derived an inspiration from the gentlemen named, which lasted all through his life-time, and which helped to cause the Art Gallery and Library to be so fittingly housed. He was a useful, member of the Street Improve- r:lent Committee, and had he lived they would have been indebted to him for many more valu- able suggestions. He had visited Councillor Birtles, and, speaking about the improvements suggested, Mr. Birtles said : "Whatever you do, oonsider the interests of the present, and then ••ast your mind 50 years forward and make your provision for the future." He was always a mall who looked ahead.

div.head: "There's Father Christmas."
div.p: "There's Father Christmas."

- - - Councillor HENSHALL said his personal rela- tions with Councillor Birtles were of the best and most intimate- Be recalled an instance which illustrated the point about his pictur- esque personality. He was in the main street with Councillor Birtles, when they met some children, who gazed at Mr. Birtles, And they wondered what was the mystery until a little girl let it out by whispering: "See, there's Father Christmas." He was not only the most striking personality in the Council Chamber, but in the town. Looking at some of Shakes- peare's descriptions• he came to this: "Of a Pleasing look, a Cheerful eye, and a most noble Carriage: as proper a man as we will see in a summer's day." That" described the late Coun- cillor Birtles. There was no better description of Councillor Birtles than that written 400 years ago by the poet Wotton : Whose passions not his masters are. Whose soul is still prepared for death, This man is freed from servile bands Of hope to rise, or fear to fall; Lord of himself, though not of lands, And having nothing, yet hath all. Councillor Roberts's Tribute.

Councillor ROBERTS, speaking on behalf of the Education Committee, referred to Councillor Birtles' educational work upon the School Attend- ance Committee and Medical Inspection Com- mittee, to which committee he gave of his best, because the questions involved especially ap- pealed to his character. The interest of children was also in front of anything he had to do. In the death of Mr. Birtles he had lost not only' a colleague but one of his best personal friends. (If ear, hear.) 7 The resolution was carried by the members silently rising in their places.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS IN THE STREETS
div.p: DRUNKENNESS IN THE STREETS
The Fears of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League.

div.head: COUNCIL DISCUSSION.
div.p: COUNCIL DISCUSSION.
Alleged "Libel" on the Working-
classes and the Police.

Some members of the Warrington Council on Tuesday were inclined to resent the Communi- cation received by the Watch Committee from the Citizens' Temperance League on the ques- tion of drunkenness in the streets.

The Watch Committee's minutes, moved by the MAxon and seconded by Dr. JOSEPH, stated that a letter was read from the' Warrington Citizens' Temperance League containing the fol- lowing resolution;- which was referfed to the Chief Constable: "That this Executive Com- mittee of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League views with apprehension the amount of drunkenness on the streets of Warrington, espe- cially among young' people, and in view of the danger to citizenship respectfully urges the Watch Committee to instruct the police to exercise increased vigilance as to the public- houses where such intoxicants are obtained,"

div.head: Pathetic and Tragic.
div.p: Pathetic and Tragic.

Councillor HENSHALL, who drew attention to the matter, asked if the Executive Committee of the League had submitted any facts. In raising the question he was expressing no senti- ment in the matter, but he thought they were 'agreed, whether they were rabid teetotalers or not, it was regrettable, pathetic, and even tragic if it was true that there was an increase in drunkenness among the young people. He wondered if there were any fresh facts brought before the Watch Committee, or had informa- tion been supplied by the (Thief Constable?
Alsrou : We had simply this resolution ,tore us; with no other facts, and we-referred it to the Chief Constable, who we expect will report to us next Thursday.
"Not Foul His Own Nest."

Councillor BROADHURST contended that to his own knowledge drunskenness in Warrington was decreasing. There was now less drunkenness and less immorality than in any town it was possible to visit. He had travelled in many towns, and he would not foul his own nest. He had visited towns from the South of England to the North of Scotland, and Warrington did not come out second best. He had been thinking about the matter, and he considered that the resolution of the League was a libel on the working classes of the town, a libel on the police, and on the Watch Committee and the Chief Constable.

If there had been some young peraiins who had been under the influence of drink it should be remembered that as long as they were not dis- orderly the police could not take action. (A Voice: "Don't be tod sure ri') He wanted to say a word in favour of the Chief Constable, whom he had previously criticised in that Chamber, and he believed that, irrespective of classes and creed, the Chief Constable would do his duty when the occasion required it without fear or favour. (Hear, hear.)

Noisy " Night Birds." Councillor SuAw drew attention to noises at night. There was so much noisy rowdyism in the street and neighbourhood where he lived, that it was hardly possible to go to sleep until 12.30 or 1 a.m. He thought some request might be made to the Chief Constable to try to find a remedy. Councillor WILSON said it was with pain he read the minutes of the 'Watch Committee. He thought Warrington had as good .a record as any town. A few years ago one might have gone into public-houses and found men and women sitting drinking, but they would not find that state Of things to-day, and unless people were prepared to place the charge on the table no notice should be taken of it. He went through the town every night during the Christmas holidays, , and even in the lowest - parts of the town he did not see a single case of. drunkenness between 10 and 11 o'clock at night. People should not be called drunk because they were a little bit noisy. It was a Slur upon their good old town that the resolu- tion had been put on the agenda.

div.head: Town End Improvement.
div.p: Town End Improvement.

Councillor Gorou thought the committee had been well advised in referring the matter to the Chief Constable. He could speak to the fact that there had been an- improvement in the drinking habits of the people, especially at Town's End. He gave credit to the Chief Con- stable for what he had done in the matter. His .men regularly visited the public-houses at Town's End on Saturday night, and it had had the effect of minimising the drunkenness which had previously existed. He was a temperance man, but,what he was saying lie said conscien- tiously, and he believed there had been nu improvement. Councillor ROBERTS expressed the view that it would have been better had the Council with- held any criticism until they had heard the Chief Constable's 'report. There seemed to he a misconception as to the memorial, which de- plored the amount of drunkenness to be seen in the streets among young people. It did not for a moment suggest there was an. increase of drunkenness. He was absolutely confident that comparing Warrington of 20 years ago, or even less, with what it was now, there had been a decided im- provement in the general conduct of the people, especially on holidays and high days, but that there was still a deplorable amount of chin-ikon- ness no one would contest. He did not think they had ever had a 'more conscientious and capable officer than the Chief/Constable, and no one did his duty—and the position was not an easy one in view of the conflicting interests in- volved—more conscientiously and without the slightest regard to one side or the pther. Hav- ing said that, he hoped they would have no further discussion. (Laughter.) The minutes were Adopted.

div.head: FIELD •F PO- 6
div.p: THE FIELD •F PO- 6

LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP. The Postponed Final. Although the, Warrington F.C.- Committee were prepared- to offer their ground to-day for the final of the Lancashire Junior Cup between Rylands' and Abram Rangers, the offer could not be accepted, as Rylands'‘are taking part in the third qualifying round of the Northern Union Cup against Runcorn White Star. The date of the match will, therefore, have to be settled by the Lancashire County Committee next week. This is rather unfortunate, because the War- rington ground will now be engaged until the end of the season.

div.head: Pithy Pars About N.U. Games.
div.p: Pithy Pars About N.U. Games.

Next victims wanted! After Huddersfield, who Will be the next to succumb? Will it be Hull Kingston to-day? Let us hope so, at least.• A few more wins and Warrington are amongst the "Four." Did Huddersfield go home singing That well-known melody, "Oh! what a surprise—oh!" ? The Fartowners were too sore To sing at all, one would think.

e e o e (10 Clare made it " clare" to The men from Fartown That he was a hit to lively For the hottest amongst them. The Thelwall lad is truly " A broth- ov a bhoy, indade." If he does not get a ticket To the land of the Golden Fleece . Then many folk will be surprised. Fearnley would be a good mate to Go with Clare to the land "down under." Perhaps the six will go to Australia.

div.head: eet etc
div.p: eet etc

Dainteth has been resurrected. He came up fresh and active. There was plenty of "soul" in his play. AS, one of the cup-tie team he Must have enjoyed the revenge. He dropped a lovely goal and The 'crowd yelled with delight. And \well, indeed, they might. And then didn't he dodge? Huddersfield were completely bluffed By some of Dainteth's smart antics.- His play ought to make him a fixture. eeeoec

Fearnley's try was also a beauty. lie is a man who is "coming one" Chesters also gave a nice try. When he gets the chance the County man can well score. Ruddick was too tricky for The visiting defence, and one was Heard to remark that Ruddick is A greater demon at threequarter than at half. " The Examiner" has said so before. Once he could not get through his own side, He doubled to the right and got right away. e e e O.

Jolley we saw in Jolly mood. As at Huddersfield so at Vibilderspool. The "little 'un" rollicked in his work. Gleeson he effectively bottled up. He did the same at Fartown in September. The Huddersfield hare, didn't like it. If Jolly was jolly: Gleeson wasn't gleeful. Nicholas and Young_Aid very well. They were against THE great half-backs. The great TRES did not shine more brightly Than did the Warrington pair of half-backs. Wildman was beat by the pair every time. e 0 It looks as if the 1160' Will be won yet, boys! You have now shaken down, So keep up the pace and win. Few teams, after a strenuous list Of holiday engagements, could have so Decisively defeated Huddersfield As Warrington did on Saturday. But "Serum" always said they would.. A few more victories—the .tlOO is yours. And what about the NA." Cup? About that we must patiently wait and see.

Ca The "A's" did it also at Fetrtown. Who would have thought it with A rather weakened team? but A victory there was splendid. Brookes was responsible for a fine try. He is another one who is "coming on. Alec Brown was the other try—er. His was likewise a splendid effort. It was a pity neither was goaled. Still Warrington "A " won by a point. And it was something to be proud of To defeat the Fartowners on their own pitch.

Warrington "A" did not fare•so well Last season against the Fartowners. They were beaten 10-6 points. The seniors at Wilderspool were Beaten by 21 points against six. For the 40-3 points defeat in September, Warrington, have in their side of the book A 50 points to nil defeat of Huddersfield. This happened in the days of Jack Fish. He was responsible for 30 of the points. , Evidently the Warrington side is again turn- ing. The team seems the best since Fish's days.

- - Latchford Second commenced the second half. of their fixtures in great style by beating Sale "B"'14-0, the goal scorers being Minards (5), Fletcher (3), Tinsley (2), .Knight (2), Banks, and Furness.

To-day's Teams. To-day the first eleven meet South Manche:iv- ter with the following team: J. Bruhl; W. Fletcher and C. Billington; J. Albinson, J. B. Wilkinson and T. Banks; F. W. Isherwood, A. Dale, J. E. Pearson, D. B. Travis and A. Knight. Umpire, Mr. P. Grounds. • The second eleven are at home to South Manchester, with: G. I‘l"ynekyme; W. T. Eccles S. E. Parkhouse, F. C. STOCKTON HEATH V. FORMBY. Stockton Heath were at home to Formby on Saturday last, and won by seven goals against one. Last season Stockton Heath won by six goals against two at Formby. From the bully Partridge got away on the right wing and pass- ing acro'ss; Richardson opened the scoring for Stockton Heath. The home team continued to press, Baxter scoring after 20 minutes. Baxter :ran right through from the bully, the goalkeeper putting behind, Richardson scoring from the corner. Partridge, with a fine shot from near the goal line, scored the fourth goal for Stock- ton Heath. Just on half-time Ayer scored from a weak clearance by the Formby goalkeeper. 'Half-time: Stockton Heath, five goals; Formby, nil. From the bully the home forwards got away. Baxter scoring in the first minute. Formby , now improved, and after a short spelA of attack- ing Leytham scored. The visitors were now playing up strongly, and: a'little steadiness in the circle would have increased their score. Play was now fairly even until ;just on time, when the home team attacked strongly. Ayer scoring. Result: Stockton Heath, seven goals; Formby, one goal.

SO the rather. despised Warrington side have beaten the Hercules of N.U. football' Hudders- field came to Warrington determined to wint, sure to win and win they did not. Not so long 'ago I was hailed as an extreme optithist when 1 ventured to say Warrington would defeat the giants at Wilderspool, even some of the War- rington Club members were inclined to laugh at my remarks—aud.now, he who laughs last is entitled to laugh best. • Anyone who keeps in touch • with the NAL game could see what was happening. Warring- have within the last month or so come along , wonderfully-, and their improved form has been 'to mere flash in the pan. It has been slow, steady and sure. - Huddersfield, on the other hand, have not improved in form, and they have not gone back. Theirs has been a sort of mark- time, and while they have not degenerated hare not advanced as have 'Warrington, we glrl, and other teams. ; It became patent „ :e" ago that Huddersfield would not walk (3r everY side, as they did last season, and ins one was able to forecast their fttte wv saw happen on Saturday.

war i A FINE VICTORY. excellergton's 14 points to 8 points win was v. ), six clear I r, and although the home side just won Points, the victory was as fine a one for Warrin f Ituddersfi 1g c' n as was the 40 points to three for Wilderspool we saw e d at Fartown on Bth September. At tw and trained . o about equally balanced teams, at Fartown we witnessed a ,superbly trained side in Huddersfield and a less well trained team in Warringtofl. t,•; was training alone ,could only that 'told in the Vartown match varly in September, and the result was what one expect between a tuned up thirteen and a side not merely •up to concert pitch. Of -course, some critics are making the usual apolo- gies for Huddersfield, but why it ;is difficult to understand, except it be that Huddersfield, like a beaten school bully, cannot take defeat in a scrupulously fair fight. Warrington's win was no fluke; it was the result of grit and persever- ance, and the fact that they were pressing more than half the game proves it.

DAINTETH'S SPLENDID GOAL The start of the game indiCated what was to come. Gleeson, the crack threequarter of Far- town, was soon sent on the run by a neat pass out from the scrum by Rogers. Nicholas dashed after Gleeson and promptly grounded him should I say "mudded" Min? Next Buddick was well away in the opposite direction, with his usual luck—pushed into touch. The best bout by the visiting threequarters followed. Tiosenfeld was tackled and Jolley found safety with a long kick well up in touch. Warringtonwaenei came. up • and pressed hard. The tiits first reaPPetl out to Dainteth, who celebrated PPCup earance against Huddersfield since p„at final 1)Y dropping a splendid goal. This hlood a • 6 necessary fire into the Warriegtonian 11 ] and Huddersfield could not get further n mid-field; It PENALTY GOAL AND THE REST. •‘,lll F tho course of an affray within the artown =5" one of the Huddersfield nien was penal- ised. The kick was taken from a diffittalt angle, ',lit Jolley does hc.st- sit, these circumstanees, and landed a fine goal. This came as a surprise to , Iluddersfield, but the yell of delight from the 'Peetators showed how they appreciated the tour Points lead. • The visitors' style of play was now completely Upset, the automatic passing game was at a dig- vount against the bustling Warrington forwards and the ever-alert half-backs. The home pack Webi] next in evidence. A quickly broken up -scrum saw Fearnley dashing away, with the ball in possession. He neatly bluffed Rogers .and others and grounded a fine try just behind the post. Jolley declined the kick—his forte is 4Lngle goaling—and Nicholas essayed the task. Beautifully the ball sailed across the bar— Warrington nine points, Huddeisfyd nil. do. BOTH SIDES SCORE. After this there seemed to be a spirit of -desperation in the Huddersfield play possibly they felt that a large score was in the brew against them. Rogers got the ball away from the scrum in a more nippy fashion than he had • Yet done, and lie sent his threequarters on. one of their characteristic runs. Moorhouse and Rosenfeld handled before the ball reached "Leeson. The latter's pace told and he crossed the line with a try. The goal-kick failed, and Warrington's lead was reduced to six points. The Warrington forwards were soon on their dribbling game, and Clare, gathering the sphere, Passed back to Dainteth, who gained additional . ground, handed the -ball. with his Messing, to Bradshaw, and the captain seemed on the verge • of scoring a fine try. He ran too near the line, and the Huddersfield defence played the only :saving game, which was to put Bradshaw into touch. A minute or two later Warrington marked and Jolley goaled. The interval found - Warrington, 4 goals 1 try (11 points); Hudders- field, 1 try (3 points). A STUBBORN SECOND HALF. The second half was stubbornly fought. Had- •-41ersfield added five points and Warrington three • to their score respectively. The visitors started in a sensational manner. Almost from the Warrington "25" Bogers handed the ball on to Rosenfeld, and from him the sphere travelled backwards through his comrades on the line. Wildman, the stand-off half-back, was the last kfte I"an in Possession and scored. Holland goaled. ida uddersfield had much more of the the sound defence of the home ym from further augmenting their dashing exhib ito Warrington were gwokeiiren übpy, and Nicholas,s e ,I);elllstteeit,slll:aßteurddick and Bradshaw, hut score they could not. As time was drawing nigh ioriaas scored onteheof his chadfacteristic tries. a splendidly fought goal, an tou b Faun? resulted in a fine win for Warring'als 2 tries (14 p ~ oints) to 1 goal tiles Points). , A SURPRISE ? NOT QUITE s lehlo soz3ni.e.the result is supposed to have come •'r a surprise. It could not be characterised as withotd doubt the better team wofb ;knee ViTilder spool men in every sense deserved dav,vintiorY; they were the better team on the is 4 8 Play. In a sense the match was remin- t of -the cup final at Headingley, but on th isil • of Warrington were on the right side, score sheet. AS one obrykshire critic puts it:leally Won Warrington controlling the ball and trusting to the impetuosity of their forwards to carry , 1 tl,lt.nn through." I would make an addition that Isluci (IS Was the most effective game to play against ee a machine-like combination as the lind- I isfi eld side. The game was to make the tilitliv'ine lump a cog and run out of gear, and tl reenusit.Bist what Warrington did, and we saw

upset the Huddersfield onlY perfect line—the threcquarters. The prompt way the Warring- tonians broke up the scrums; and the way they were, down upon the visiting,half-backs ere they could part with the ball, wiis'a treat to watch, and a sore thorn in the Huddersfield flesh. Clare and Fearnley were more conspicuous in this, and it is doubtful if a brace of forwards could be found in the League equal to them. The other four did well. • Nicholas Q. nd Young were pitted against Tni half-backs of the League, but their lights were not hidden under a bushel. They cOmpared quite favourably with Rogers and Wildman.

DAINTETH'S RESURRECTION. Naturally, in point of combined, aggressive work the Warrington threequarters were not in the same class with the Huddersfield quartet, and no one would expect them to be so, but the Warrington four played a fine game, and In tackling they were superior to the superioi quartet. Ruddick, Tranter and Bradshaw were hard workers all the way. ' Dainteth was the J 1). n Ja3.ost in the spectators' eye. His fine goal has already been referred to, and there was no more aggressive " three " on the field than was Dainteth. His bluffing tac- tics bathed his opponents. . In a word, Dainteth surprised everyone, and he should now be a fixture in the threequarter line. Jolley played up to his usual standard and was a glutton for work. Few mistakes he made, and if he had the score would have been different. The fact that GleeGon did so little .is an eloquent, tribute, "1 to 'the: fine work acc plished by Warrington's little, alert back.' 7* WAS THEIR miss ION?

_ I was pleased to see present at the Hudders- field, match the two managers who will take out the Northern Union team to Australia—Messrs. Clifford, of Huddersfield, and Houghton, of St. Helens. These gentlemen will' have a large voice in the selection of the team, and, after the way the Warrington men showed how they can play, particularly the forwards, there should be no doubt as to the invitations that will come in this direction.

WARRINGTON'S LEAGUE POSITION. Recent matches ~have wonderfully improved the Warrington team's position in the League table. They have now reached seventh place, and in the matter of points for and against they are once more almost on a level, with 151 for and 152 against, this despite the heavy drubbing at Huddersfield and defeats elsewhere. There Seems every chance of them not only greatly improving upon that, but of them at least finishing in the first four. If the present form is maintained they should soon be in one of the four positions at the top.

WARRINGTON "A" WIN BY A FOINT. A Fine Achievement at Fartawn. Warrington " A," with rather a weakened team, made the trip to Huddersfi43ld and gained a fine victory by the odd point in eleven, an achievement of which the Warringtonians had every reason to be proud. The final score of six points for Warrington against five for Hud- dersfield 'indicates the level character of the game... _

In the first half Warrington had rather the greater share of the game, and a splendid try was scored by Brookes. This was not converted and the interval found Warrington leading by three points. In the second portion some fine play was shown by both sides, and A. Brown scored again for Warrington. Another attempt at goal failed. Then Huddersfield came away with a dribble, and Howell Davies, the Welsh Internationalist, scored. Holroyd got the goal. The game ended: Warrington, two tries; Huddersfield, one goal one try.

WARRINGTON TEAM MUCH CHANGED. Stan. Young on the Injured List. The Warrington Committee have been com- pelled, owing to injuries and other causes, to make several changes in the team which goes to Hull to-day to meet the Kingston Rovers. On the other hand, the Rovers are at full strength, and are playing the side which recently defeated Wigan. Stan. Young, who has not recovered from the gruelling he got in the Wigan match, is under medical treatment and cannot possibly turn out. Dainteth, in consequence, goes back into the half-back line. Bradshaw has been dropped, and Ruddick makes his first appearance on the right wing, Waywell going on the left. With even this re-organised team Warrington should be able to es give a good account of themselves and i a win s just possible. The sides will be:
WARRINGTON. Jolley. Waywell, Dickenson, Tranter, Ruddick. Nicholas, Dainteth. Cox, _Cheaters, Skelhotne, Clare, Thomas, l'earnley. •
Mann. olleponald, Hoskins, 'Trump, Sandham, Moore, Watson, McGeiver. Lord, Oliver, Hicks, Marshall. Carmichael. KINGSTON ROVERS.

NEW FACES AMONG THE "A's." Fearnley's Brother Gets a Trial. Wigan Highfield are engaged in the qualify- ing round of the N.U. Cup, and consequently ! cannot fulfil their engagement with the "A" team at Wilderspool to-day. A friendly has been fixed up with Sutton. In the "A's will appear several new faces. Page and Aspinall, two locals of mudi promise, are given a trial amongst the threequarters. Worrall is another newcomer, and G. Fearnley, brother of the crack forward, now playing for Cadishead, should do well in the forward line. The Warrington team, who ought to win com- fortably, will be: Jordan; Baker, Page, C. Brown, Aspinall; A. Brown, Brookes; Naylor, Harmer, Green, Boardman, Worrall, G. Fearn- ley.

RE-ARRANGED FIXTURES. At a meeting of the N.U. League on Tuesday night the following matches were re-arranged : Barrow v. St. Helens, from March 7 to January 17; Rtmeorn V. Warrington, from January 1 to March 18; Runcorn v. Rochdale Hornets, from January 3 to March 25; Swinton v. Salford, from January 1 to January 17; and Warrington "A" v. Runcorn "A," from January 1 to February 28.

div.p: WHAT HAS GONE.WRONG WITH STOCKTON HEATH?

The chief match was the meeting of Latchford and L in the preliminary round for the AitrinYni chamin' Amateur Oup, and Latchford secured a 4-71 in. There is great rejoicing in the are now pitted against Oughtrington United in the Ist round of the competition proper, and as tile team i atch have notcampover this result, as they forgotten' the defeat in the Ist round of the, Senior Cup they are out for revenge this time. , „ In the Warrington and District League, First Division, Stockton Heath and the Weaver Re- fining Company Played their return match at West-avenue. In the first meeting of these clubs the game ended in a division of points, and in the return it was up to the " Heathens," in order to keep in the running for the top place, to secure both points in this mateu, but such did not happen and the game was drawr. Great Sankey had Weston as visitors to the Penketh Recreation Ground in their return fixture, and the home club were minus a player the whole of the game. However, they proved themselves too good for their visitors, and ulti- mately won by five goals to none. One of the keenest and most interesting games in the .League took place at Moore between Daresbury and Crosfield's. The result was a win for Daresbury by one goal to nil. There was much enthusiasm in the home camp, as this was their first victory in the League.

ALTRINCHAM AMATEUR CUP. . Preliminary Round. Latchford v. Lymin• At Thelwall-lane. Neither team were fully represented, E. Webb and Hindes being the absentees, both of them preferring to play for Altrincham instead of their own clubs, Teams: Latchford—Kite; Haspell and .Robinson; Sid_ dall, Downs and Carter; S. Smith, P. Webb, Lees, Fogg, and Tinder. Lymm—Haddon ; Clare and Taylor; Daniels, Woods and Lee; Barber, Guest, Whitfield, Jones and Owens. Referee, Mr. F. Shaw, Northwich. The home- sters made a raid on the visitors' goal, when Taylor relieved with -a timely kick, but the visitors' forwards found the home half •ba?.ks in their best humour and they were compelled to retire to their own half, where the game uas carried on for the first fifteen minutes. The Lytnm backs and goalkeeper had a busy time. From a goal-kick they gained a little relief, but their forwards could not get past the home defenders, and their visits were only of a brief duration. Downs made a long pass out to the right. Taylor missed the ball and Smith beat him in the race for possession, and the latter finished with a good oblique shot, which : beat Haddon. This was one of the best goals ever seen scored on the ground. From the centre_ kick the visitors made strenuous efforts to retrieve, but they were met in a stubborn fashion by Haspell and Robinson, the ball never reaching Kite. Half-time found the seer, in favour of Latchford by one goal to nil. ' Tinder made a fine attempt, but failed with his final shot. However, he made amends, and, being successful in snapping up a centre from the right, scored the second goal. The visitors' goal was hotly besieged, ffaddon saving many well-intended shots. The home team were driven back by offside tactics, when Lees made a splendid individual effort, tipped the ball just over the visitors' backs, rushed between them, and registered a third goal. The visitors, stung by these reverses, made a determined attempt, and for a short time theY did not meet ... ith success, but when near the home goal they appealed for a penalty, which was awarded them. Owen was entrusted with the kick and he successfully beat Kite. This made the home ' team respond with more enthusiasm, and again the visitors' goal was hotly bombarded. Respell came down the field from the back divisiou to •help his forwards, and he managed to steer the ball past Haddon for a fourth time. Result: Latchford, four goals; LYinin, one goal. \ Smith was the most dangerous forward On the home side. The half -backs were good, and Haspell has proved himself a worthy successor to Bardsley. Robinson Played his usual re- sourceful game, while, liite in goal had only three or four shots to stop during the vhole game. The visitors have to thank lladdon that the score against thou was not doubled, as lie had many awkward shots to deal with. Clare and Taylor played well, as also did Woods. Owens was the best forward of only a moderate line. ,_.—... —____--- ,

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.I Division. First x Great Sankey v. Weston. On the Penketh Recreation Ground. Teams: Great Sankey—Bond; Gloveran Stephens; Ire- ! land, Gardiner and Payne; "Ltrlington,, Poulter; Houghton and Ditchfield. Weston—Nancolli; . Barnes and Woods; Smith, AaPeY and Leach; ! Flanigan, Kirkham, Coow9', Hope and Hulse. The home forwards took the ; v-sitors by sur- prise by taking the ball from the kick-off and combining very well, and this led to their first goal within half a minute. , The homesters came again with a fine run by Darlington, but th,e danger was .-cleared in a half-hearted fashion. Penner registered a second goal, Nancollis mak- hir, a splendid,, attempt to save. Darlington aadded a third goal, and Hongl iton got a fourth. The interval found the home team leading by four goals. On resuming play was more even and in mid- field, until Payne set Hough ton gcdng, the latter sending in a grand shot, which Navaeollis saved. Foll3wing this the visitors had a period of defensive play, and Woo _dm. Frs, Barnes ' and Aspey displayed good form. , Nancollis rom a break- away they came near to scoring, awing to a mis- understanding between Bond and Stephens, Conwayl3 final shot going the wrung- side of the l'post. Houghton scored t i the fifth and best goal !of the match. The home team won by five goals i to none.

(30:n liWigilkainn Wilkinson; Evans, ' Stockton Heath- v. Weaver Refining Co. On the West Avenue ground. The visitors Id only muster ten .players.osl Teams—Stock-' could Jefferson; 1.14-I:atorioil:dlisw°Glatrd ; Woodhead, Sankey, Vernon. Weaver Jones, Simcock and 1 d Refining Referee, S. C. Essenhigh. The Beans and Johnston; Leicester. Newton, All- tCGoll Glover, : heath:e Collier;De'l with a rush and some fine this success the visitors vecolsemiktboailnisllcitteiPaononilevelialelltv. laveeu their forwards brought them into the home goal area. Johnston opened and the home delViTee the score with a shot that completely beat Har- 1 rpilsaoyne.d wit m Encouragedoe i vim, was seVerely taxed. They were again beaten by Evans, who registered a second goal for the visitors. The home team did not appear to be able to get. into their stride, and the opposing half-backs held the forwards in check and kept the ball in the home.half• Beans added a third goal with a long shot which beat Harrison. Jones scored finely for the Heathens. At the interval the visitors were leading by three goals to one.
By " LillOSMane"'

The homesters next showed up to better ad- vantage and were soon at the visitors' end. Sim- cock, getting possession, passed out to Vernon on the left. The latter raced along the lines and with his final shot he beat the visitors' cus- todian, and registered the second goal for the home team. The home team failed to improve on several corner kicks. On time approaching the homesters made,a final rally, and Vernon was suecessful in equalising the score. Result: Stockton 'Heath, three goals; Weaver Refining Co., three goals.

Daresbury v. Crosfield's Reserve. At Moore. Teams—Daresbury: Ravenscroft; De Prez and Forster; Cash, Forster aqd Ryder; De Prez, Hallam, Forster, Lee-Jones and Fors- ter. Crosfield's Reserve: Ellison; Claymore and Calligan; Collins, Worrall and Pagett; Rowlands, Munn, Sherratt and Jackson. For a while play was confined to midfield, where the exchanges were very evenly distributed, but as the interval was drawing near the home team played up more strongly, and a neat pass out to Forster on the left, the latter worked into a favourable position centred well in the goal- mouth, where Lee-Jones dashed up and scored a capital goal for the homesters. Half-time was called with the home team leading by 1-0. The visitors went off with, a rush, but the home defence was on the alert and proved too good for the visiting forwards. Towards the close the visitors made strenuous efforts to equalise, but owing to fine goalkeeping by 'Raveriscroft and partly bad shooting by the visitors, no score was made, and when the final whistle blew the result was: Daresbury, one goal; Crosfield's Reserve, nil. .

div.head: Second Division.
div.p: Second Division.

Emmanuel Old Boys V. Orford St. John's. In Victoria Park. Good , play 'by the Boys' half-back line resulted in IsherWood making an individual effort, and beating the opposition, passed the ball out to Wainwright, who corn- Pleted a fine effort by sending the ball past Forber, with a rattling good shot, thus open- ing the score. There was no further scoring, and the result was: Emmanuel Old Boys, one goal; Orford St. John's, none.

div.head: LEAGUE MEETING.
div.p: THE LEAGUE MEETING.

- - - The monthly meeting of the Warrington ana District League was held last Tuesday night at the Lion Hotel, Mr. Wright occupying the chair. There was a good attendance of delegates, and a lengthy business agenda was gone through, at the conclusion of which the secretary placed before the meeting the report of the sub-com- mittee with respect to the Minor Medal Compe- tition, which they had decided to hold during the present season. The rules were read and ap- proved, and it was decided that the first round should be played on the first Saturday in Febru- ary, the competition being open to • all junior clubs within ten miles of Market Gate. , The Secretary reported that the committee of the League had been presented with a cup, to be played for, its an open age competition, open to all clubs in the Warrington area. Rules and regulations for the same will be presented to the next meeting. Mr. Starkey, dentist, War- rington, is the donor of the cup, which in all probability will be on view in the town at an early date.

ASSOCIATION ITEMS. - The Latchford team have taken three points from their near and dear rivals—Lymm. For Latchford's two homes matches, Christ- mas Day and New Year's Day, no official referee put in an appearance. Haddon, the Lymm custodian, gave a brilliant exhibition on New Year's Day at Latchford. _ .

Without a doubt, he is one of the best goal- keepers in the North Cheshire League. In the Warrington and District League, First Division, Great Sankey and the Adult School teams are yet undefeated. The Warrington Excelsior are also undefeated in the Second

---..-- - - hi the Widnes and District Minor Medal Competition there are three Warrington League clubs in the semi-final. Orford St. John's are looked upon as favourites for the medals. In the Altrinchain Amateur Cup preliminary round Latchford proved victors against Li.rmm by four goals to one. _ Smith was the best forward on the field, mak- ing many sparkling runs on the extreme right, and scored one of the best goals ever seen got on the Thelwall-lanegrou,nd.

Haddon, in goal, for the visitors, gave a splendid exhibition, in spite of the four goals that beat him. E. Foster, the captain of Crosfield's Recrea- tion, and their inside-left, has had an extended trial during the holidays with the Middles- brough reserve team. He has given every: satisfaction, scoring three goals, besides making splendid openings for his colleagues. He has taken -part in fire matches, all of which have been won.
