div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1914.
DISTRICT NEWS.
Continued from Page 11.
GRAPiEiN HALL.
Confirmation.—ln the provisional list of con- firmations for the current year it is announced that the Bishop .of Chester will confirm at Grappenhall Church on Tuesday. March 3rd.

Choir Social.—The choir and friends of the Independent Methodist Church held a very in- teresting social on Wednesday night, foll-Wing upon their arduous task of Christmas carolling, when they handed over a little above ..t2O to- wards the purchase of a piano for the use of the church. The order of the evening was a hotpot supper, followed by an entertainment, ' consisting of gramophone selections, games and singing, under the direction of Mr. Gough.

Parish Church.—The scholars attending the! Parish Church were given their annual treat! on Thursday night. Book prizes were distri- ! bUted for attendance and conduct. Mrs. Far- rant, of Victoria-road, made the presentations,' and was supported by the Rector and Mrs. Pigot. The much coveted prize for the choir- boys, which is given by Mr. A. Down, was secured by James Shepherd. Mr. W. Parkin- , son, of Warrington, gave a cinematograph ex- hibition, which added greatly to the enjoyment ,of the evening. The film of the recent Royal visit came in for a special round of applause.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
Women's Guild.—The annuartea Nmg--given in St. Mary's Infant School on Thursday evening. A concert, arranged by Mr. Owen, proved a great success.

Labour Party Children.—The Labour party gave the children a merry time on Saturday. Mrs. P. Davies and a band of hard-working ladies splendidly carried through the arrange- ments. Toys from the Christmas tree were dis- tributed by Mr. P. Davies, an ideal " Fathez Christmas."

div.head: WELL-KNOWN WESLEYAN'S DEATH.
div.p: WELL-KNOWN WESLEYAN'S DEATH.

Mr. Bell, of Chapel-road, died on Saturday in his 50th year. Born at Workington, he started life in the employ of the late Mr. Wil- liam Walker, tanner, Whitehaven, and after a short period there he came to Penketh, and had been an employe of the Penketh Tanning Co. ever since. _

The deceased, who was of a quiet disposition, was an earnest worker, and the loss to the Wes- leyan Church will be great. Nearly all the offices open to a layman, both in the church and Sunday school, he had held. Mr. Bell held office in the Penketh Labour party. He was a most ardent supporter of the temperance cause and was a life member of the Ancient Order of Rechabites. • The funeral took place on Tuesday at Sankey Cemetery. A service was held in the Wesleyan Church, the Revs. Gunnell and Middlewood officiating. Mr. C. E. Parker also spoke of the good work Mr. Bell had done during his life.

div.head: RIGHT OF WAY QUESTION.
div.p: RIGHT OF WAY QUESTION.
District Council Now Move in the
Matter.,
EVIDENCE TO BE GATHERED.

The Penketh right-of-way question was again discussed at the ktural District Council meet- ing on Wednesday. The Clerk reported having written to Capt. Hughes, detailing all the particulars of the grievance, and stating that the Council having received a clearly expressed resolution, passed at a Parish Council meeting, felt it their duty to enforce the powers provided by Statute in that behalf. He asked Capt. Hughes to remove the obstacles. and allow free use of the path within the present month. Capt. Hughes had replied to the effect that he had nothing further to add to his previous replies, and stating that he would hold the Council responsible for any damage and tres- pass. He would like to know the date when they would remove the obstacles, so that he could have a representative there, in order that full proof could be given in any proceedings. The Clerk observed that he had not discovered any ground upon which a technical objection could be raised. Councillor Garnett: If the navigation on the river were to increase its it decreased 40 years ago, the boatmen would find it an advantage to use this path. The Chairman: Is it likely or possible to in- crease? Councillor Garnett: Ask Mother Shipton. I could not answer that.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Parish Council—The quarterly meeting of Council was held in the C.E. Schoolroom on Wednesday. ' Mr. R. Denham Presided. A letter was read from Mr. William Bennett, in which he urged that if the present drainage systems were improved by piping, not be necessary to incur expenditure &c., it would the large of an elaborate scheme of sewage for a consider- able number of years. The Clerk was instructedto interview the Surveyor of the Rural District Council, and obtain his opinion as to the prac- ticability of the suggested improvements, in Tidal-lane and Bruche-avenue.

Tea Meeting.—This annual gathering in con- nection with Christ Church took place on Thurs- day. A larger number than usual sat down to a substantial tea, provided under the able super- intendence of Mrs. Grounds. The Vicar (Rey. G. W. Dickinson) opened the entertainment. in a brief review of the principal events affecting the church during the past year. A dialogue, " Who's who?" was rendered by four young ladies. The "Dandy Coons," who provided the entertainment, proved themselves a Pierrot troupe of no mean order. Their leader, Mr. W. H. Rigby, is to be congratulated on the refine- ment and cleverness of his troupe.

Wesleyan Tea.—The annual tea meeiiing in connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School was held on Thursday. The entertainment which followed was presided over by Dr. Ben- nett. The report for the year was presented on behalf of the Sunday School Council by Mr. A. Ward. It showed that the total income frem all sources was .tB4 18s. 7d. The total number of scholars at the end of the year, inclusive of a cradle roll of 35, was 333. The officers elected for the present year are: Superintendents, Messrs. Wright and Roscoller; secretaries, Messrs. A. Ward, L. Bennett and R. Lunt; treasurer, Mr. Gaudy; club secretary and librarian, Mr. George Brough. The miscel- lanepus entertainment provided reached a high level. The programme was sustained by Miss Dorothy London, Mr. Warburton. Miss Nichol- son, Miss Ella Royston, Mr. Hawthorne (31an- chesfer), and Mr. Ir. M. Ashton.

div.head: HATTON.
div.p: HATTON.

Farmer's Death.—The death of a prominent Hatton farmer, Mr. Henry Mawdsley, of Quiesty Birch Farm, occurred on Thursday. Mr. Mawdsley was a prominent figure in the local shows. a lover of all English sports, and a large man of genial presence.
"OUR NAVY" AT NEW PICTURE HOUSE.

-- The programme at the New • Picture House for next week promises to be of unusual inter-, est, mainly by the fact that Parts 1 and 2 (Monday and Thursday) of "Our Navy" will be shown. The pictures describe life in the Navy from the, recruiting stage onwards, and are the only authentic films taken of the subject.' • -

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
REALISM AT THE ROYAL.
"The Ever Open Door" Amid the Slums and the Palaces of Westminster.

This week the Royal Court Theatre has given us an intellectual treat in bringing to the town "The Ever Open Door," one of the many suc- cessful productions of Mr. A. M. Loader. The Ever Open Door" is one of the most I realistic plays ever staged. The extremes of abject poverty and overwhelming misery and of unnecessary and unjust riches are presented on the stage cheek by jowl just as they jostle each other in the slums and palaces of Westminster.: It is a masterpiece in its way, and amounts tq a serious indictint,nt of the social condition of civilised England. The work of a rescue home for children has been selected with unerring wisdom as the medium through which to reveal a canker that sadly needs eradicating—it is the children that suffer, and it is the children in whom the true hope of the future resides. It is a remarkable play and grips the attention of the most blase of theatregoers from begin- ning to end. It is unique in its way, because the ordinary hero and heroine have no place. Substituted we have the child-life of the sons and daughters of the slums. The play, as acted by the splendid company at the theatre this week, is one to be remembered. Robbie, as por- trayed by Miss Vida Flower, leaves absolutely ntyoptehin g at without all atnoy exaggeration and delineates be desired. She gives us the the character with faithfulness and skill. Mr. Wilfred E. Payne shows us with dignity what a polished schemer can be. Ile is to be con- gratulated upon the fact that, even in his angry moments, he never forgets that he must live up to his blue blood and act the gentlemanly villain, Lord Dereham, with due deference to his aristocratic lineage. Miss Jamieson, as Miriam, is convincing that above all else the children must be cared for, and in this light her acting appeals to us. Miss Maude Locker, as Molly, is splendid in showing us the type of a low-class woman of the slums. She brings out its idiosyncrasies with all the characteristics belonging to such an individual. Mr. F. Beres- ford played his part as Father Clement with dignity due to his clerical profession and stood out with forceful vigour in his various and try- ing positions. Mr. Harry McClelland wafted us back to Dickens' Land, for we saw in him, as Jim Dundon, a worthy confrere of his prototype, Bill Sikes. His "make-uP" was fine, and his acting even more excellent. Mr. Miller Wilson, as Swankie Dottles, was inimitable, and his quaint style irresistible. Charles Grenville played his part as Sergeant in a forceful manner and quite with a policeman-like air showed us the dignity of duty. The lively Sister Lil (Miss Margaret Withers) makes us understand that in spite of dismal surroundings, low quarters, and squalid slums, one can.stilt be happy. Miss Anna Cuka's Maggie was pathetically touching. She played her child-life in the slums in a most realistic manner. The worthy M.P., Hon. C. Aveling, was finely acted by Mr. Fred Castle- man, wile brought out his timorous qualms at finding himself alone in squalid Westminster with real ability. nary was acted very beau- tifully by Miss Adah Rothwell, and Mr. David Kemp, as Tom Slater, was ably Portrayed. The other members of the company played their parts with skill. The scenery was exceptionally fine in its reality. In the second act. the scene of the Black Bull, Peter-street, was wonderful, and readily took one back (if one has ever been in such squalid surroundings) to the dismal slums in our great cities and its ever flaunting, gaily- lighted gin palaces. The church scene was mag- nificent, with its stained glass windows above the altar, decorated with candles and crucifix. Rarely has a truer representation of a sacred edifice been seen anywhere on the stage. The dresses, too, were quite the latest fashion and extremely pretty. To the success of this Play, as of all the others which come to the theatre, the ever-energetic and indefatigable enthusiasm of the acting manager is largely - accountable.

- - DISTINGUISHED VISITORS. Mr' G. it. Sims visited the Royal Court on Tuesday present last night. 13oth expressed pleasure night and Sir Joseph Beecham was at the way the play has been presented locally. There have been large houses during the week.

' " DICK WHITTINGTON " NEXT WEEK. King Pantomime is to Nightingale, again reign at the Royal Court Theatre next week, when an ex- cellent company will be brought by Mr. Richard who will Pr° duce "Dick Whit- tington." This well-known itself admirably '`. panto " lends to fresh adaptations, and "Dick ng Whittington," as it will be presented on Monday night, will be plus manY pleasing and nerd variations. There will be an array of charm- i ladies in new dresses, and the numerous scenes will all be new. The dances and the singing will be a special feature: A charming principal boy has been found n Miss Doriy Ross. and we can truthfully say she will please. i Idle Jack will receive full attention from Bob Stevens, who is no stranger to similat char- acters. The performance will be given twice nightly.

div.head: "CHINA SHOP" FUN AT THE HippoDROBIE.
div.p: "CHINA SHOP" FUN AT THE HippoDROBIE.

The varietydrome this week is only excelled by the superb ominates in the fast and furious of the--programme at the Hippo- drome quality of the "turns" appearing. Fun, of the pantomimical sketch, " Fan in a China Shop," presented by Howard and Collinson trio. The comedy element is introd order, prod uced through the medium of a "doll," which is attached to a china clock, and the lady. who plays this part does so with consummate skill, for one Can scarcely see the flicker of an eyelid. Laughable knockabout passages are introduced, , and the whole is ludicrous to the extreme. A splendid shadowgraphic entertainment is given by Mr. and Mrs. Gordon Wilde. With the hands alone silhouettes of great men are shown on the cur- tain. Probably the best in this branch is that ! of King Edward VII. Additional items, hum- orous and otherwise, are given in a very skilful and Praiseworthy manner. The Two Rodriquez give a novel acrobatic act, which might appro- priately be termed ~ up the pole." Balanced on the shoulders of one is a long pole, at the top Of Which a horizontal bar is fastened, and it is on this that the other performer goes through a series of daring and marvellous tricks. Mdlle. Quin's dogs Perform a number of clever tricks, which prove that much time and Patience has been expended in their training. Cissie Lupin° is a clever, character dancer, her changes being executed with commendable rapidity. Gordon Brown, the bey tenor, delights with, his singing. and Fannie Needham proves herself an ideal comedienne, her songs being breezy and catchy. Jeavon and Jena are loudly applauded for their clever entertainment in which they introduce balancing feats and tricks with dogs and pigeons. The pictures include “ Gussy Rides a Pony " and -ri " —eParture of the Orient liner, Orama, for Australia." .. _ _

"BABES IN THE WOOD." Pantomime holds sway at tb next week. "The Babes in the Wood" come to tell their popular story, and along with the " babes " will be Robin Hood and his merry Hippodrome men. The dashing outlaw will be played by Miss Maur Beaumont, and other parts will be taken by the following talented artistes : Miss Baia Walters, Sisters St. Julien, Miss Minnie Saunders, Miss Vi Saunders, Messrs. Fred Dun- stone, Goodall and Knox, Clarence Turner, Hilly Curzon, Walter Pearson, Bert Bose and Dudley Hoard. Laurie and Elsie will be the "Babes." The show teems with fun, good sing- ing and smart dancing. it should prove a great attraction.

"THE RED DUKE" AT PARK PALACE. There is every evidence that the management of the Park Picture Palace will give , a good exhibition next week, when the principal films willv b th e "The Re 4 Duke" and "Through e Cliouds." "A Message .from n Mars" is a sensa- tional picture that is to be here shortly.

div.head: COMEDY OF DULNESS.
div.p: A COMEDY OF DULNESS.
J. J. BELL (Author of " Wee Macgreegor," " Jack of All Trades," etc.).

"Why will people write dull books ?" Mrs. Methven murmured impatiently, flinging the red-covered novel aside and rising from the couch whereon she had been reclining for a long hour. " Life is dull enough in all con- science, without any addition from the lib- raries." Languidly she crossed the spacious drawing-room and halted by one of the large windows. She was a dark, handsome woman of twen- ty-five, and she had been a widow for over a year. The late Mr. Methven had married at an. age when the average man is either a grandfather or a confirmed bachelor. The or- phan girl on whom he had set his venerable but virgin heart had accepted him quite hon- estly for the home and wealth he could give her, yet she made earth such a cheerful place for him that he had been sorry indeed to leave it at sixty-eight. Now she was free, and rich enough to indulge her freedom as she chose, and—desperately dull. Few people were moving in the square on which she idly looked, but presently a tall, slight, black-coated figure caught he:: atten- tion.

" I do believe that is Dick Charterliouse,'' she said to herself, after a brief scrutiny. "Haven't seen him for years. How earnest he looks! It would be rather nice to have a chat with him again. Why does he not think of calling? He knows perfectly well that I live here."

The black-coated figure went on without Looking to right or left. On an impulse Mrs. Methvcn rushed to the bell. On the appearance of a maid she said quickly, but calmly— " Eliza, a clergyman has just passed the house—to the left. Run after him and say that I desire to speak to him." Roused from a dulness almost as heavy as that of her mistress, Eliza obeyed with alac- rity, "What a goose I am!" muttered Mrs. Methven. " I have nothing to say to him. I hope Eliza does not catch him." Ile entered the room, looking somewhat bewildered.

" It was good of you to come back," she said, after the formal greeting which was rather awkward on his part. "Good of you to ask me, Mrs. Methven. I have passed your house frequently, of late, and have intended calling upon you. ' "Bolton Square is paved with good inten- tions, I suppose. You have not come to see me since I was married. I never had a host of friends, you know." "You have been having a sad time," he began lamely. " Dulness, :leer dulness, is mv chief trou- ble at present I don't know What I want. But let us have tea, and please tell me about yourself." My-self !—a limited. subject, Mrs. Meth- yen. Only my work—" " It was always your work, I remember." " Ah! you remember! Well, well," he con- tinued, with a sigh, "there's nothing new to tell you. I go into the same sad corners as of yore, and I have to confess that I don't see much change for the better." ' The poor are strong conservatives," she remarked. "You remember when I tried my little hand at slumming ? Oh, dear! tha flesh was weak."

" Still," he went on, "it is my work—" She shook her head. " You don't believe in it ?" he asked quietly. " Well, you confess it is a failuse." " Oh, no," be returned quickly, with a note of bitterness; "I am the failure." " Why not give it up ? You've done your share of the dirty work. Now you deserve to be presented with a sweet little living in the country. The town appears to be wearing you out. Why, you look ofteen years older than at our last meeting. five years ago. You ought to have learned wisdom." "It is kind of you to consider my wel- fare," he said gravely, rem,nnbcring their last meeting. Mrs. Methven proceeded to pour' out tea. "Two lumps ?"- she asked lightly. " What a wonderful memory!" " Merely for trifles, Mr. Charterhouse. Do von know, you are making me feel almost merry ?" "You should always be merry," he ssaid softly. No; I ought to be serious, but I never get deeper than dulness." "But you must meet so many people now- adays. Surely—" " Yes, yes. But they are all too like my- self. They are all rich or pretend to be. Oh, if you come when I'm 'at home,' I shall in- troiluee you to some extraordinary ordinary People. They are distinguished by being yl com- monplace. They try to appear so worldly and only succeed in appearing foolish." "You are severe on them—and on your- self."

"No; I'm different. I try to be foolish and end in being worldly." They talked on for half an hour, and then he looked at his watch and mentioned an en• gagement. ' Is it very important ?" she asked in a way that redeemed the forwardness of the question. Charterhouse was tempted. It was sweet to be in her presence again, after a period such as he had passed through. The fascination of her eyes and the enchantment of her voice seemed even stronger than in the old days; the very flippancy of her speech was a delight to him. He hesitated, and con. suited his watch once more.

" It's kind of you, Maud," he said, grate. fully. " It's good to be your friend once more." " I'm selfish, as you know," she returned, "and I'm often lonely. Take pity, and come to see me sometimes.' "Whenever I can get away from my work Pshall come," he said. "Always your work!" she cried, a little impatiently. He smiled. " Yes; and I'm neglecting it now." "Then, if you must go--" She expected him to resume his seat, but he held out his hand.

" I must go." A minute litter he was hastening from the square towards the station, whence the un- derground railway would bear him to the eastern slums of the city. He had a particu- larly disagreeable case of chronic drunken- ness to visit, but he went in company with Hope. Mrs. Methven watched his departure from the window. Her dulness seemed to have lifted a little.

Mrs. Methren laid aside her mourning, nr suddenly, but by artistic gradations through greys and violets. It seemed to Dick, who was now her frequent visitor, that each suc- ceeding shade set off her beauty in a new and clearer light. But at times he was ashamed of himself. lie had not reached the point of neglecting his work, but he knew that his interest in it was in danger of being chilled. It began to be an effort. An illness in the spring might have been held as an excuse—had .he been less a man. He had been very near to death, and his recovery was slow, made bearable, however, by the cheering messages and kind- ly gifts of invalid luxuries from Maud, and the prospect of seeing her again. But Maud was never more than friendly, and whatever he may have hoped during. the period of his convalescence appearen mere folly to him at the first meetinr, after his recovery. More. over, as he told ° himself with sad repetition, his circumstances were utter poverty com- pared with hers. _ Still, the charm drew him, and he con- tinued to find his way to Bolton Square on every possible occasion, if the widow was secretly amused, it was in a tender fashion. She ,perceived his straggle between duty a,nd inclination, and ,accepted the compliment. 'idt would be too much to say that she actually tempted him to ncglect nus work. hut she

certainly did nothing to stimulate the ma en- thusiasm which appeared to be failing. But at last an incident occurred to check the fall of Dick. He was sitting talking to Maud one autumn afternoon, when the maid entered with a basket of hot-house blooms. Mrs. Methven laid them carelessly on the table.

"So you've given up the idea of going eastward to-day, Dick ?'' "Well, I didn't promise I would-go," he answered weakly. "I'm afraid your poor people will be of. fended," she said teasingly. "You know you've got them into the bad habit of expect- ing you nearly every day." "Do you think I ought to go, Maud ?" " Oh, no, my friend. I require you more than they. I want you to preach to me, for a change.' "Maud

"So you think I'm hopeless. Oh, Dick T." she cried, with a little laugh. " Tell me, do you love the people you preach to 9" He was silent. " You used to—at least you told me so. And yet, you are sitting here with me—" She broke off suddenly, observing hi. 3 face. Maud, you don't know what you are say- ing 1"
Ileigh-ho!" she sighed lightly. "I'm aware I'm very dreadful. That's why I want you to prea:•ll to me. Or, stay! Let me make a confession first."
She picked up the basket of flowers and nanded them to him.
" They are beautiful," he said; and then his eye caught sight of the name on the card in their midst. " They are beautiful," he re- peated.
" Sir Lewis Morton wants me to marry aim,- the said.
I must congratulate you," he returned, feebly. "But is it not rather soon to consider such a thing ? I want your advice. Besides," she added, "I don't specially care for him."

" Then, what advice can I give you I" he said endeavouring to speak natuFally. " On the other hand," she continued, " I'm not sure that I specially care for anyone. But I'm getting tired of myself." " How an I advise you ? I d2n't know Sir Lewis Morton except by name. I've heard he is an exceedingly brilliAnt scholar. He left lollege the year I entered." ".But. would it be right for me to marry

again ?" " Maud, Maud, how can you ask me ?" lie cried hotly. " Why ?"—innocently—" am I rude ? I've told you before that you are my only real friend. If I asked my aunt she would dissolve in tears. My uncle would congratulate me: and straightway fly to borrow money from my probable fiancé, as he did from poor Mr. Methven. Can't you understand, Dick, why I'm not after the exact pattern of the aver- age. woman ?"
-Dick was touched, and he said very gent- ly:7

" I wish I could help you, but you must please yourself." " You're a most unsatisfactory friend," she sighed. " I know it," he said ruefully; "I make a very poor friend to you. But now I must be going; I've stayed too long as it is." " Then you leave me to my fate ?" she questioned with a faint smile. "TO yourself, Maud," he replied. When he had gone, Mrs. Methven seated herself at her desk, and, after much delibera- tion, indited a letter to Sir Lewis Morton.

Once more dulness had settled upon Mrs. Methven. It was nearly a month since Dick's last call, and she was angry with him. A week's visitation from her uncle and aunt had not left her in a cheerful mood. Ana now, apparently, her friend had deserted her, She tried to make herself believe that she re- gretted the letter she had written four weeks previously to Sir Lewis Morton. When Dick did call he was received with the coldness his recent neglect merited. I'm sorry I could not come before this," he said.

"Pray don't mention it. and hardly noticed the time." " It will be four weeks to-morrow since I saw you." " Really ?"—with polite dubiety. . "Yes; and I fear it will be a longer period ere I call again," lie said sadly. You needn't trouble to be rude."
I've been busy

" You understand me, Maud. to tell you that I am about to le Methren became interesl she clapped her hands.
I've come
"I i.tiew it, I knew it! And I'm delight- ed!"
"It is you who are rude now," said Dick rather sulkily.

"It is you who misunderstand now," she replied. " But I'm glad for your sake. Oh, I was sure it would come! Is it a nice place ? Oh, my friend, you do deserve a beautiful country home after the slums of London." But my destination is China." She gave a little gasp, but said nothing. " Maud, you know how discontented I have been of late. I've felt that I was doing little or no good in London, and when I heard, about a month ago, of a man being wanted for China, I volunteered. My steamer sails on Saturday." " How foolish you have been," she a helpless sort of voice. "I have been foolish, and that is perhaps my best reason for making this change." Ah, you will take me up wrongly. Have you not considered how your poor folk will miss you ? You may shake your head. but I know they used to depend on you, and I be- lieve they still do. And don't you think it's just a little cowardly to throw up your work here because you haven't been able to right the wrongs of half a million souls in a few years ?" The curate flushed. " Maud, I like to hear you talk like that," lie stammered. She nodded sagely and continued. •‘ Don't you feel that you are exhibiting a sad lack of faith in giving up here ? And yet"—suddenly changino her tone—" I can't understand you. Yon bhave always set your mind against a comfortable country charge for the sake of these London poor, and all of a sudden you throw them over for the atro- cious Chinese." " I know you don't understand me, Maud, and so it would be vain to try to explain why I am taking this step." "Quite vain to try, to explain folly." "However, it's' all arranged now, and I feel it's for the best "—the tone of his voice scarcely agreed with the words. Of course, I'm sorry to leave the home country and the people. I hope you will write occasionally to me, Maud."
said in
I'll think over that," she said. "And I'm glad that you and Sir Lewis Morton will—"

"Are you ?" "Have you not—" "No; I have not," she replica quickly And ere he could make further remark, she deftly changed the subject, and for the next half-hour kept the ball of conversation roll- ing among the slightest everyday topics. At last they both wearied of it all, and Dick rose to go. There was no reason, he considered, why his farewell should be longer delayed. He was ,pale, while Maud's colour and ready smile did not desert her, despite her nervousnces. She wondered he would speak at the very last moment. If not— Good-bye, Maud. You'll think over iny annual letter," he said, with a poor attempt at lightness. I've a shocking memory," she said cruel- ly. " I can't forget you, Maud," he blurted out in a boyish fashion. You are very kind." "Good-bye, Maud." And is this all thought Mrs. Methyen, with a strange sharp misery in her heart. But she smiled sweetly. " I shall honour your last visit, Dick, by seeing you to the door myself." They went downstairs. together. "Don't you feel like changing your mind at the eleventh hour ?" she asked, laughing- ly. Ile shook his head. Think once more of the poor folk in the East End. Think of your own people." ' I have done so, Maud. I have decided." He laid hold of the handle of the door— one or the handles, rather, for the door had two. Mrs. Methven held the other. "Think how dull I shall be," sla,( said with a great effort. "And oh! how dull you are !" she added under her breath. He gripped the handle hard. " I must go, Maud. Good-bye," he said, duskily, attempting to open the door. " The wrong handle, Dick," she managed to say. Row stupid
the an was! His hand

.., did oetieve that T your work' cheaply ? I didn't know before, though I do now, that I was jealous of it. Stay at home, and see if I'm not interested in all your schemes. We'll make it up to the Mission in other ways. Or, if you must go— take me."

WYCLIFFE P.S.A. New. Year's Sunday was marked- by a good attendance at Wycliffe P.S.A. Mr. Farrar, the secretary, presided, and proposed a vote of sym- pathy with Mr. Street upon the death of his wife, and a vote of condolence was passed to Mr. Ratcliffe in his affliction. The Rev. T. T. James, the president, delivered his monthly address, remarking that it was the first New Year's Sunday he had passed amongst them. He was pleased to meet $o many P.S.A. friends upon such an occasion. He thought an appropriate subject for his address would be "Looking forward." They should remember that indifference and want of serious hope robbed them of much pleasure in life. David Livingstone set an example in looking ahead , when he entered upon unknown lands to open Ahem up for Christ. Of the past Livingstone knew little; he pressed forward for the future.. Paul had- also looked forward when he deter- mined to do nothing but Christ's work. The soloist was Mr. Dawson, and he sang taste- fully " Thou art passing hence" and ".rm. arm, ye brave." These solos were greatly appre- ciated. lir. Payton presided at the organ with his usual skill, and Mr. H. Osborne also took part in the meeting. One new member was wel- comed.

"Maud, would you mind taking me back to the drawing-room, for a minute ? There's something I forgot." But he could not wait until they reached the drawing-room. At the bend of the stairs he suddenly halted, and said his say in three words. But words, after all, are not every- thing. And even after they had mounted the remaining steps, an hour elapsed before Dick remembered that in a few days he must leave for China. Good, earnest man though he was, he was aghast at the prospect. As for Maud, she merely laugned and said, in her old flippant manner: "Send them word that you've found a bet- ter engagement." "But, dear, I can't turn back now," he protested, " it would be cowardly." " Pouf ! It would be cowardly not to con- fess that you want to stay at home. October, its "Monthly Notes" attacked this campaign with bitterness, but in November its "Fortnightly Notes" approved the farmers in their action. The official Press cries "Ulster first," but the farmer reads the cry as "Manufacturers first," and feels that if anyone is shelved by Ulster it must be the wealthy merchants and factors of Birmingham and Sheffield, who can- not be seriously affected by waiting a little longer; whilst the present fiscal proposals, in the words of a 'famous Protectionist, " mean something like ruin to the farmer." "Base Vote-catching." I The cry of "Ulster first," coupled with the boycott of any protest, assumes a sinister aspect to the threatened agriculturist. If anyone searches the files of the "Morning Post," "Pall Mall Gazette," "Spectator," "Observer," &c., last January, they will find outspoken denunciation of the Edinburgh com- pact; the situation Was not changed, hut these papers are now silent. You, sir, at Newcastle, a short time ago, made a speech to the effect that the Unionist party would never stoop to base vote-catching 1 marapuvres, but would sooner stay out of office I indefinitely. ... What do you think the farmer feels about your action, _and how do you think he contrasts it witTi'your statement? A great party can never carry this country by such tactics, nor would it be well for it if it could.—Yours, &c., BERNARD GILBERT. When Freedom of Thought Is Again Permitted.. WARRINGTON ADULT SCHOOLS. Annual Meetings Instead of Services. On New Year's Sunday the an.nual meetings were held for. the election of officers at all the Schools. There were no Bible lessons and no lecturettes for the day. Instead, the annual letter from the Chairman of the National Coun- cil of Adult Schools was read, not only in the Warrington, but in all the British and Colonial Schools as well. STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S. The first annual meeting was held on Sunday Morning. The progress of the school was re- ported as very satisfactory, both as regards the membership, the tone of the school, and finan- cially. Remembering the condition of the 'school building six months ago and the willing and strenuous work the members, men and women, had put into it to make it what it is, they deserved every praise for their achieve- ment. Mr. W. T. Rowland was unanimously re- eleeted.president, Mr. J. F. Fergusson was re- elected secretary, and Mr. Frank Lynch secre- •

tary of the i Social Club. Mr. W. H. Sherburn also retains his office as lecture secretary. ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S. At the annual meeting on Sunday, Mr. George Walker was re-elected president, and Messrs. Herbert Berry and IL A. Webb joint secretaries. It was reported that all the many organisations of the school were in a healthy condition. SANKEY BRIDGES MEN'S. This school have elected Mr. Robert Williams, 108, Evelyn-street, secretary for the year. BEWSEY. A irimorial service was held on Sunday evening for the late Mrs. Robinson, a much esteemed member of the Women's School.

From Everywhere. Conscience never gets on the job until you've quit having a good time. The man under 25 is the one most pleased when he is addressed as "old boy." Fame, like life insurance, never matures until we are too dead to enjoy it. Many a fellow who is a light weight is really a heavy weight to his friends. Some courtships end in marriage and some in the courts. The conversation of women may not be as in- teresting as that of men, but there is more of it. The worst feature about the skeleton in the closet is that it hasn't sense enough to stay there. A man naturally has a drawn look when his head and heart are drawing in opposite direc- tions. Men don't understand women, women do understand men; that's why men love women. —" The Taller." The Same Result. 1 If we say we don't understand someone we infer something to their discredit, while if we say that they don't understand us they are still in the wrong.—" The Taller."

VICAR'S "COMING OF AGE.' Rev. B. Percival's 21 Years of Strenuous Labour. EXAMPLE OF PERSEVERANCE. Twenty-one years of strenuous labour in St. Peter's, one of the poorest parishes in Warring- ton, has been the record of the Rev. B. Percival, and the highly esteemed Vicar on Sunday cele- brated his parochial "coming of age." Be preached to large congregations and briefly ovt- lined his feelings upon the celebration of that interesting event. I have been with you 21 years, he said, and I can honestly say I have tried to realise my responsibility. The feeling amongst his parish- ioners is that he has nobly realised his respon- sibility, and that he has worked faithfully and well. The Vicar was the subject of numerous congratulations upon the celebration of the interesting event. Worked at Fourteen. Mr. Percival's career has been an intensely interesting- one, as lie has risen from the ranks to the high station which lie now occupies in the Church to which he belongs. He was born in 1856 at Burgh-by-Sands, a little village tucked away in Cumberland, and here he lived with his father, the late Mr. Matthew Perci- val, who laboured on the land. While quite young Mr. Percival lost his father, and at tire age of 14 be had to turn out to work. Ile had a great love for the Church and spent most of his leisure time in studying Church work and theological questions gener- ally. For three years he studied at Ayerst Hall, Cambridge, where he was under the guidance of the Rev. W. Ayerst. In 1887 he was successful in passing the Cambridge Theological Prelimin- ary Examination, and in the same year he was ordained deacon by Dr. Ryle, the late Bishop of Liverpool, and commenced his ministry at • • ::;"; • , 4t: , • • , ' 41, Le •,?•& • , • •-• , • THE REV. B. PERCIVAL.

HIGH LECH SENSATION. The Injured Old Man Dies in the Infirmary. SHOT IN A WOOD. Joseph Skitt, 74, ex-gamekeei)er, of Hollowell 1 Brow, High Legh, the victim of a mysterious , shooting affair in a • wood a month ago, as exclusively' described in "The Examiner" mit, the time, died in 'Warrington Infirmary on g through the wood when his , foot caught a wire, which exploded a hidden trap gun. The old man fell, Severely wounded . in the thigh. He shouted for help, but none being forthcoming, proceeded to crawl home. En route he fell into a ditch, and with difficulty got out. The old man managed to crawl within a short distance of his home, where he collapsed, and was found later by two young men Passing. They summoned medical aid from Lymin, and after treatment Skitt was removed to the Infirmary. The inquest will be held to•day.
